before the boome for a guard etc. chap. 5 the relation of the jacob a ship of Bristol of one hundred and twenty ton which be about the end of October 1621. take by the turkish pirate of Argier and within five day after four english youth do valiant overcome thirteen of the say turk and bring the ship to saint Lucas in Spain where they sell nine of the turk for gallie-slave with mention of some other like english adventure near the latter end of October last 1621. a ship belong to the city of Bristol be about the burden of one hundred and twenty tun be meet withal and set upon by turk or pirate of Argier where after a long and sharp fight be in the mouth of the straits of Gibraltar the english ship be oppress with the multitude of their enemy be take their ordnance cables anchor sail ship and man pillage ransack and at the mercy of the insult barbarian who to make their work the sure take all the englishman out of the ship except four youth who name be John Cook William ling David jones and Robert tuckey into which ship the turk do put thirteen of their own man to command the english and to bring the ship as a prize to Argier amongst which one of the pirate be appoint captain be a strong able stern and resolute fellow these four poor youth be thus fall into the hand of merciless infidel begin to study and complot all the mean they can for the obtain of their freedom first they consider the lamentable and miserable estate that they be like to be in as to be debar for ever from see their friend and country to be chain beat make slave and to eat the bread of affliction in the galley all the remainder of their unfortunate life to have their head shave to feed on course diet to have hard board for bed and which be worst of all never to be partaker of the heavenly word and sacrament thus be quite hopeless hapless and for any thing they know for ever helpless they sail five day and night under the command of the pirate when on the five night God in his great mercy show they a mean for their wish for escape for in the dead of the night the wind begin to arise and in short space it blow so stiff that they be enforce to strike both their top sail and at last it increase to such a gust or storm that they must take in their main sail and be unable to do it themselves John Cook and William ling do call to the turk for help whereupon the captain himself come to help they who stand by the ship side between the foresay John and David jones lend his hand to hale in the sail the say John and David sudden take he by the breech and throw he overboard but by fortune he fall into the of the sail where quick catch hold of a rope he be a very strong man have almost get into the ship again which John Cook perceive leap speedy to the pump and take off the pump break or handle and cast it to William ling bid he knock he down which he be not long in do but lift up the wooden weapon he give he such a pelt on the pate as make his brain forsake the possession of his head with which his body fall into the sea. a objection may be make here why the Turk cry not to his fellow at first for help or how these thing can be do but the rest of his company must either see or hear it to which I answer that at sea a gust flaw or storm have many time a loud voice than a man beside when mariner do hale or pull any thing they do make a noise as it be cry ha woet hale man hale which with the noise of the wind whizz and hiz in the shrowd and cordage will overcome and drown the voice or cry of any man whatsoever beside his companion be all busy some at the mizzen some at the spritsail some to trim the foresail and the night exceed dark all these thing concur and chief God gracious assist thus these brave lad begin the business lucky nor must I forget Robert tuckey who be employ all this while in a place of main importance for he stand at the helm and in all the weather guide the ship now after the captain be thus cashier John Cook run hasty up the half deck to the master cabin near which be stand six or seven turk but he be nothing daunt or discourage for they slip rough by they and get out two good cuttleax or short sword one of which he deliver to William ling withal say courage my fellow and countryman God strengthen and assist we with that they lay about they so manful that they drive the turk from place to place in the ship and have course they from the poop to the forecastle they there valiant kill two of they and give another a dangerous wound or two who to escape the further fury of their sword leap sudden overboard to go seek his captain thus four of the thirteen turk be make sure for do any harm they chase and follow the other nine so close that they to save themselves be also many of they before hurt and wound run between the ship deck whereupon the english man fasten the deck to keep they under the Turk not know how to be revenge run afterward towards the helm and unshipt their whip-staffe or as some call it a whipstock which be the staff that a mariner hold in his hand when he guide or steer a ship by which mean the english man be in some distress by reason the sip lie tumble and roll unguided in the rage and boisterous billow of the sea at last John Cook and William ling get each of they a musket which they quick charge and go down where the nine turk be make offer to shoot at they at which they be much terrify whereupon they quick ship their whipstock again deliver the helm to Robert tuckey and then present they stow all the turk under the hatch where they keep they close till the next morning and then as they have occasion to use they they will call up two or three of they at a time to hale and pull sheet tack brace and bolein to hoist and strike sail or any such necessary and laborious employment in all which the english make the turk attend they and direct their course for the port of saint Lucas in Spain they in short time by God aid happy and safe arrive at the say port where they sell the nine turk for galleyslave for a good sum of money and as I think a great deal more than they be worth nor do I write this to the intent that any man shall presume that their own strength valour or courage be sufficient to do these or the like action for they be not ordinary and therefore man be but make the ordinary instrument of a extraordinary power and he that shall attribute such thing as these to the arm of flesh and blood be forgetful ingrateful and in a manner atheistical one John fox a expert mariner and a good approve and sufficient gunner be in the see the history in hack. voyages reign of queen Elizabeth take by the turk and keep eighteen year in most miserable bondage and slavery at the end of which time he espy his opportunity and God assist he withal that he slay his keeper and flee to the sea side where he find a galley with one hundred and fifty captive christian which he speedy weigh their anchor set sail and fall to work like man and safe arrive in spaone by which mean he free himself and a number of poor soul from long and intolerable servitude after which the say John fox come into England and the queen be right inform of his brave exploit do gracious entertain he for her servant and allow he a yearly pension captain Nichols with a ship of London call the dolphin fight a long and bloody fight cap. Nicholes with many of the turkish man of war at one time at which time he sink some of they slay many of their man and have his own ship exceed rend and tear with the enemy great shot yet at last it please God to deliver he from they so that he safe arrive at home master William of Rotherhith within these three year be set upon by these rover master and after a long fight be much hurt by the ordnance of the turk the night come on which make the fight to cease when the general of the pirate past his word and bind it with a oath that if master will come aboard his ship all night that he shall well and safe be set aboard again his own ship the next morning upon which word and oath master go aboard the Turk and a merchant with he but first before he go command his mate to watch his opportunity and steal away with the ship in the night if he can which fall out as he wish whereby all the merchant good be save and the ship safe arrive here at London but in the morning when the turk do perceive the english ship be go then will they have put master and the merchant that be with he to death whereupon he urge he with his oath and promise which be that he shall come and go safe and that if a christian have make he or any man such a promise and bind it with a vow he will have keep his word and that for any thing he know his ship be so dangerous hurt by they may be sink in the night and not escape away as he imagine now while they be in this discourse present come a sail in sight which afterward they find to be a small scottish ship bind for England who the turk quick take and pillage at their pleasure take from they their sail cable anchor and all thing necessary for their use or preservation and have rob a rifle the poor scot in that manner they put master and the merchant into she to try their fortune either to sink or swim but it please God they safe arrive in the west part of England where they come home by land sad and disconsolate because they can not hear any news of the ship but the same night that he come home before day there be happy tiding bring of the ship safe arrival into the river of Thames all these thing be true upon my own knowledge and these worthy mariner that have be so deliver do and ever do attribute all the mean of their deliverance to the mighty hand of God and they be so far from take any of these thing to their own praise or glory that some of they have ever do their best to suppress they from be print chap. 7 the wonderful recovery of the exchange of Bristol from the turkish pirate of Argier publish by JOHN RAWLINS here abbreviate in the year 1621. the first of November there be one John Rawlins bear in Rochester and dwell three and twenty year in Plymouth employ to the strait of Gibraltar by master Richard and Steven trevile merchant of Plymouth and freight in (...) ark call the Nicholas of Plymouth of the burden of forty tun which have also in her company another ship of Plymouth call the George Bonaventure of seventy tun burden or thereabout which by reason of her greatness beyond the other I will name the admiral and John Rawlins bark shall if you please be the vide-admiral these two accord to the time of the year have a fair passage and by the eighteen of the same month come to a place at the enter of the strait name trafflegar but the next morning be in the sight of Gibraltar at the very mouth of the strait the watch descry five sail of ship who as it seem use all the mean they can to come near we and we as we have cause use the same mean to go as far from they yet do their admiral take in both his top sail that either we may not suspect they or that his own company may come up the close together at last perceive we christian they fall from device to apparent discovery of hostility and make out against we we again suspect they pirate take our course to escape from they and make all the sail we possible can for Tirriff or Gibraltar but all we can do can not prevent their approach for sudden one of they come right over against we to windward and so fall upon our quarter another come upon our and so threaten we there and at last all five chase we make great speed to surprise we their admiral be call Callfater have upon her main topsail two top-gallant sail one above another but whereas we think they all five to be turkish ship of war we afterward understand that two of they be their prize the one a small ship of London the other of the west-country that come out of the quactath lade with fig and other merchandise but now subject to the fortune of the sea and the captivity of pirate but to our business three of these ship get much upon we and so much that ere half the day be spend the admiral who be the best sailer fetcnt up the George Bonaventure and make booty of it the vide-admiral again be near unto the lesser bark whereof John Rawlins be master show he the force of a strong arm and by his turkish name call villa-rise command he in like sort to strike his sail and submit to his mercy which not to be gainesaied nor prevent be quick do and so Rawlins with his bark be quick take although the rear-admiral be the worst sailor of the three call reggiprise come not in till all be do the same day before night the admiral either loath to pester himself with too much company or ignorant of the commodity be to be make by the sale of english prisoner or dare not to trust they in his company for fear of mutiny and excite other to rebellion set twelve person who be in the George Bonaventure on the land and diverse other english who he have take before to try their fortune in a unknown country but villa-rise the vice-admiral that have take John Rawlins will not so dispense with his man but command he and five more of his company to be bring aboard his ship leave in his bark three man and his boy with thirteen turk and moor who be questionless sufficient to overmaster the other and direct the bark to harbour thus they sail direct for Argier but the night follow follow they with great tempest and foul weather which end not without some effect of a storm for they lose the sight of Rawlins bark call the Nicholas and in a manner lose themselves though they seem safe a shipboard by fearful conjecture what shall become of we at last by the two and twenty of the same month they or we choose you whether arrive at Argier and come in safety within the mould but find not our other bark there nay though we earnest inquire after the same yet hear we nothing to our satisfaction but much matter be minister to our discomfort and amazement for although the captain and our overseer be loath we shall have any conference with our countryman yet do we adventure to inform ourselves of the present affair both of the town and the ship so that find many english at work in other ship they spare not to tell we the danger we be in and the mischief we must needs incur as be sure if we be not use like slave to be sell as slave for there have be five hundred bring into the market for the same purpose and above a hundred handsome youth compel to turn Turk or make subject to more vild prostitution and all english yet like good christian they bid we be of good cheer and comfort ourselves in this that God trial be gentle purgation and these cross be but to cleanse the dross from the gold and bring we out of the fire again more clear and lovely yet I must needs confess that they afford we reason for this cruelty as if they determine to be revenge of our last attempt to fire their ship in the mould and therefore protest to spare none who they can surprise and take alive but either to sell they for money or torment they to serve their own turn now their custom and usage in both these be in this manner first concern the first the bashaw have the over-seeing of all prisoner who be present unto he at their first come into the harbour and so choose one out of every eight for a present or fee to himself the rest be rate by the captain and so send to the market to be sell whereat if either there be repine or any draw back then certain moor and officer attend either to beat you forward or thrust you into the side with goad and this be the manner of the sell of slave second concern their enforce they either (...) turn Turk or to attend their filthiness execrable torture by hellish pitat inflict on the english to make they renegado and apostate and impiety although it will make a christian heart bleed to hear of the same yet must the truth not be hide nor the terror leave untell they common lay they on their naked back or belly beat they so long till they bleed at the nose and mouth and if yet they continue constant than they strike the tooth out of their head pinch they by their tongue and use many other sort of torture to convert they nay many time they lay they their whole length in the ground like a grave and so cover they with board threaten to starve they if they will not turn and so many even for fear of torment and death make their tongue betray their heart to a most fearful wickedness and so be circumcise with new name and bring to confess a new religion other again I must confess who never know any god but their own sensual lust and pleasure think that any religion will serve their turn and so for perferment or wealth very voluntary renounce their faith and become renegado in despite of any counsel which seem to intercept they and this be the first news we encounter with at our come first to Argier the 26. of the same month John Rawlins his bark with his other three man and a boy come safe into the mould and so be put all together to be carry before the bashaw but that they take the owner servant and rawlings boy and by force and torment compel they to turn turk then be they in all seven english beside John Rawlins of who the bashaw take one and send the rest to their captain who set a valuation upon they and so the soldier hurry we like dog into the market whereas man sell hackney in England we be toss up and down to see who will give most for we and although we have heavy heart and sale of the english. look with sad countenance yet many come to behold we sometime take we by the hand sometime turn we round about sometime feel our brawn and naked arm and so behold our price write in our breast they bargain for we accord and at last we be all sell and the soldier return with the money to their captain John Rawlins be the last who be sell by reason of his lame hand and buy by the captain that take he even that dog Villa rise who better inform himself of his skill fit to be a pilot and his experience to be a overseer buy he and his carpenter at very easy rate for as we afterward understand by diverse english renegado he pay for Rawlins but one hundred and fifty dooblet which make of english money seven pound ten shilling thus be he and his carpenter with diverse other slave send into his ship to work and employ about such affair as belong to the well rig and prepare the same but the villainous turk perceive his lame hand and that he can not perform so much as other slave quick complain to their patron who as quick apprehend the inconvenience whereupon he send for he the next day and tell he he be unserviceable for his present purpose and therefore unless he can procure fifteen pound of the english there for his ransom he will send he up into the country where he shall never see Christendom again and endure the extremity of a miserable banishment but see how God work all for the best for his servant and confound the presumption of tyrant frustrate their purpose to make his wonder know to the son of man and relieve his people when they least think of succour and releasement while John Rawlins be thus terrify with the dogged answer of Villa rise the exchange of Bristol a ship former the exchange of Bristol surprise by the pirate lay all unrig in the harbour till at last one John goodale a english Turk with his he speak soft leave they shall all fare the worse for his distemperature the worse quoth Rawlins what can be worse I will either attempt my deliverance at one time or another or perish in the enterprise but if you will be content to hearken after a release and join with i in the action I will not doubt of facilitate the same and show you a way to make your credit thrive by some work of amazement and augment your glory in purchase your liberty I prithee be quiet say they again and think not of impossibility yet if you can but open such a door of reason and probability that we be not be very superstitious be content wizard or witch carry to sea by turk to be direct by their Hoshea who with we signify a witch and be of great account and reputation amongst they as not go in any John Rawlins and sometime make he take in all his sail and sometime cause he to hoist they all out as the witch find by his book and presage then have they two arrow and a curtleaxe lie upon a pillow naked the arrow be one for the turk and the other for the christian then the witch read and the captain of some other take the arrow in their hand by the head and if the arrow for the christian come over the head of the arrow for the turk then do they advance their sail and will not endure the fight whatsoever they see but if the arrow of the turk be find in the open of the hand upon the arrow of the christian then will they stay and encounter with any ship whatsoever the curtleaxe be take up by some child that be innocent or rather ignorant of the ceremony and so lay down again then do they observe whether the same side be uppermost which lie before and so proceed accord they also observe lunatics and changeling and the conjurer write down their saying in a book grovel on the ground as demonstration that all be finish the people in the ship give a great shout and cry out a sail a sail which at last be discover to be another man of war of turk for he make towards we and send his boat aboard we to who our captain complain that be becalm by the southern cape and have make no voyage the turk deny to go any further northward but the captain resolve not to return to Argier except he can obtain some prize worthy his endurance but rather togoe to salle and sell his christian to victual his ship which the other captain apprehend for his honour and so persuade the turk to be obedient unto he whereupon follow a pacication amongst we and so that Turk take his course for the straits and we put up northward expect the good hour of some beneficial booty all this while our slavery continue and the turk with insult tyranny set we still on work in all base and servile action add stripe and inhuman revile even in our great labour whereupon John Rawlins resolve to obtain his liberty and surprise the ship provide rope with broad specke of iron and all the iron crow with which he know a way upon consent of the rest to ram up or tie fast their scuttel grating and cabin yea to shut up the captain himself with all his consort and so to handle the matter that upon the watchword give the english be master of the gunner room ordnance and powder they will either blow they into the air or kill they as they adventure to come down one by one if they shall by any chance open their cabin but because he will proceed the better in his enterprise as he have somewhat abrupt discover himself to the nine english slave so he keep the same distance with the four hollander that be free man till find they come somewhat towards they he acquaint they with the whole conspiracy and they affect the plot offer the adventure of their life in the business then very wary he undermine the english renegado which be the gunner and three more his associate who at first seem to retract last of all be bring in the dutch renegado who be also in the gunner room for always there lie twelve there five christian and seven english and dutch turk so that when another motion have settle their resolution and John Rawlins his constancy have put new life as it be in the matter the four hollander very honest accord to their promise sound the dutch renegado who with easy persuasion give their consent to so brave a enterprise whereupon John Rawlins not care whether the english gunner will yield or no resolve in the captain morning watch to make the attempt but you must understand that where the english slave lay there hang up always four or five crow of iron be still under the carriage of the piece and when the time approach be very dark because John Rawlins will have his crow of iron ready as other thing be and other man prepare in their several place in take it out of the carriage by chance it hit on the side of the piece make such a noise that the soldier hear it awake the turk and bid they come down whereupon the botesane of the turk descend with a candle and danger of discovery present search all the slave place make much ado of the matter but find neither hatchet nor hammer nor any thing else to move suspicion of the enterprise more than the crow of iron which lie slip down under the carriage of the piece they go quiet up again and certify the captain what have chance who satisfy himself that it be a common thing to have a crow of iron slip from his place but by this occasion we make stay of our attempt yet wer^ resolve to take another or a better opportunity for we sail still more northward and Rawlins have more time to tamper with his gunner and the rest of the english renegado who very willing when they consider the matter and perpend the reason give way unto the project and with a kind of joy seem to entertain the motive only they make a stop at the first onset who shall begin the enterprise which be no way fit for they to do because they be no slave but renegado and so have always beneficial entertainment amongst they but when it be once put in practice they will be sure not to fail they but venture their life for God and their country but once again he be disappoint and a suspicious accident bring he to recollect his spirit anew and study on the danger of the enterprise and thus it be after the renegado gunner have protest secrecy by all that may induce a man to bestow some belief upon he he present go up the scottle but stay not aloft a quarter of a hour nay he come soon down another danger and in the gunner room sit by Rawlins who tarry for he where he leave he he be no soon place and enter into some conference but there enter into the place a furious Turk with his knife draw and present it to Rawlins his body who very suppose he intend to kill he as suspicious that the gunner have discover something whereat Rawlins be much move and so hasty ask what the matter mean or whether he will kill he or no observe his countenance and accord to the nature of jealousy conceit that his colour have a passage of change whereby his suspicious heart condemn he for a traitor but that at more leisure he swear the contrary and afterward prove faithful and industrious in the enterprise and for the present he answer Rawlins in this manner no master be not afraid I think he do but jest with that John Rawlins give back a little and draw out his knife step also to the gunner sheath and take out his whereby he have two knife to one which when the Turk perceive he throw down his knife say he do but jest with he but as I say when the gunner perceive Rawlins take it so ill he whisper something in his ear that at last satisfy he call heaven to witness that he never speak word of the enterprise nor ever will either to the prejudice of the business or danger of his person notwithstanding Rawlins keep the knife in his sleeve all night and be somewhat trouble for that he have make so many acquaint with a action of such importance but the next day when he perceive the coast clear and that there be no cause of further fear he somewhat comfort himself all this while Rawlins draw the captain to lie for the northern cape assure he that thereby he shall not miss purchase which accord fell out as a wish will have it but his drift be in truth to draw he from any supply or second of turk if God shall give way to their enterprise or success to the victory yet for the present the six of February be twelve league from the cape we descry a sail and present take the advantage of the wind in chase she and at last fetch she up make she strike all her sail whereby we know she to be a bark belong to Tor bay near Dartmouth that come from lade tor bay. with salt ere we have full dispatch it chance to be foul weather so that we can not or at least will not make out our boat but cause the master of the bark to let down his and come aboard with his company be in the bark but nine man and one boy and so the master leave his mate with two man in the same come himself with five man and the boy unto we whereupon our turkish captain send ten turk to man she amongst who be two dutch and one english renegado who be of our confederacy and acquaint with the business but when Rawlins see this partition of his friend before they can hoist out their boat for the bark he make mean to speak with they and tell they plain that he will prosecute the matter either that night or the next and therefore whatsoever come of it they shall acquaint the english with his resolution and make towards England bear up the helm while the turk sleep and suspect no such matter for by God grace in his first watch about midnight he will show they a light by which they may understand that the enterprise be begin or at least in a good forwardness for the execution and so the boat be let down and they come to the bark of Tor bay where the master mate be leave as before you have hear apprehend quick the matter and hear the discourse with amazement but time be precious and not to be spend in dispute or cast of doubt whether the turk that be with they be able to master they or no be seven to six consider they have the helm of the ship and the turk be soldier and ignorant of sea affaires can not discover whether they go to Argier or no or if they do they resolve by Rawlins example to cut their throat or cast they overboard and so I leave they to make use of the renegado instruction and return to Rawlins again the master of the bark of Tor bay and his company be quick search and as quick pillage and dismiss to the liberty of the ship whereby Rawlins have leisure to entertain he with the lamentable news of their extremity and in a word of every particular which be befit to the purpose yea he tell he that that night he shall lose the sight of they for they will make the helm for England and he will that night and evermore pray for their good success and safe deliverance when the master of the bark of Tor Bayliff have hear he out and that his company be partaker of his story they become all silent not either diffident of his discourse or afraid of the attempt but resolve to assist he yet to grating and cabbine he have also in the gunner room two curtleax and the slave have five crow of iron before they beside in the scuffle they make no question of some of the soldier weapon then for the of sight see or find whereat the captain begin to storm and swear command Rawlins to search the sea up and down for she who bestow all that day in the business but to little purpose whereupon when the humour be spend the captain pacify himself as conceit he shall sure find she at Argier but by the permission of the ruler of all action that Argier be England and all his wickedness frustrate for Rawlins be now startle lest he shall return in this humour for the straits the eight of February go down into the hold and find a great deal of water below tell the captain of the same add that it do not come to the pump which he do very politic that he may remove the ordnance for when the captain ask he the reason he tell he the ship be too far after the head then he command to use the best mean he can to bring she in order sure then quoth Rawlins we must quit our cable and bring four piece of ordnance after and that will bring the water to the pump which be present put in practice so the piece be usual make fast thwart the ship we bring two of they with their mouth right before the biticle and because the renegadoe fleming will not begin it be thus conclude that the ship have three the time of Pharaoh it also produce abundance of fish in shape and quality much differ from we but by reason of the muddy channel not altogether savoury nor wholesome throughout this country there be no wine yet want they none in that they desire they not neither be here any tree to speak of but such as be plant and those in orchard only palmetree except palm which delight in desert and be natural they do grow without limit of these they have plenty please the eye with their goodly form and with diversity of benefit enrich their owner of body straight high round and slender yet unfit for building crest about and by mean thereof with facility ascend the branch like sedge slit on the neither side and ever green grow only on the uppermost height resemble fair plume of feather which they yearly prune by lop of the low and at the top of all by bear a little of the bowl of these there be male and female both thr^st forth cod which be full of seed like knot string at the root of their branch but the female be only fruitful male and female and not so unless grow by the male towards who upright growth she incline her crown and have of his seed commix with she which in the begin of march they no more fail to do then to sow the earth at accustom season their date do grow like finger and be thereof name not ripe until the fine of December which begin to cod about the begin of February they open the top of such as be fruitless or otherwise perish and take from thence the white pith of old call the brain which they sell up and down a excellent salad not much unlike in taste but far better than a artichoke of the branch they make bedstead lattice etc. of the web of the leave basket mat fan etc. of the outward husk of the cod good cordage of the inward brush etc. such and such like afford they yearly without impair to themselves this tree they hold to be the perfect image of a man and by the same represent he first for that it do not fructify but by next as have a brain as it be in the uppermost part which once corrupt as man even so it perish and last in regard that on the top thereof grow certain string which resemble the hair the great end of the branch appear like hand stretch forth and the date as finger and because the palm be never to be suppress but shoot up against all opposition the bough thereof have be propose as reward for such as be either victorious in arm or exercise wood then be here but scarce in regard of the quantity and yet enough if their use for the same be consider for they eat but little flesh fresh cheese sour milk make solid root fruit and herb especial ancient call the egyptian bean though bear no bean but like the leaf of a Colewort be their principal sustenance bake their bread in cake on the hearth and mingle there with the seed of coriander as for cold they know it not have sufficient of the refuse of palm sugarcane and the like to furnish they with fuel answerable to their necessity but foreigner that feed as in cold country do buy wood sell by weight their wood by weight which be bring in hither by ship the galleon also of Constantinople always go into the black sea for timber before they take their voyage for cairo omit I must not the sedgy reed which grow in the marsh of Egypt call former of which they make paper and whereof we make of rag assume that name they divide it into thin flake english ship England with who we consort to furnish the ship with fresh water and other provision they have supply our necessity so on the second of tune be Sunday we enter the haven that lie on the a voyage by sea to my nature so irksome and so be I leave alone on a naked promontory right against the city remote from the concourse of people without provision and not know how to dispose of myself remain Malta do lie in the lybian sea right between Tripoli of Barbary and the southeast angle description of Malta of Sicilia distant a hundred fourscore and ten mile from the one and threescore from the other contain also threescore mile in circuit call former melita of the abundance of honey a country altogether champion be no other than a rock cover over with earth but two foot deep where the country people for fuel who need not much in a clime so exceed hot hot by much than any other which be seat in the same parallel yet sometime temperate by the comfortable wind to which it lie open a true relation of master RICHARD jobsons uoyage employ by sir WILLIAM saint JOHN knight and other for the discovery of Gambra in the Zion a ship of two hundred tun admiral and the saint John fifty vice-admiral in which they pass nine hundred and sixty mile up the river into the continent extract out of his large journal we set sail from Gravesend on Saturday the five of October 1620. from Gravesend on the five and twenty we depart from Dartmouth we sail from Dartmouth to the canary the fourteen of February we come to a anchor in Travisco the Katherine betray road where we find three frenchman and one Fleming Francisco a Portugal here dwell be busy to inquire if we go to Gambra have a letter as he say from m. cramp who have late depart thence for Sierra Liona set forth by the company this Portugal fear just revenge for the ship portugal which trade take and man betray and murder by they in Gambra have procure a letter in behalf of some of his friend in the river of borsall we enter where we take a small boat belong in part to Hector Numez the principal in that treachery and murder aforesaid and detain some of his good therein for satisfaction take thereof a public inventory that if any other can lay just claim they may be restore this be do by punish Numez and to terrify other the general wind from like treacherous attempt not without effect the portugal be glad they so escape know and curse Numez his villainy the portugall which trade here and inhabit the river be banish man renegado and base people and behave themselves accord we build a shallop and launch it the two and twenty the next day we set sail up the river and the tide spend anchor against a little island on the southside some four league up from October till May the wind be general easterly and down the river which much hinder our course up the same we pass up by tide intend to stay at a town call taukorovalle but over-shot it in the night and the next morning be against another town four tankorovalle league high call tindobauge our ship with her ordnance may here come both side the river tindobauge here dwell Emanuel corseen a Portugal which tell we that master Tomson be kill by one of his company and that the rest be in health it be intend the Zion shall stay here and therefore the king customer be pay who dwell some six mile from the river but have his drunken officer to receive they leave she with five and twenty man and boy on Wednesday the nine and twenty the voyage up the river the saint John and two shallop we set sail up the river twelve man in the big with Henry lowe and thirteen in the lesser with myself which with the boat tow she up in calm on the first of December we come to pudding island sixteen league from the ship the pudding island maugegar second we anchor against a little creek which lead into a town maugegar we go to this town meet by the way a Portugal call bastian Roderigo who give i a ounce skin on Monday the four the king with his Alcade come aboard and drink himself with his consort so drink that the custom be defer till next day Henry low agree for a house and leave there Humphrey davis John Blithe and one Nicholas a pretty youth which two last die there on the seven we pass thence by a town on the north-side call Wolley Wolley big than any we have yet see and in the afternoon come to a anchor at Wolley Wolley cassan. Portugal perfidy cassan where the Katherine be betray where no Portugal will now be see this king be under the great king of Bursall the Al^ade show we friendship and tell we that the portugal have the neglect of bring salt through ignorance or emulation oranto be a hindrance the king of oranto abode on the other side of the river his name a blind man and subject to the great king of Cantore we sometime by his wife sometime by his daughter but every day his son be there and likewise diverse other of the better sort but count from many great person which word they use for commendation you must return something again or it will be ill take on Christmas day Ferambra send we as much elephant flesh as one can well carry new (...) faith kill this Ferambra go four mile off and be a friend of yet the negro be displease they may not eat he on the seventeen on both side the river we see thousand of baboon and monkey a sea horse give the boat a shrewd blow but do no harm we have still our Canoe before we to sound the depth on the eighteen we be force to enter the river naked very fearful of the so they call the crocodile and carry the boat against the current and over or through the sand heave and shove till we come in deep water the nineteenth we meet with a violent current that all the strength of six oar can prevail but a mile in a hour the twenty on the sear-board side we have Cantore river which have a fair entrance where Ferran cabo be the great king. on the one and twenty we send a shore to the mountain top whence may be perceive only desert replenish with terrible wild beast who roar we hear every night the black be so afraid of the that they dare not put their hand into the water diverse of they be by they devour yet do they avoid from we whether it be our noise or multitude which cause it some we see thirty foot-long yet will not come near we on the two and twenty walk on the bank I espy sixteen great elephant together hard by i a black with i fall a tremble the sedge in the place be almost as high again as our head so that we can not be see till we be within pistol shoot of they we see diverse little one by their side we make a offer to shoot but the piece will not off which they perceive begin to run in a mile space not so much as turn nor look behind they make speed to the mountain like a dear in the forest the moor wonder at our adventure on the three and twenty we be fain to enter the water and by strength of hand to carry the boat a mile and a half into deep water on the four and twenty we tow she sometime add hale by the boat side as shold and tree permit and meet with one vehement current overthwart break rock so that we be force to hold she by force till one take the anchor on his neck wade above that quick fall and let it so rank with a musky water distatefull musky send of the crocodile as we suppose that it be distatefull whereas this be pleasant one of our moor be take and like to be lose in a whirlpool notwithstanding he can swim well have not one of our man lay hold on he as he rise the three time almost spend from under water on the six and twenty we be comfort with the sight of the hill of Tinda be high rocky land we send three moor thither with a present to the king and to buckor Sano a merchant of Tinda entreat he to come down to we with provision for we have no flesh dear and fowl be see sometime twenty crocodile musky fish one by another and in the night special towards break of day they will call one to another much resemble the sound of a deep well and may be easy hear a league we pass the shold and against Tinda river recover steep water and see many sea horse which love deep water on the thirty we kill a Anthelope big than any Windsor antelope stag the blood of he draw a world of eagle and other fowl amongst which come one stalker a foul high than a man which we likewise kill present after come our man back with buckor Sanos brother and a servant of the king with hen our deer be kill in good season for their entertainment the report pass among they current that with gun-thunder our thunder so they call our gun we can kill whatsoever we will they much fear the same as have never see or hear it whereof we make good use on Thursday the first of February come buckor Sano with a troop of forty people amongst which his wife and daughter have taste of our strong water he lay drink aboard that night he be never so after and be sick the next day he give we a beef and many of the people bring goat cock and hen which we buy easy on Saturday we begin to trade our salt which be the chief thing they desire other thing they ask for which we have salt chief trade not provide salve he tell we be the thing they hold dear for any thing else we shall have if we will maintain our come thither he will provide it we have some elephant tooth negro clothes Cotten yearn and some gold of they we refuse to buy hide because we will not lade our boat down the river the water fall every day which we keep note of by the shore the people come daily more and more to we and upon the shore they build house we also have a house open to trade under so as it seem like a pretty town our black go over the river and three day after bring other people which build a siege town on the other side the river and within three day there be five hundred which be a more savage people have breech of beast skin neither have they ever see any white people before the woman will run and hide themselves when we come near they at their first come but after grow bold to buy and the north and southside thereof lose the land but southward from the point about half a mile from the land there be a island see whereon many fowl breed and great number of egg be find therein behind this island there lie a great rock a little separate from the land. this island be very unfit to raise shallop on you may sail between the land and this island with a ship of three hundred and twenty tun but not without great fear for that there be many rock lie under the water but for the best security of ship and good it be better to sail on the west side of the island to the other island where shallop may be set together which you may see be right against the first island lie about three mile southeast from the other these land be not inhabit and there be nothing to be have in they but great store of ballast and wood to burn but for that there be a convenient valley to make shallop in therefore those place be much use and be the cause that many ship sail to they but on the firm land there be great store of negro inhabit which traffic with all nation the country people go naked only that they hang a piece of linen cloth before their the people and their apparel privy member but their governor as captain and gentleman be better apparel then the common sort of people and be well know by their garment to be such they go in a long Cotton garment close about they like a woman smock full of blue stripe like feather bed tike on their arm they wear many foure-cornerd leather bag all close join together and the like upon their leg but what be within they I know not because they will not let we see about their neck they wear bead make of sea-horse tooth and some coral or bead which we bring they on their head they wear cap of the same stuff that their clothes be they be people that be very industrious and careful to get their living their chief trade be husbandry to sow Rice and corn their great riches be in cow which there be very scant and dear but further into the country there be great store for that man lade whole ship full of salt hide at porta which they take in exchange or barter for iron which place lie but seven or eight mile from cape Verde they make very fair iron work and in that country there be great store of iron spend special fair long bar whereof they be as curious as any man in the world can be those they use to make instrument of wherewith to fish and to labour upon the land as also to make weapon as bow arrow aponer and * * kind of dart make javelin-fashion at both end Assagayen they have no knowledge of God those that traffic and be conversant among strange country people be civil than the common sort of people they be very greedy eater and no less drinker and very lecherous and thievish and much addict to uncleanness one man have as many wife as he be able to keep and maintain the woman also be much addict to lechery special with strange country people of their woman who they be not jealous as of their own country people and neighbour their religion be after the manner of Mahomet law for circumcision and such like toy they be also great liar and not to be credit the principal commodity that man traffic for there be commodity hide ambergris gum of Arabia salt and other ware of small importance as Rice graine tooth and some civet. the portugal also dwell there with other nation wherewith they may free traffic because they be not subject to the king of Spain and beside that they be not master of the country and have no command but over their slave the negro be under the command of their own governor which be call algaier in their language which be a captain of a village for every village have his several algaier and when any ship come to anchor there than the captain come present aboard with a Canoe to ask anchoridge money which be common three bar of iron but of such as know not their custom they take as much as they can their body be very black and of a good proportion when they the presence of her friend which come to the banquet make a promise and swear to be rite of marriage true to her husband and not to use the bodily company of any other man but the man take no such oath but be free thereof now if she chance to commit whoredom with a other man either willing or against divorce and forseiture her will and that her husband hear thereof than he must put she away for it and the man that have commit the act shall forfeit to the king four and twenty Pesos which after our account be nine ounce of gold but if it be a dutch man he pay no fine because he be a stranger and know not whether the woman be marry or not which excuse he yet the fault be lay upon the woman that have do such a offence and she must pay to her husband four Pesos or half a ounce of gold because she commit adultery with another man if she have get any thing but if she have nothing and can pay the fine to her husband it excuse she not for if he have no great fantasy to his wife or that they have little affection one unto the other if he will he may put she away from he and as then the band of matrimony be break between they and he may take a other wife when he will but if he can learn that his wife have commit such a fact by information of other man but presume it of himself or suspect that his wife have lie with any other man trial of jealousy he charge she with it and make she eat certain salt use other ceremony of their idolatrous Fetissos wherewith the woman know herself to be clear and not to have commit adultery with a other man willing take her oath but know herself to be faulty she dare not take her oath fear that if she shall forswear herself her Fetisso will make she die whereby oftentimes the wife discover she own offence and proour the mean to move her husband to be divorce from she which chief happen by mean of the jealousy which the man have of his first wife for it cause a great hatred and contention between they because it be a great scandal unto he and oftentimes there grow so great strife about it that he seek to murder the man that do the fault and although he have pay the fine impose upon he the marry man have the privilege to drive she live and put she not away but she be force to serve the young wife and shall never trouble herself with any thing but only to eat and drink well to have a care to please her husband and to do whatsoever he command although a man have as many wife as he be able to keep yet all be not of one but of several age the one young than the other that they may be the better serve by their wife for when the elder can do no more for age that he may not want work and that the young wife may do he more pleasure they make most of the young and every wife dwell in a house by herself although he have evening the woman go home to their house again and be together but in the day time the man and wife lie each of they in a several room at night spread a mat upon the ground and lay a wooden stool under their head in stead of a pillow and then make bed a little fire of wood when it burn they lie down with the sole of their foot before it that the heat thereof may draw out the cold which they by day have draw up into they from the irish do the like the earth by go barefooted esteem it to be very good for they which we must also acknowledge now when he have a desire to use any of his wife either he call or fetch she and that night heli with she and the next day she go to her house again where she dwell not once make any of the rest acquaint what she do that night or that her husband she go to the water to wash and make clean herself not once dream of a month lie in nor of make caudle of hippocras and other wine as woman here with we use to do they use no nurse to help they when they lie in childbed neither seek to lie dainty and soft but they present take a spoonful of oil and a handful of Manigette or graine whereof they make a drink and drink it up the next day after they go abroad in the street to do their business as other woman do they give their child such a name as they think good to themselves and bless the same name with their Fetissos and other witchcraft and when time serve circumcise both boy and girl at which time they make a great feast whereof they make great account but where the woman be most shameless at the time of the birth of their child the man in three month after lie not with that wife nor once have the use of her body which nevertheless I think they do not for any shame or regard that they have to deal with that woman but only because they have other wife enough they take the young child as soon as it be bear and wrap a clean cloth about the middle thereof lay it down on a mat upon the ground and not in a cradle and there let it turn and sprawl about and do what it will and when it be two or three month old the mother tie the child with a piece of cloth at her back and so let it hang there as the high duchess wife use to follow their husband in the war when the child cry to suck the mother cast one of her dug backward over her shoulder and so the child suck it as it hang the woman go up and down from place to place and still carry their child in that sort as light as if they have nothing at their back the child head lie just upon her shoulder and so she go shake of the child most pitiful to behold whereby usage of child we wonder that they break not the child joint by bear they in that sort be so young and yet you find very few or no lame person in those country they teach their child to go very young for they make no reckon thereof and suffer they to creep and run abroad when they be very little and teach they to speak very soon whereby you find many child there among they that can both go and speak ere they be a year old and some of they speak so plain that you may understand what they say in their language for they speak and go far soon than our child do which we wonder at beside this they be strong fat and well dispose whereof we will speak hereafter in another place the child be a month or two old than they hang a net about the body thereof like devilish preservative against the devil a little shirt which be make of the bark of a tree which they hang full of their Fetissos as golden cross string with coral about their hand foot and neck and their hair be fill full of shell whereof they make great account for they say that as long as the young child have that net about he the devil can take nor bear the child away and leave it off the devil will carry it away for they say the child be so little it will not be strong enough to resist the devil but have that net upon the body it be arm and then the devil have no power over it the coral which they hang about the child which they call a Fetisso they esteem much for that hang such a Fetisso about the child neck they say it be good against vomit the second Fetisso which they hang about his neck they say it be good against fall the three they say be good against bleed the four be very good to procure sleep which they hang about the neck thereof in the nighttime that it may sleep well the five be good against wild beast and the unwholsomenesse of the air with diverse other such like Fetissos each have a name apart to show what virtue it have and what they be good for and they credible believe they to be good against vomit fall bleed which they present help and for sleep they feed their young child with all kind of gross meat almost from the first for when they leave suckling they suffer they not to suck long than they begin to learn the child to eat of their gross meat and to drink water when they be use thereunto than they take little heed to they but beat the child lie down in their house like dog root in the ground like hog whereby it fall out that the young child soon learn to go every woman bring up her own child and each child know the mother and remain with she until the father either buy it of she or that it go away from the mother it oftentimes fall out that the husband take the child from the mother and sell it to other man for a slave when they begin to go they present learn to swim and to colour run into the water and when they be first bear they be not black but reddish as the brasilian be and then by little and little begin to be black and at last to be as black as pitch and grow big run up and down like savage man boy and girl together fight one with another take each other meat from they and from their childhood upward begin to be envious one against the other and so grow big and exercise all kind of villainy and knavery their parent not once teach they any civility nor show they what they shall do suffer both boy and girl to go stark naked as they be bear with their privy member all open without any shame or civility they use to beat and chasten their child most cruel strike they with great staff in correction such sort that we wonder that they do not break their bone which they do not but for some great cause whereby their child respect they much and for that they beat they cruel so that they do not easy forget it other good discipline they teach they not but they grow up like wild tree have spend their time thus uncivil and beginning to be eight ten or twelve year old than their parent begin to instruct and teach they to do some thing and to labour with their hand the father teach their son to spin thread make of bark of tree and to knit net which have learn they go to sea with their father to fish and when they know how to row and to guide a boat than two or three boy will go out together Arts. in a Canoe or Almadia to fish and that which they take they carry to their parent for food but when they be eighteen or twenty year old than their son begin to deal for themselves and leave their father and go and dwell two or three of they together in a house buy or hire a Canoe which be one of their boat and therewith go to sea together and what fish they get they sell for gold first keep as much as serve for food for themselves with that they sell they buy a fathom of linen cloth which they hang about their first apparel body and between their leg wherewith they cover their privy member for than they begin to be shamefaced whence they proceed further and begin to deal and traffic with merchandise and to carry it aboard the ship in their canoe and serve merchant to carry they to and from their ship and so learn to deal with gold and to get some thing after that begin to be amorous and to look after young wench than they be esteem to be man which when their father perceive they look they out wife and then they marry which wive they do very young so that in those country child get child touch the g^rles they also begin to work and that somewhat soon than the boy they learn to make basket mat and str^w hat of green rush which they fold with their hand they also learn to make cap purse and apparel make of bark of tree die with all kind of colour most cunning do as if they be fasten together with cord much to be wonder at they also learn to grind their corn or and thereof make bread which they go and sell for their mother and bring they the money to buy other meat withal and whatsoever they get they give it to their mother who for that when they marry give they some gift as I have say before in this sort the girl begin to labour and to learn to do household work wherein accord to their manner of house keep they be very curious and exceed the man in cunning workmanship the man in those country be of a very good proportion with fair member strong leg and well-shaped body which be easy to be see for that they go almost naked of their body they have round face and no great lip nor wide mouth as the barbarian moor have but their nose be flat which they make flat when they be young for they esteem a their limb and member flat nose to be a great ornament unto they and to say truth it do not amiss in they for that accord to the proportion of body it beautify their face their ear be small their eye white their eye brow very great white tooth in their mouth for they keep their tooth very clean scour they with small stick and thereby make they very smooth and shine like ivory they have little beard and be at least thirty year of age before they have any they have broad shoulder thick arm great hand and long finger and let their nail long nail a sign of idle gentry grow very long which they keep very clean with scrape for some of they let they grow as long as the joint of a man finger which they esteem for a great ornament for that cause think themselves to be gentleman the merchant also that dwell within the land use those long nail for a great show for they keep they as white as ivory by scrape they and again they have good use for they for that sometime when they have not a spoon by they and that they untie their purse to weigh gold and want a spoon to take it out for haste they use their long nail and therewith put the gold into the scale and I have see some of they at one time take at least half a ounce of small gold like sand out of their purse they have small belly long leg broad foot and long toe little hair upon their body curl hair upon their head but not so much curl as the tawny moor for they be almost like bristel and not like wool in the palm of their hand under their foot and under their lip they be very white their skin be as soft as velvet and smooth which they raze not they likewise have a great privy member whereof they make great account therein they much surpass our countryman as they grow in year they become black and black at thirty year of age be in their best time but when they be seventy or eighty year old than their blackness begin to decay and their body become yellowish and their skin begin to be rugged and to wrinkle like spanish leather they exceed all other moor in Africa for proportion and stature of body the man be industrious and subtle person as can be good workman or labourer strong of body straight and very upright ingenious to learn any thing and ready to conceive it for any thing whatsoever they see do before they they will soon imitate and counterfeit they be of a very sharp fight and see further than our netherlander for if there be any ship at the their wit be subtlety sea they will see they soon than we they be subtle merchant to traffic with all and every day more and more learn of the netherlander so that in time they will surpass they for they have good skill and knowledge in the merchandize which we sell they they be hard of complexion and have very hot stomach for they be able to digest raw and most strange meat whereat we wonder for if they have a ostrich maw they can not better digest stomach such raw meat as they many time eat as I will further declare when I speak more of their manner of feed they be very envious and spiteful one against the other and will bear stomach and revenge malice against a man ten year together and when they have the mean to be revenge than they will make their malice know and until then keep it secret they be idolatrous and very superstitious in their religion they have a strong complexion or savour of their body much like oil of palm wherewith they often anoint themselves superstition nicety they be very curious to keep their body clean and often wash and scour they they be much trouble with louse and flea they be not ashamed to show their naked body but they be very careful not to let a fart if any body be by they they wonder at our netherlander that use it so common for they can abide that a man shall fart before they esteem it to be a great shame and contempt do unto they when they ease themselves they common go in the morning to the town end where there be a place purposely make for they that easement they may not be see as also because man pass by shall not be molest with the smell thereof they also esteem it a bad thing that man shall ease themselves upon the ground and therefore they make house which be bear up above the ground wherein they ease themselves and every time they do it they wipe or else they go to the water side to ease themselves in the sand and when these privy-house be full they set fire in they and let they burn to ash they piss by job as hog do and not all at one time they be very covetous and much covetise and beg addict thereunto and they can beg so well and be so expert therein that they surpass all the beggar in our country who although they have set ten or twelve year ordinary at the church door in Holland or Zealand or go from door to door to beg a alm yet they can have their lesson so perfect as these and although they be very hard and niggardly and will give but little yet when they have get any thing by their beg than they will be somewhat liberal thereof when it cost they nothing they be very lecherous and much addict to uncleanness especial with young woman lechery whereby they be much subject to the pox and other unclean disease that be get thereby which they make small account of and be nothing ashamed of they they be no less give to drink for they be great drunkard and dainty mouth and can eat and drink drunkenness and greediness of the best in their feed they be very greedy they can endure that any rain shall fall upon their body and therefore they shun it they be very great liar and not to be credit they be likewise much incline to theft for they will steal like dog for their king and lie and steal captain practise it and they be so well use thereunto that they can leave steal they be very expert and cunning to fish and to till the land and in their apparel and go very proud they be very stout proud and curious in all their action they be not to be trust nor credit for they be no good paymaster you be as good give it as trust they with any thing they be of a very good memory and will remember a thing long they be by nature warm and hot and therefore can endure cold they be not frugal for whatsoever they get they spend it present for it grieve they to keep it so that therein they be like to little child that can keep nothing they be excellent swimmer and diverse in the water and be so expert therein that they much surpass our country man @. 3 of their apparel custom within door manner of diet merchandise the they for it the woman have the government of their house and the man take care as much as lie in their housewiferie they to earn something but the woman provide the meat to serve for their daily food although they eat a part they buy no more meat every day then serve they for that day or they can eat at a meal in the evening they go to their house that stand without the town make of bread and be full of which be their kind of corn where they take a certain quantity as much as they need for their house and with a staff stamp it as we use to stamp spice in a grocer shop and that be their manner of thresh than they fan it in a wooden dish till it be clean but such as have slave make they do it this be a fair white seed when it be break as hereafter I will show over night they steep this with a little maize in fair water and in the morning after they have wash and make themselves ready they take the and lay it upon a stone as painter do when they grind their colour than they take another stone about a foot long and with their hand grind the as small as they can till in a manner it be dough and then it show like bake buckway cake they temper their dough with fresh water and salt and then make roll thereof as big as two fist and that they lie upon a warm hearth whereon it bake a little and this be the bread which they use the negro of the castle bake fair bread of maize which be almost like our wheaten bread raw food and that they cut in rowles they can also bake it so hard that it will keep two or three month sweet and hard for they furnish their ship and jact with such bread when they send they to the land of saint Thomas or to angola other that have not the mean to have such bread they go to market to buy it and call it kangue when the fisherman come out of the sea with their fish than the woman carry it to the market where every one come to buy that and flesh fruit and other thing they use altogether raw and strange kind of meat as handful of grain or Manigette and will drink up whole romer full of aquavite at a filthy food draught dog cat and filthy stink elephant and buffold flesh wherein there be a thousand magget and many time stink like carrion in such sort that you can endure the smell thereof there be likewise little bird as big as a bulfinch of a grey colour with red bill which very cunning make their nest upon the small end of the branch of tree thereby to preserve themselves from snake or other venomous beast those they eat alive feather and all I have be tell by some of the moor that the country people dwell within the land eat dry snake and the boor or slave as also the common people which dwell upon the seaside although they have better provision of meat then those that dwell further into the land yet they be of so hot a nature that they eat raw dog gut and never seethe nor roast they which we ourselves see and there be one of their boy leave aboard a netherlander ship for a pawn for debt which boy be so greedy to eat raw meat that although he have sufficient meat with they in the ship yet he will eat the hen meat out of their trough this boy make a stick and at the end thereof he drive a nail with the point upward a greedy boy and go and lie by the hen cage and when any of they put out their head to eat meat he strike they in the head and kill they and then he go and show the sailor that some of the hen be dead which he do to the end he may eat their raw gut and will not stay so long until the gut be make clean but take they and eat they raw as they come out of the hen belly they eat also great store of old stink fish which be dry in the sun but to say that they eat such kind of raw meat for necessity and no other be untruth for they also be very dainty and can eat good meat when they have it there be woman that dwell in the castle among the portugal that can dress meat well they eat also many hen goat ox and heart but such meat be not eat by the common people but those that eat they be gentleman or such as be rich and be able to buy they they also eat jugnamis Bannanas and patate they have three kind of tree as the palmtree whereof their tree some be female which yield no wine but bear grape as big as plum of a orange colour at the one end be somewhat blackish those grape they peel to the stone and palme-oile thereof they make oil which they call palm oil which be very delicate and good which they use to dress their meat withal and make good sauce thereof for their fish the thick of this oil they use to anoint their body withal to make they clean and the woman use it to frizell their hair the vein be as great as acorn and as hard as a stone at the end thereof have three round hole they beat they in piece and within they find certain nut like little earthen pellet much like hazell-nut but when you eat they they taste of the wood and be very dry they likewise have many bean and pease whereof some be like Turkey beanes of a purple colour those bean be good and fat which they dress with oil of palm and it be a very excellent meat and nourish well but the other kind of bean and pease they use not to eat for they have no great quantity of they grow thereabouts the jugnamis also they use in many place in stead of bread their drink common be nothing but water but yet in some place they brew a little maize in water which be sod together be almost like a kind of beer which they also use much to drink and call it poitou other buy a pot of palme-wine and because that will not continue long therefore four or five of they go together and buy a drink pot or two a pot of they be ten pot of we and that they pay for together which they pour into a great Cabas which grow upon tree whereof some be half as big as a kilderkin and will hold at least twelve khan and then sit down round about it to drink whereof every man send he love and true wife a little pot full home to drink and the first draught that they drink they take it out of the Cabas with a small Cabas and when the first man drink the rest stand up and take his cap or hat off lay their hand upon his head and with a loud voice cry Tautosi Tautosi at the first draught they drink not the Cabas full out but leave a little in it which they throw upon the ground say i OV as give their Fetissos that to drink and if they have other on their arm or foot they spit drink out of their uncivil feed mouth upon they as if they give they drink also for they be of opinion that if they do it not or forget to do it they shall not drink their wine quiet together but that their Fetissos will let they natural they be great drinker and use no less unseemliness in their feed but eat as unmannerly and greedy as if they be a company of hog for sit down upon the ground to eat they stay not till they have eat one morsel up but still cram strange hunger in so hot a climate in and they put not their meat into their mouth but pull their meat in piece and take it up with their three middlemost finger and gape cast it so right into their mouth that they never fail nor cast it beside their mouth whereat we wonder much they be always hungry and will willing eat all day long which show that they have very hot maw and although the country be very hot whereby the heat of the air common shall fill man stomach yet they be hungry and we netherlander be not weak stomach there but always have good appetite whereby I be of opinion that heat in those country make man hungry but because I be no doctor of physic I will not entreat thereof and because they make great account of that drink together they be very earnest and industrious to get something and to make provision of gold which have get they can be frugal or spare good fellowship or prodigality but present go and drink it with their companion now one and then another every one his turn and if one get more than his fellow than he must be liberall than his fellow that be when they begin to deal with the merchant and to go aboard the ship and he that be poor or have not much can hardly bear company to drink because they be not spare when they have get any thing as I have understand by the inhabitant of those country before the portugal come thither to deal with they they have very little or no kind of merchandise to traffic withal or their trade to live by but live upon that which they get from other by force which be not much special to get any thing to apparel themselves for before that time they go all naked as I say before much less have they any cattle or victual for their maintenance but only such as the portugal bring thither and by that mean the country be fill and replenish with diverse kind of beast and corn whereby at this day there be almost all kind of thing that be first simplicity necessary and needful for man sustenance and otherwise to be have in those country and within a while after the portugal begin to traffic and deal with the savage inhabitant they likewise begin to know their merchandise at the first in former time they come and bring their gold unto the portugal and buy of they such thing as they want as linen cloth etc. but the people dwell further within land dare not venture to come to the portugal to deal with they as wonder at first trade they it be a fearful thing unto they to see white man apparel and they themselves black and unapparelled as the like happen unto our man for at the first they be afraid to see black moor and therefore they bring their money to those that dwell on the sea side where the portugal traffic and tell they what ware they will have and they go to the castle and buy such thing as they desire as iron tin copper basin knife cloth linen kettles coral and such like ware and the merchant that send they to the portugal pay they for their pain upon every of gold by they disburse so that if they bestow many pesoe they receive a good deal of money for their factoridge and by that mean they get their living but after that when we begin to traffic thither the first that go from hence thither first Dutch trade out of Holland to deal with the negro be call barent erickson of medenblicke and find what profit the portugal do there we increase our trade thither and send more ship with the say baront as a fit man for it because he know the coast as have be there with the portugal but have no place upon the land as the portugal have to carry our ware ashore and to lay it in warehouse to traffic with they as time serve and dare not or else may not go on land we be constrain to stay with our ship at anchor before their town attend for the merchant that come aboard our ship with their canoe at which time the negro see that we have merchandise aboard embolden themselves to traffic with we and bring their gold aboard our ship and for that at this present they deal but little with the portugal but only with our countryman therefore I will show in what manner they deal with we in the morning betimes they come aboard our ship with their canoe or scute to traffic with we and the cause why their merchant come so early aboard be for that in the morning the wind which they call Bofone blow off from the land and then it be calm smooth water for wind in the morning from land and calm about noon the wind which they call agom Brettou begin to blow out of the sea and then they row to land again for the people that dwell within the land can hardly brook the sea for when they be aboard the ship they can scarce go or stand but lie down and spew like dog and be very seasick but their rower and pilot that bring they aboard be hardy enough and never be sick by reason of their daily use to the sea but some of their merchant when they come aboard our ship be so sick that they cast out all they have within their body and by reason of their be so sick infaire weather they be so afraid of the wind when the wave go any thing high that they make as much haste home as they can and some of they dare not venture upon the sea to go aboard the ship but deliver their money to the pilot or factor tell they what merchandise they desire to buy and those tolken come with the gold aboard the ship have a purse which hang about their middle wherein they put their gold and every several man gold be in a piece of cloth or paper by itself and they can tell which be every man and what ware he desire to have for it and sometime they have twelve or ten man gold to bestow which be call a english of gold and of some two three or four and when any of their money be not weight than they put it into their purse and carry it to the man again for if they shall put any thing to it to make it full weight the merchant will not give it they again for they weigh their gold first upon the land and know how much it be before they send it aboard the ship for they credit not one the other and when they have bestow their money than we must give they somewhat to boot which they call dache dache when we begin to traffic here in the country with two or
