here pursue a poor sailer a Englishman for offer but to carry a little bag of corent aboard uncustome and kill he run up a pair of stair for succour he be weary of his life that have a difference with any of they and will walk abroad after daylight but cowardice be join with their cruelty who dare do nothing but sudden upon advantage and be ever danger of remiss law private arm encourage to villainy by the remissness of their law for none will lay hand upon a offender until fourteen day after that he be call to the scale a eminent place where one do stand and public cite the offender who in the meantime have leisure to make his own peace or else to absent himself if then he appear not they banish he and propound a reward accord to the greatness of the offence to he that shall either kill or take he alive and if it be do by one that be banish his own banishment the least reward be release the labourer do go into the field with sword and partisan as if in a enemy country bring home their wine and oil in hogs-skin the inside turn outward it be a custom amongst they to invite certain man unto their marriage who they call compeer every one of these do bestow a ring which the priest do put upon the bride and bridegroom finger interchangeable shift they and so he do the garland on their head of these they be never jealous a abuse in that kind repute as detestable a crime as if against enchantment for here it be a common practice to bewitch they make thereby impotent with their wife until the charm be burn or otherwise consume insomuch that sometime as they say the mother of the betroth by way of prevention do bewitch they themselves and again unloose they as soon as the marriage be consummate the nuptial sheet as in some case command by the Mosaical law be public show will look back upon no occasion until they come unto the salutation of Mahomet at which time they reverse their face first over the right shoulder and then over the left believe that his come will be behind they when they be at their devotion the priest do sometime read unto they some part of the Alcoran hold it in reverence to the book as high as his chin sometime some of their fabulous legend intermix exposition and instruction which they harken unto with heedy attention and such steady positure of body as if they be entrance their service be mix with song and response and when all be liturgy do they strike down their face and beard with look of devout gravity if they find a paper in the street they will thrust it in some crevice of the adjoin wall imagine that the name of God may be contain therein and then profane to be tread under foot or otherwise defile they number their often repetition of the name of God and his attribute with other short ejaculation of prayer and praise upon bead some shake their head incessant until they turn giddy perhaps in imitation of the suppose trance but natural infirmity of their prophet and they have a order of monk who be call dervish monk who I have often see to dance in their mosque on tuesday and friday many together to the sound of barbarous music dance that consist of continual turn until at a certain stroke they fall upon the earth and lie along like beast be think to be rapt in spirit unto celestial conversation now the woman be not permit to come into their temple yet have they secret place to look in through grate partly for trouble their devotion but especial for that they be not circumcise as be the woman of Persia and Aethiopia nor circumcise they the male until they be able to answer the priest and promise for themselves which be for the most part at the age of eight they be circumcise in the house of their parent at a festival meeting and in the midst of the assembly the child hold up his forefinger in token that he be a mahometan as soon as cut the priest wash the wound in water and salt and bind it in linen who change not his name but be from thenceforth call a Musselman which be a true believer this do he be carry unto the where his hair before that time wear at full length be shave and so keep ever after all save a lock on the top of his crown by which they dream that they shall be assume by Mahomet into paradise then put they on he a white turban and so return with drum and Oboe be with great solemnity conduct to the mosque and present with gift accord to his quality the turk do fast one month in the year which they call Ramazan which change yearly so that in thirteen year they fast one wherein they say that the Alcoran be deliver lent. unto Mahomet by the angel observe by all but the infirm and traveller who be to fast for as long a time when so they recover or come to the end of their journey but they fast but during the day in the night they feast and then be all their steeple stick round with lamp which burn till the morning afford a object of great solemnity such as in stead of abstayn from meat do abstain at that time from their mosque they carry about in scorn and severe chastise but such as then drink wine they punish with death upon the discovery of the new moon which they superstitious gratulate esteem he happy that discover it first and by the course thereof do reckon their year fall out this year on the seven of December the feast of the great byram do begin which do continue for three day together observe by they as easter be with we on the first day the grand signior ride to Sophia in all the pomp and glory of empire of which we shall speak hereafter upon his return we see a sort of christian some of they half earth already crooked with age desperate impiety and tremble with palsy who by the throw away of their bonnet and lift up of their fore-finger do proffer themselves to become mahometans a sight full of horror and trouble to see those desperate wretch that have profess Christ all their life and have suffer no doubt for his sake much contumely and oppression now almost die to forsake their redeemer even then when they be to receive the reward of their patience to these the tyrant a little incline his body who fore not so much as cast his eye aside but sit like the adore statue of a idol for they hold it a great grace and a act of singular piety to draw many to their religion present they with money change of raiment and free they from all tribute and tax insomuch that if a christian have deserve death by their law if he will gravity convert they will many time remit his punishment but they compel no man during this festival they exercise themselves with various pastime but none more in use and more barbarous than their swing up and down as boy do in bell rope for which there be gallow for they bear that form of a exceed height erect in sundry place of the city when by two join rope that be fasten above they will swing themselves as high as the transome perhaps affect in that it stupefy the sense for a season the cause that opium be so much in request and of their fore say shake of their head and continue turn in regard whereof they have such as have lose their wit and natural idiot in high veneration as man whether be the most fool and mad ravish in spirit and take from themselves as it be to the fellowship of angel these they honour with the title of saint lodge they in their temple some of they go almost stark naked other clothe in shred of several colour who necessity be supply by the with couple chain together by the neck who beg to satisfy their creditor in part and be at the year end release of their bond provide that they make satisfaction if they prove afterward able at their death they usual give legacy for the release of prisoner the free of bondslave repair of bridge build of cane for the relief of passenger and the great man to the erect of mosque and hospital which they build not seldom in their life time but Mahomet the great and Solyman the magnificent have in that kind exceed all other who stately and sumptuous structure do give a principal ornament to the city where the sick and impotent be provide for and the stranger entertain for here be no inn the revenue of that of Mahomet amount to a hundred and fifty thousand sultany to these therebelong to feed and provide they kennel to litter in most of they repair to the sea side nightly where they keep such a howl that if the wind sit southward they may be easy hear to the upper side of the city of Pera. with the stoic they attribute all accident to destiny and constellation at birth since death can be neither hasten nor avoid be withal persuade that they die brave that die fight and that they shall be reward with paradise that do spend their blood upon the enemy of their religion call shahid which be martyr by they for although they repute murder to be a execrable crime that cry to heaven for vengeance and be never forgive yet be they command by their law to extend their profession by violence and without compassion to slaughter their opposer but they live with themselves in such exemplary concord that during the time that I remain amongst they it be above three quarter of a year I never see mahometan offer violence to a mahometan nor break into ill language but if they now that we speak of the person of the turk their disposition manner their person and manner and fashion they be general well complexioned of good stature and full body proportionable compact they nourish no hair about they but a lock on the crown and on their face only esteem it more clean and to be the better prepare for their superstitious washing but their beard they wear at full length the mark of their affect gravity and token of freedom for slave have they shave insomuch that they will scoff at such christian as cut or natural want they as if suffer themselves to be abuse against nature all of they wear on their head white sash and turban the badge of their religion as be their turban sash the fold of the one and size of the other of their vocation and quality sash be long towel of calico wind about their head turban be make like great globe of calico too and thwart with roll of the same have little cop cap on the top of green or red velvet be only wear by person of but if a christian out of ignorance wear green he shall have his clothes tear off from his back and perhaps be well beat they carry no weapon about they in the city their knife only they thrust under their girdle great crooked knife of a dagger-like size in sheath gate of metal the haft and sheath of many be set with stone and some of they worth five hundred sultany they bear their body upright of a stately gate and elate countenance in their familiar salutation they lay their hand on their bosom and a little decline their body but when they salute a person of great rank they bow almost to the ground and kiss the hem of his garment the ornament of their head they never put off upon any occasion some of they perfume their beard with amber and the inside of their turban and all of they affect cleanliness so religious that beside their customary lotion and daily frequent of the they never so much as make water but they wash both cleanness their hand and privity at which business they sequester themselves and couch to the earth revile the Christian who they see piss against a wall and sometime strike he this they do to prevent that any part of either excrement shall touch their garment esteem office of nature it a pollution and hinder the acceptation of prayer who then be to be most pure in heart and habit so slothful they be that they never walk up and down for recreation nor use any other Sloth exercise but shoot wherein they take as little pain as may be sit on carpet in the shadow and send their slave for their arrow they also shoot against earthen wall ever shoot keep moist in shop and private house for that purpose stand not above six pace from the mark and that with such violence that the arrow pass not seldom through nay I have see their arrow shoot by our ambassador through target of steel piece of brass two inch thick and through wood with a arrow head with wood of eight inch their bow be for form and length not unlike the lath of a large cross bow make of the horn Bowes of buffoloe intermix with sinew of admirable workmanship and some of they exquisite gild although there be wrestler amongst they yet they be such as do it to delight the people and do make it their profession as do those that walk upon rope wherein the turk wrestler be most expert go about when they have do to every particular spectator for his voluntary benevolence of card and dice they be happy ignorant but at chess they will play all game the day long a sport that agree well with their sedentary vacancy wherein notwithstanding they avoid the dishonest hazard of money the better sort take great delight in their horse which be beautiful to the eye and well ride for service but quick enure if hold to a good round trot for amble they do not in a horse indifferent journey but the turk do not light ride so fast as to put they unto either their saddle be hard and deep though not great plate behind and before and some of they with silver as be their massy stirrup and the rein of their bridle suit unto their costly caparison when they stand in the stable they feed they for the most part if not altogether with barley be here of small value and only serve for that purpose they litter they in their own dung first dry in the sun and puluerate which keep their skin clean smooth and shine the turk do great reverence their parent so command to do by their law as the reverence to superior leave hand before right inferior his superior and the young age ready give the priority to who it belong the left hand as they go in the street prefer before the right in that make master thereby of the sword of the other and the chief place the far from the wall live together as if all of a brotherhood yet give they no entertainment unto one another nor come there any they eat three time a day but when they feast they sit all the day long unless they rise to exonerate nature and forth with return again they abstain from hogs-flesh from blood and drink from what have die of itself unless in case of necessity their usual drink be pure water yet have they sundry sherbet so call they the confection which they infuse into it some make of sugar and lemon some of ignorant obedience moreover a number that live by write will be undo who be for the most part of the priesthood the turkish tongue be lofty in sound but poor of itself in substance for be original the infringe that precept and the grand signior himself have a fan whereon the battle of Hungary be paint colour also they have nor less fair than durable every one have some trade or other not so much as the grand signior except their trade every man have a trade be light such as serve for their own use neither much supply foreign mart nor frequent they a lazy people that work but by fit and more esteem of their ease then their profit yet be they excessive covetous and although they have not the wit to deceive for they be gross-headed yet have they the will break all compact with the christian that they find discommodious so that they seldom will deal with they but with one another they buy and sell only for ready money wherein the most of their substance consist the occasion that few suit do happen amongst they I have speak sufficient at lest what I can of this nation in general now convert we to the person and court of this sultan he be in this year 1610. about the age of three and twenty strong limn and of a just sultan describe stature yet great incline to be fat insomuch as sometime he be ready to choke as he feed and some do purposely attend to free he from that danger his face be full and due proportion only his eye be extraordinary great by they esteem as be say before a excellency in beauty phlegm have the predominancy in his complexion he have a little hair on his upper lip but less on his chin of a darksome colour his aspect be as haughty as his empire be large he begin already to abstain from exercise yet be there pillar with inscription in his seraglio between which he throw a great iron mace that memorize both his strength and activity be on a time rebuke by his father Mahomet that he neglect so much his exercise cruel policy and study he make his reply that now he be too old to begin to learn intimate thereby that his life be to determine with his father whereat the sultan weep bitter for he then have two elder brother of who the elder be strangle in the presence of his father upon a false suspicion of treason and the other by a natural death do open his way to the empire perhaps the consideration thereof have make he keep his young brother alive contrary to their cruel custom yet strong guard and keep within his seraglio for he be of no bloody disposition nor otherwise notorious vicious consider the austerity of that government and immunity of their religion yet be he a unrelenting punisher of offence even his acts. in his own household have cause eight of his page at my be there to be throw into the sea for sodomy a ordinary crime if esteem a crime in that nation in the night time be let to know by the report of a canon that his will be fulfil among who it be give out that the viceroy natural son of Sicilia be have the ground to our bed a stone to our pillow as jacob in his travel have and the sky to our cover and many poor traveller in these part who come unprovided have nothing but the air for their supper except they can meet with the first-fruit of tree or herb of the field we meet in some place with village of tent where our janissary paravan bashaw be partly fear and partly love amongst they bring unto we from they bread and water often time their bread be make all in cake after the ancient manner as Abraham entertain angel with hearth cake at one place we have also present to we very good sweet goat milk and also good sour milk turn by art which be the most common cake dish in those hot country the day follow we come about noon to a village call Hanadan eight mile on this Hanadan side Aleppo over against which village on the right hand on the top of the hill there be as the jew report the sepulchre of the prophet jeremy at this village Hanadan there be many jeremy his sepulchre pigeon house whereof the poor people make much profit bring they to Aleppo to sell. at this village we dine with musmelon sambouse and a mucclebite and after dinner we sambouse be little pasty muclebite a dish make of egg and herb Aleppo in the title of psal. 60. sleep a hour or two as the custom of the country be and then ride forward towards Aleppo whither we come by five of the clock and be kind entertain at cane Burgol by the worshipful Richard colthurst esquire consul for the english nation there aram Sobah some think to have be that city which be now call Aleppo and of this aram Sobah I find mention make 2. sam. 8. 3 4 5. and also in the title of the sixty psalm where mention be make of the salt valley which be but half a day journey from Aleppo which be a very great plain without grass grow on it the very sand whereof be good salt natural after rain be dry again by the sun they gather it there be also a little island or mountain in the midst thereof plain on the top which yield the best salt. some jew there dwell do also say that Aleppo be the city sepheruaim but I think it to be a better city which some say be call Apollonius but I know no reason for it except it be build by one of that name howsoever it shall seem this city Aleppo have often change her name and that if it be not aram Sobah yet to be build not far from the place where aram Sobah stand but the turk change the name of all place where they come call Aleppo at this day Halep which signify milk because it yield great store of milk Aleppo be inhabit by turk moor arabian jew Greek armenians Chelfalines Nostranes and people of sundry other nation the turk come of Magog the son of japheth the moor be more ancient dweller in Aleppo then Turk and more forward and zealous in mahometism than turk yea all the churchman amongst the turk be moor who the turk count a base people in regard of themselves and call they t^ts yet their churchman they have in great reverence and not only they but they reverence churchman of all Turk reverence churchman of all sort nation and call they holy man saint and man of god. I myself have have great experience hereof both in the place of my abode at Aleppo and in my journey towards jerusalem and in other place in Aleppo as I have walk in the street both turk and moor and other nation will very reverent salute i after the manner of their country yea their very soldier as I have walk in the field with many other of our nation without a janesarie to guard we though they have be many hundred together yet have they not offer either i or any of my company wrong for my sake but have say one to another Hadah cassy that be this be a churchman and therefore take heed what you do unto he for he be a good man etc. at jerusalem many stranger of sundry nation understand that I be a english preacher come and kiss my hand and call i the english patriarch yea in all my ten year travel I never receive neither be offer wrong by any nation but my own countryman and by they chief who it chief concern to protect i from wrong yet have I find they most forward to offer i wrong only for do my duty and follow the order of our church of England know that I have none of the reverend father of our church to defend i so will it be in England if we have not the reverend father in God the lord bishop of our church to protect we all other nation both heathen and Christian go before we herein in reverence and provide for their churchman the turk honour mad and foolish sanctity sheh Boubac sheh Mohammet a naked Santone their mufti which be their chief ruler in ecclesiastical matter next under the grand signior as a the nostrane Greek armenians Chelfalines and christian of all other nation perform double honour unto they only in England where there be a more learned ministry I speak by experience then in any nation in the world they be least of all regard which make our adversary the papist say as I have hear some of they speak in my hear many thousand mile from England that if we ourselves be persuade of the truth of our religion we will reverence our churchman as they do and not scorn they and contemn they as we do they also account fool dumb man and mad man santones that be saint and whatsoever such mad man say or do though they take any thing out of their house or strike they and wound they yet they take it in good part and say that they shall have good luck after it and when such mad man die they canonize they for saint and erect stately monument over their grave as we have here many example especial of one who be mad go always naked who name be sheh Boubac at who death they bestow great cost on his funeral and erect a house over his grave where to this day there be lamp burn night and day and many idle fellow who they call daruise there maintain to look unto his sepulchre and to receive the offering of such as come to offer to sheh Boubac which they take to themselves and there be no week but many come out of the city of Aleppo and other place to offer for this sepulchre be build on a hill three mile from Aleppo between the king garden and the fountain of fish if any be sick or in danger they vow that if they recover or escape they will offer so much money or this or that good thing to sheh Boubac there be also such another bedlam saint in Aleppo yet live who they call sheh mahammet a Santone who go always naked with a spit on his shoulder and as he go through the street the shopkeeper will offer he their ring and if he thrust his spit through their ring they take it for a favour and sign of good success the like account they make if he take any thing from their shop-board or box they or any of their house yea they be yet more mad upon this mad man then so for both man and woman will come unto he and kiss his hand * * pag. 455. (@) and syr. mention this naked fool and say that each other day he wash his naked body at the fountain of the great can and present the water be repute holy drink and carry to sick folk by the moor his cell be like Vulcan shop where he lie on the ground be attend with daruise which beg alm and gather beast bone to make fire sometime he sometime they sign some woman desire issue kiss his general member which be always naked and depart joyful H^e (@) fly dog eye raw and with his spit use to pursue any D^g he see for that purpose etc. a fit glass to look upon suporstition daruise or any other part sometime his thigh and ask he counsel for they hold that mad man soul be in heaven talk with God and that he reveal secret unto they in regard whereof the pasha themselves oftentimes and chief captain will come unto he with some present and kiss some part of his naked body and ask he whether they shall go to battle or not and what success they shall have in war and look whatsoever he say they hold it for a oracle not long since the turk have a victory against the christian and at their return they report that this naked Santone sheh mahammet of Aleppo be see naked in the field fight against their enemy and that by his help they over-came they although he be not near they by many thousand mile whereby you may see how the devil do delude they still as he do their forefather at the first by Mahomet Machiaveilian device their daruise also they have in such reputation that oftentimes great pasha when they be in disfavour with the king and fear either loss of life or good or both to avoid danger will turn daruise and then they account themselves privilege person from the rigour of their law. the witness of a daruise or of a churchman will pass better than any man witness beside yea better than Shereffes who they account of Mahomet kindred and they be know from other by their green sash which no man else may wear for green they account Mahomet colour and if they see any christian wear a garment of that colour they will cut it from his back and beat he and ask he how he dare presume to wear Mahomet colour and whether he be kin to God or not this I have know put in practice upon christian not acquaint with the custom of the country since my come one for have but green shoestring have his shoe take away another wear green breeches under his gown be espy have his breeches cut off and he revile and beat the turk have no print amongst they but all their law and their religion be write in the morisco tongue that be the arabic tongue and he be account a learned man amongst they that can write and read and as for the latin tongue he be a rare man amongst they that can speak it some few amongst they have the italian tongue and many especial in and about Constantinople speak the vulgar greek that be tongue for in Constantinople there be as many grecian and Hebrew as turk the poor amongst the moor and Syntana turk at Aleppo beg oftentimes in the street in the name and for the sake of Syntana who be as they say a whore of charity and will prostitute herself to any man bacsheese as they say in the arabic tongue that be gratis free the diet of the turk be not sumptuous for the most common dish be Pilaw which be good diet of the turk Pilawe savoury meat make of Rice and small morsel of mutton boil therein and sometime roast buckone that be small bit or morsel of flesh their more costly fare be sambouse and muclebite sambouse be make of paste like a great round pastry with variety of herb and meat therein not mince but in buckone a muclebite be a dish make of egg and herb their small sambouse be more common not so big as a man hand like a square pastry with mince meat therein they have also variety of Helloway that be sweet meat compound in such sort as be not to be see elsewhere the poor sort feed on herb and fruit of the tree their most common drink be Coffa which be a black kind of drink make of a kind Coffa of pulse like pease call Coava which be ground in the mill and boil in water they drink it as hot as they can suffer it which they find to agree very well with they against their crudity and feed on herb and raw meat other compound drink they have call Sherbet make of water and sugar or honey with snow therein to make it cool for although the country be hot yet they keep snow all the year long to cool their drink it be account a great courtesy amongst they to give unto their friend when they come to visit they a fin-ion or Scudella of Coffa which be more wholesome than toothsome for it cause good concoction and drive away drowsiness some of they will also drink Bersh or opium which make they forget themselves and talk idle of castle in the air as though they see vision and hear revelation their Coffa house be more common than alehouse in England but they use not so much to sit in the house as on bench on both side the Coffa house street near unto a Coffa house every man with his fin-ion full which be smoke hot they use to put it to their nose and ear and then sup it off by leisure be full of idle and alehouse talk while they be amongst themselves drink of it if there be any news it be talk off there they have also excellent good fountain water in most place of that country which be a common drink amongst they especial in summer time and in their travel at all time of the year some of our merchant have weigh their water and we in England when they have come water light there than here home and have find their water light than we by four ounce in the pound and the light the water be the more pleasant it be to drink and go down more delectable as if it be milk rather than water in great city where the fountain be either far off or not so plentiful there be certain poor man which go about the street from morning to night with a bear skin full of water sew up and fasten about his shoulder like a tinker budget with a bowl of brass in his hand and offer water free to they that pass by except they give they any thing in courtesy some seldom time the great part of they salutation of the turk be very courteous people amongst themselves salute one another at their meeting with their hand on their breast for they never uncover their head with these word Salam alike Sultanum that be peace be unto you sir. whereunto the other reply Salam that be peace be to you also and sometime thus Elph Marhabba or in turkish thus hosh Geldanos sophi Geldanos that be welcome my dear friend and in the morning subalky Sultanum that be good morrow sir and in the evening thus misalker Sultanum that be good even sir. and when friend and acquaintance meet who have not see one another many day before they salute one another in turkish thus neder halen that be how do you in arabic thus that be how do you sir and ish babtac that be how do thy gate mean all within his gate and so proceed by particular to ask how do thy child slave horse cat Dog ass etc. and every thing in the house except his wife for that be hold a very unkind question and not suuall amongst they and if a man come to their house and at the door inquire of the child for their father they will answer he but if he inquire for the mother they will throw stone at he and revile he their woman as have be show before have little liberty to come abroad except it be on the Eeve before their sabbath which be Thursday to weep at the grave of the dead or to the bannio or hot bath to wash themselves as the use of the country be and when they come abroad they be always mask for it be account a shame for a woman to be see bare-faced yea they be so jealous and suspicious over they that father will not suffer their own son after they come to fourteen year of age to see their mother these be their common salutation one to another their more special salutation to great personage be these when a man come to salute the great Turk or grand signior himself into who presence few be admit except ambassador and great personage they be lead between two by the arm for fear of a stab by which mean one of their grand signior be once kill and when they return they go backward for it be account a disgrace to turn their back part to a great man in like manner they salute their pasha and other great man but not lead by the arm but with their hand on the breast bow down their head to kiss the skirt of his garment pronounce these word Ollah towal emrac that be God prolong your day sir. and so long as they talk with a bashaw they stand with their hand on their breast maiden-like and bow low at their departure and go backward they never uncover their head unto any man no not to the king himself yea it be a word of reproach amongst they to say when they mislike a matter I have as lief thou show i thy bare head they call one another diverse and not always by their name but sometime by their father call trade or degree as eben sultan that be the son of a king eben Terzi the name son of a tailor and sometime by their father quality as eben Sacran that be the son of a drunkard and sometime by their mark as Colac that be a man without ear Sepher that be Sepher with the thin beard and sometime by their stature as towill that be a tall man sgire rugiall that be a little man and sometime by their office as i-asgee that be a secretary nibe that be a clerk etc. and sometime by their humour as Chiplac that be a naked man or one who be of a humour to wear no clothes but breech but their common word of courtesy either to stranger or such who name they know not or who they purpose to reverence be Chillabee that be gentleman and there be no man amongst they of any degree will refuse to answer to any of these name but if nature have mark they either with goggle eye bunch back lame leg or any other infirmity or deformity as they be know by it so they be content to be call by it but they have go on pilgrimage to their holy city Mecha where their prophet Mahomet be bury at their return be call hogy that be pilgrim as hogie Tahar Hogie Mahammet etc. which be count a word of great grace and credit amongst they and the witness of a hogie will be take before any other there be also many arabian in Aleppo call vulgar arabs or bedween they have two king at this day viz. Dandan and Aborisha the one their lawful king the other a usurper and some follow the one and some the other and be bitter enemy one to another yet have I seldom hear of any great war betwixt they for they seldom meet they never come into any wall town or city for fear of treason but live in tent and be here to day and many hundred mile off within few day after they be a base beggarly and roguish people wander up and down and live by spoil which they account no sin because they be Mahomet countryman and he allow they liberty to live by theft yet their king do no great harm but take toll or tribute of the caravans as they pass by which if they pay willing they pass quiet and be not rob but a little exact upon one of their king have often time pitch his tent near unto the city of Aleppo and many merchant be desirous to see they and their order take occasion to present he with some small present or other which he take very kind and admit they to his table and give they a tent to lodge in all night on the morrow for breakfast one of they make he a minsed pie and set it before he hot as it come out of the oven and when he see it cut up and open and perceive smoke to come out of it he shrink back fear it have be some engine to destroy he and that the fire will follow after the smoke but when he perceive no fire follow the smoke he be content to taste of it and high commend it as the dainty dish that ever he taste of in his life these arabian king never keep any money in their purse but spend it as fast as they find it and when they want with their sword they seek a new purchase some be soldier fight faithful on any side that will give they pay some of this roguish arabian race follow neither of their king but wander from place to place in cave and rock and live by their sword not only rob but kill such as they can overcome other of they of a better mind so journey in city of trade and traffic and make themselves servant to any nation that will set they on work and well reward they some of they be horse-keeper some bastage that be porter and some under-cooke in kitchins and be very serviceable but for the most part their lodging be on some dunghill or other or odd corner of the city with some silly tent over their head their wife wear ring in their nose either of silver or brass fasten to the middle gristle of their nose and colour their lip blue with indigo and go always barelegged and barefooted with plate or ring of brass above their ankle and bracelet of brass about their hand they be people which can and do endure great hardness and misery both for diet and lodging their woman be skilful in mourn and cry by art and therefore they be hire to cry at the funeral of turk and moor oftentimes tear their hair and make all their face blue with indigo there be here speak so many several language as there be several nation here dwell or sojourn every nation amongst themselves speak their own language and here be of most nation in the world some who either come with their merchandise to sell or buy commodity or sojourn here as stranger or else have access and recess to this city as traveller but of all christian language the italian tongue be most use and therewithal a man may travel further but of all the oriental tongue these four be most speak in these part arabic turkish armenian and persian or Agimesco beside all these mahometan which I have already name there be many jew in Constantinople Aleppo Damascus Babylon cairo and every great city and place of merchandise throughout all the turk dominion who be know by their hat for they be accustom to wear red hat without brim at my first come but late the head Vizier be their enemy they be constrain to wear hat of blue cloth because red be account too stately and princelike a colour for they to wear they be of more vile account in the sight of turk than christian insomuch that if a jew will turn Turk he must first turn Christian before they will admit he to be a Turk yea it be a word of reproach amongst the turk and a usual protestation amongst they when they be false accuse of any crime to clear themselves they use to protest in this manner if this be true than God grant I may die a jew. and the jew in like case use to say if this be not a false accusation then God grant I may die a Christian pray better for themselves then they believe and as all of they must be that shall be save and the poor christian sojourn and dwell in these part do hate they very uncharitable and irreligious in that we read rom. 11. many argument prove that they shall be convert again for on good Friday in many place especial at zante Jew stone on good Friday they throw stone at they insomuch that they dare not come out of their house all that day and yet be scarce in safety in their house for they use to throw stone at their window and door and on the roof of their house on Thursday about noon the jew begin to keep within door and continue there with their door shut until Saturday about noon for if they come forth before that time they be sure to be stone but after noon on easter Eeve if they come abroad they may pass as quiet as ever they do and some ignorant christian refuse superstition to eat of their meat or bread their reason be because the jew refuse to eat or drink with christian to this day or to eat any meat that christian kill but it be not unusual amongst christian of better knowledge to eat of the jew meat which ordinary they buy of they for the jew to this day eat not of the hinder part of any beast but only of the former part and sell the hinder quarter of their beef mutton kid goat etc. to christian they observe still all their old ceremony and feast sacrifice only except yet some of they have confess that their physician kill some christian patient or other who they have under their hand at that time in stead of a sacrifice if a man die without child the next brother take his wife and raise up seed unto his brother and they still marry in their own kindred many of they be rich merchant some of they drogomen and some broker most of they be very crafty and deceitful people they have no beggar amongst they but many thief and some who steal for necessity because they dare not beg all matter of controversy betwixt themselves be bring before their Cakam to decide who be their chief churchman most of the jew can read Hebrew but few of they speak it except it be in two place in Turkey and that be at Salonica former call thessalonica a city in Macedonia by the gulf thermaicus and at Safetta in the holy land near unto the sea of Galilee which two place two university be as it be university or school of learning amongst they among all the sort of christian there be amongst the maronites a ancient company of christian call vulgar nostrane nazaritan of the sect of the nazarite more civil and harmless people than any of the rest their country be mount Lybanus as I write unto you heretofore but many of they dwell at Aleppo whereof some of they be cassise that be churchman some of they be cook and servant unto english merchant and other some artificer all of they live somewhat poor but they be more honest and true in their conversation then any of the rest especial at their first come from mount Lybanus to dwell in Aleppo and many during their continuance there if they be not corrupt by other wicked nation there dwell in who I observe more by experience than I hear of they or note in they when I be amongst they at mount Lybanus and especial for the manner of their marriage and how they honour the same they buy their wife of their father as other there dwell do but never see they until they come to be marry nor then neither until the marriage be solemnize betwixt they for there be a partition in the place where they meet to be marry and the man and his friend stand on the one side and the young woman and her friend on the other side where they may hear but not see one another until the cassy bid the young man put his hand through a hole in the wall and take his wife by the hand and while they have hand in hand the mother of the maid come with some sharp instrument make for the purpose and all to beprick the new marry man hand and make it bleed and if he let her hand go when he feel his hand smart they hold it for a sign that he will not love she but if he hold fast notwithstanding the smart and wring she hard by the hand until she cry rather than he will once shrink than he be count a love man and her friend be glad that they have bestow she on he and how they honour marriage above other I observe by the name of their first manchild for as amongst we the woman when they be marry lose their surname and be surname by the husband surname and child likewise so amongst they the father lose his name and be call by the name of his elder son in this manner I have know a nostrane who name be mou-se that be Moses who have a manchild name he Useph that be joseph and then be the father no more call mouse Moses but above Useph that be the father of joseph another who name be Useph name his elder son pher-iolla after which he be no more call Useph but above pher-iolla the father of pher-iolla another man call I^brael that be Gabriel his son at the time of baptism be name mouse he always after be call above mouse that be the father of Moses such a honour do they account it to be the father of a manchild these nostrane reverence their cassise great and kiss their hand wheresoever they meet liturgy read they yet be most of they altogether unlearned have only the knowledge of the syriac tongue wherein their liturgy be read they keep their feast at the same time as we do viz. Christmas Easter and Whitsuntide and at Christmas on the twelve day in the morning call Epiphanie their young man have a custom betimes in the morning to leap naked into the water I can never hear any reason of their so do but Uzansa de press the custom of their country and though it be then very cold yet they persuade themselves and other that then it be hot than at any other time and that the water than have a extraordinary virtue to wash away their sin on Monday in Easter week and Whitsun week these nostrane go with their cassise to the grave of the dead and there kneel down and burn incense and pray at every grave the Chelfalines be christian dwell upon the border of Persia between Mesopotamia and Persia at a place call chelfa these bring silk to Aleppo to sell. they be plain deal people if a man pay they money and by over-reckoning himself give they more than their due though there be but one piece over so soon as they perceive it though it be many day after they will bring it back again and restore it and think they shall never return safe into their country if they shall not make restitution thereof these people persuade themselves and report unto other that they dwell in that place which be call Eden whereinto Adam be put to keep it and dress it the Greek in Aleppo be very poor for they be there for the most part but broker or Eden bastage that be porter and many of their woman as light as water maintain their husband themselves and their family by prostitute their body to other and their own husband be oftentimes their pander or procurer to bring they customer but the Greek that live at Constantinople be many of they great merchant and very rich but exceed proud and sumptuous in apparel even the base of they and especial their woman who though they be but cobbler wife or poor artificer wife yet they go in gown of satin cobbler wife in satin gown and taffeta yea of cloth of silver and gold adorn with precious stone and many gem and jewel about their neck and hand they care not how they pinch their belly so that they may have fine apparel on their back and at the time of their marriage the woman condition with their husband to find they decent apparel and convenient diet and bring they before their patriarch of Constantinople to confirm it which if it be not perform accord if they complain to their patriarch they be divorce present and she take a he instance of one Sophia which for brevity be omit other man to her husband better able to maintain she and he may marry another woman if he please and both at Constantinople Aleppo and other place of Turkey where there be traffic and trade of merchant it be no rare matter for popish christian of sundry other country to cut cabin as they call it that be to take any woman of that country where they sojourn Turkish woman only except for it be death for a Christian to meddle with they and when they have buy they and enroll they in the cadies book to use they as wife so long as they sojourn in that country and maintain they gallant to the consume of their wealth diminish of their health and endanger of their own soul and when they depart out of that country they shake off these their sweetheart and leave they to shift for themselves and their child and this they account no sin or at leastwise such a sin as may be wash away with a little holy water and these be the virtue which many christian learn by sojourn long in heathen country every bashaw who have government over other in a city or country tyrannise over those which be under their regiment and sometime strangle sometime behead and sometime put unto terrible torture those who offend yea oftentimes without offence only because they be rich and have fair house the bashaw will lay to their charge such thing as he himself know to be untrue and put they to death that he may seize upon his good there be a sheriff or a green-head in Aleppo who they account Mahomet kindred who offend the bashaw and brave he in term as though he dare not punish he he cause one of his officer to go with he home and when he come before his own door open in the street to break both his leg and arm and there let he lie and no man dare find fault or give he food or physician or chirurgeon come to he or wife or servant take he into house but there he lie all day and shall so have continue until he have die for hunger or dog eat he have not his friend give money to the bashaw to have his throat cut to rid he out of his pain and this be a common punishment amongst they and sometime for small offence they will lay a man down on his back and hoist up his foot and with a cudgel give they three hundred or four hundred blow on the sole of their foot whereby many be lame and some they set on a sharp stake naked which come from his fundament up to his mouth if he find not favour to have his throat cut soon and some be ganch in this manner they be draw up by a rope fasten about their arm to the top of a gazouke or gibbet full of hook and let downward again and on what part soever any hook take hold by that they hang until they die for hunger and some in like sort be draw over a gibbet and they be compass about the naked waste with a small cord the cord be draw by two man to make they draw up their breath and still pull straight and straight until they be so narrow in the waste that they may easy be cut off by the middle at one blow and then the upper part be let down on a hot grid-iron and there sear up to keep they in sense and feel of pain so long as be possible and the neither part be throw to the dog etc. they who they call francke or freeman live in great security amongst they than their own people by reason that they be govern by consul of their own nation and those consul also be back by ambassador for the same nation which be always leiger at Constantinople and when their consul abroad be offer wrong they write unto the ambassador how and by who they be wrong and then the ambassador procure from the great Turk commandment to the bashaw of Aleppo to redress their wrong and punish such as offend they otherwise there be no dwell for franc amongst they but they shall be use like slave by every slave and notwithstanding their consul and ambassador to yet they be oftentimes abuse by turk both in word and deed in word they revile they as the egyptian do the israelite and call they gour that be infidel and Cupec that be dog and Canzier that be hog and by many other odious and reproachful name and though they strike they yet dare they not strike again leave they lose their hand or be worse use they also oftentimes make Auenias of they that be false accusation and suborn false witness to confirm it to be true and no christian word will be take against a Turk for they account we infidel and call themselves musselman that be true believer this misery abroad will make we love our own country the better when we come thither and that be the best lesson which I have learn in my travel that be the contempt of the world and saint Paul lesson phil. 4. 11. in whatsoever state I be therewith to be content oh how happy be you in England if you know your own happiness but as the prodigal son until he be pinch with penury abroad never consider the plenty of his father house so many in England know not their own felicity because they do not know the misery of other but if they be here in this heathen country they will know what it be to live in a christian commonwealth under the government of a godly king who rule by law and not by lust where there be plenty and peace and preach of the gospel and many other godly blessing which other want and GOD long continue his mercy to our noble king james and his whole realm and give we grace as far to excel other nation in thankfulness as we do in happiness and thus for present I commend you to the most gracious protection of the almighty Jehovah beseech he if it be his will to send we a joyful meeting both in this world and in the world to come amen part of another letter of master WILLIAM biddulph from jerusalem worshipful and my singular good friend I be now by the providence of GOD at for the love I bear to you and delight I conceive in this famous place where our sweet saviour Christ vouchsafe once his bless bodily presence I can not but remember you with some salutation from hence have such choice of messenger by reason of the great concourse of people unto this place at this present from sundry place of Christendom to transport my letter unto you nothing doubt but that as my former letter which I have heretofore write unto you both from Aleppo and other place concern my former voyage and such thing as by diligent observation I note in my travel be acceptable unto you so that this shall be much more acceptable both in regard of the place from whence it come as also of the matter subject herein contain be my voyage from Aleppo in Syria Comagena to jerusalem undertake this present year 1600. not move as pilgrim with any superstitious devotion to see relic or worship such place as they account holy but as traveller and merchant occasion by dearth and sickness pestilence and famine in the city where we sojourn which two be such fellowlike companion that the grecian distinguish they but by one letter call the pestilence (@) (@) (@) (@) (@) and the famine (@) (@) (@) (@) (@) by reason whereof all traffic be hinder and those merchant who they call frank or freeman either remove to other place or such as stay in the city cause their gate to be shut up and come not abroad until Sol enter into Leo which be usual the twelve or thirteen the plague cease by instuence of the heaven day of july at which time the plague still cease in this place though it be never so great and all that be then sick amend and such as then come abroad need not fear any danger the turk moor arabian and other mahometan never remove for fear of any sickness nor refuse any man company infect therewith for they say every man fortune be write in his forehead and that they shall not die before their time not know what it be to tempt God and to refuse ordinary mean but in this interim from the begin of this sickness which be in march until the expect and undoubted end when the sun enter into Leo we who name be subscribe for cause above mention take our voyage from Aleppo towards jerusalem have letter of commendation from Venice consul and sundry other of the chief italian merchant to their Padres at jerusalem for our kind usage there with liberty of conscience dom. 1600. the nine of march after dinner we set forth guard with janissary and accompany with sundry english italian and french merchant who in kindness ride with we seven or eight mile to bring we on the way and then return to Aleppo but most of our english merchant bring we to cane toman ten mile from Aleppo where we make merry cane toman with such good cheer as we bring with we for there be nothing to be have for money but goat milk whereof we have as much as we will here we purpose to have sleep all night but have no other bed but the hard ground with lacobs pillow a good hard stone under our head unaccustomed to such down bed we can not sleep but spend the time in honest mirth until it be past midnight and then our friend take their leave of we and return towards Aleppo and we proceed in our journey towards jerusalem the night be dark and the way dangerous and thievish our janissary byram bashaw will we every one to take a match light in our hand and to whirl it about that the fire may be see the further to terrify the thief leave they shall surprise we on the sudden and when we come to suspicious place as cave rock barn or odd cottage in the way our janissary use to ride before and as fowler beat upon bush for bird so he with his lance will strike and beat upon such place lest wild arab which lie lurk in such place shall steal upon we on the sudden when the day appear our way be pleasant and comfortable unto we until we come to a village call saracoope whither we come about noon the ten of march. and Saracoope^ because our seisenar or Sumptor horse which carry provision for man and horse as the custom of the country be be tire and we ourselves also for want of sleep the night pass weary and hungry we be constrain to lodge there all night on the hard ground by our horse heel in a old cane distant from cane toman eight and twenty mile the eleven of march betimes in the morning we depart from saracoope and come betimes in the afternoon to a fine village call Marrah where there be a very fair new Marrah cane build by amrath common call m^rat Chillabee sometime Defterdare that be treasurer of Aleppo and afterward of Damascus who for the refuge of traveller and their protection against thief build a stately strong cane like unto manner of their cane leaden hall in London or rather the exchange in London where there be fair upper room for great man in their travel and the neither room be for ordinary traveller and their horse but in hot weather the best make choice to sleep on the ground in low room rather than in their chamber the founder hereof also ordain that all traveller that way shall have their entertainment there of his cost he allow they bread Pillaw and mutton which our janissary accept off but we scorn relief from the turk without money send unto the village where beside our own provision which we bring with we we have also other good thing for money Marrah be distant from saracoope four and twenty mile the twelve of march be a very rainy day yet we travel all the forenoon until we come to a village call lacmine which a far off make show of a very fair village but when we come thither we find it so ruinous that there be not one house able to shroud we from the extremity of the shower the inhabitant thereof have forsake it and flee into the mountain to dwell for fear of the ay (...) ies of Damascu^ who travel that way use to take from they not only victual for themselves and provender for their horse without money but whatsoever thing else they find in their house only there be a little church or chapel wretel ed slavery in good preparation wherinto for a little money we obtain leave to enter ourselves with our horse and carriage and there we bring out our victual and refresh ourselves and bait our horse and rest until it leave rain after the shower while our horse be prepare we walk into the field near unto the church and see many poor people gather mallow and miserable poverty three leave grass and ask they what they do with it and they answer that it be all their food and that they boil it and do eat it then we take pity on they and give they bread which they receive very joyful and bless God that there be bread in the world and say they have not see any bread the space of many month the shower cease we ride from this chapel and village of lack money I shall have say lacmin but may say lack man and money too and ride forward until we come unto a village or town call Tyaba where because it be near night we desire to lodge but can not be admit into any house for any money whereupon our chief janissary byram bashaw go into a house and offer to pull man woman and child out of the house that we may bring in our horse and lodge there ourselves but when we see what pitiful lamentation they make we entreat our janissary either to persuade they for money or to let they alone and understand that there be a fair city in our way ten mile off we five with our janissary be well horse ride thither and leave our carriage with the rest of our company at Tyaba to come to we Tyaba betimes in the morning this city be now common call aman but of old it be call Hamath 2. king 17. here we lodge in a fair cane but on the cold ground and upon the hard stone and think aman. ourselves well provide for that we have a house over our head to keep we dry Hamath be from Marrah about five and thirty thereof and buy bread and wine of Charrah the christian there dwell it be inhabit by Greek and turk but govern by turk only there be but one church in the town which be dedicate to saint Nicholas by the christian who first build it but both christian and turk pray therein the christian on the one side or i will of the church and the turk on the other but the christian be overrule by the turk and constrain to find they oil to their lamp in the church for the Turk not only burn lamp in their church every night but during the whole time of their lent they beset the battlement of their steeple round about with lamp but when their Lent be end they burn lamp in their steeple only once a week and that be on Thursday at night which be the Eeve before their sabbath after we have refresh ourselves here half the day be not yet spend we ride from hence to a poor village call Nebecke or as they pronounce it Ne^^keh where we lodge in a old cane distant from hassia seven and twenty mile and understand at this place that the way that we be to pass on the morrow Nebecke be full of arab and that two day before many man be find in the way kill by they we fear to go any further yet meet with company contrary to expectation march the seventeen we go forward and see no house nor company all the day long beside ourselves until we come to a village call Cotifey where we lodge in a very stately new cane C^tifey build by Synan bashaw and not altogether finish this cane do far exceed that at Marrah before mention for hereunto be adjoin a fair new church and a Bazar that be a market sleep on the hard ground as most man that travel that way be wont to do the eighteen of march from Cotifey we have not much more than twenty mile to Damascus dangerous way the first ten mile be a desert and dangerous way and we hardly escape danger for a arabian horseman see we come stand as a spy in our way to view our strength and mark every one of we very narrow and what weapon we have and have many fruitful village fine river and pleasant garden thereon at our entrance into this plain or valley ride down a hill we behold the prospect of Damascus ten mile off whither we come about two of the clock in the afternoon and take up our lodging in the middle of the city at a cane call in morisco cane Nebbe that be the cane of the prophet but by the turk cane Haramin where we hire three weary body the nineteenth and twenty of march we stay at Damascus to rest ourselves and see the city Damascus be a most ancient city and as Esay speak of it in his time the head of aram be Damascus Damascus isa. 7. 8. so Damascus be the chief city of Syria to this day the situation thereof be most pleasant be build on a plain ground strong wall about and a strong castle therein with many fine river run on every side of it especial Abanah and pharpar mention 2. king 5. which now be divide into many head the turk say that their prophet the pleasant situation Mahomet be once at Damascus and that when he see the pleasant situation of it and behold the stately prospect of it excel all other that ever he see before refuse to enter into the city lest the pleasantness thereof shall ravish he and move he there to settle a earthly paradise and hinder his desire of the heavenly paradise it have also many pleasant orchard and garden round about the city and some way for the space of a mile and more about the city there be many orchard and great variety of first-fruit some call Adam apple and Adam fig and sundry other strange fruit Damascus be call by the turk shame and they call it the garden of Turkey because there be no place in all the turk dominion especial in Syria that yield such abundance of Fruit. here we stay two day and three night to rest ourselves and see the city and dwell there ever since the time of Paul and therefore may keep a memorial of the very place but to let the place pass the thing itself we know to be true he show we also the house of ananias which be under the ground whereinto we be lead down a pair of stair from the street as it be into a cellar and the door be unlock we enter with candle into the place where we see two dark chamber where a man can see to read in the day time without candle here they say he live in secret for fear of the jew many christian come thither to see that place with a coal write their name on the wall and there be so many name there already that there be scarce room for any other to set his name some of they report Damascus to be build in the place where kain kill his brother Abel and some say it be near it and offer to bring we to the place but we refuse they take upon they also at Damascus to demonstrate the place where saint George be bury saint George so they do likewise at Aleppo but I think the one to be as true as the other there be a fine town near unto Damascus about two or three mile distant on the side of a hill call Salhia from whence a man may behold the prospect of the city of Damascus most pleasant Salbia with the garden and pleasant place about it at Damascus we meet many thousand turk go on pilgrimage towards Mecha in Arabia pilgrimage to Mecha to visit Mahomet sepulchre as they usual do every year about their byram time for they hold that whosoever once in his life time shall not go on pilgrimage to Mecha to see the sepulchre of their prophet shall never enter into paradise and therefore some of they go thither often in their life time partly for devotion and partly to buy merchandise for there be bring thither at that time of the year great store of commodity from India Persia and other place and none may buy or sell there but mahometans and it be forbid to all christian upon pain of death to come near Mecha within five mile partly lest they shall mar their market but chief lest they shall see their folly or rather madness in worship a iron sepulchre after the sight whereof many of their old man which think never to come thither again use to pull out both their eye after they have see so holy a sight and whosoever say they die in his pilgrimage thither or return from thence be sore to get to heaven present and they that have be there but once be always after call hogy that be pilgrim and be call by that name in this manner if his name before be Mahomet hogy he be at his return call hogie Mahomet if before Mustapha he be always after call hogie Mustapha etc. and they that have be often at Mecha and return again be call great hogy and every year when the caravan of pilgrim return from Mocha he that have be there often be call the great hogie and be great honour of they all for he ride before they all in more stately apparel than they with flower and garland about his horse and when they come near any great city the chief man in the city ride forth to meet he and bring he into the city with great solemnity they false affirm that this their temple at Mecha in Arabia be build by Abraham and they prepare themselves with great care to go to worship there than many christian do when they come to the lord a angell-devill supper for they disburden their heart of all hatred and malice and reconcile themselves one to another etc. otherwise they hold that all their labour be lose and that they shall be never awhit the better for their pilgrimage but if they forgive one another and repent they for their former sin they think there to obtain full remission of all their sin and that at their return they be pure and without spot march twenty one we depart from the city of Damascus and about five or six mile from the city pass by a village call Daria near unto which we see a great multitude of man Daria woman and child on their knee in the high way and by that time they have end their devotion we draw so near as to salute they and ask what they be it be tell we that they be all christian of sundry nation viz. armenians Greek Chelfalines Nostranes and sundry other who go to jerusalem to visit and worship the holy place there we ask further what they mean to fall on their knee in that place they answer we that it be the place where * * fur or Sauli libere pauli Paul be convert and that it be their custom when they travel that place of Paul conversion way to fall on their knee and pray unto God to convert they they be in number at the least four or five hundred people there be a greek patriarch and a armenian bishop in their company many of they know we have see we in Aleppo and salute we by our name we ride a while in company together and lodge all together that night at a cane call Sassa distant from Damascus six and twenty mile Sassa march twenty two we ride before the rest of the company our way that we travel all this day be exceed bad rocky waterish and barren call Arabia Petrea where our horse Arabia Petrea oftentimes stick fast in the puddle and miry place and sometime ready to break their own leg and their rider neck among rock and stone it be neither pleasant go on foot nor ride this way for there be no path nor even ground but huge stone and rock so near together that our horse can go but a footpace and oftentimes meet with such marsh and ill way quagmire that we be constrain to go far about before we can find better way to pass over it be also exceed cold in this place always in respect of other place in that great cold country for there be neither tree nor house nor high hill to keep away the violence and force of the wind the caravans that travel usual that way betwixt Damascus and Egypt say that this day journey trouble they more than all the rest and that they never pass by that way but they leave two or three of their camel behind they some misfortune or other befall unto they we see also in sundry place this way the carcase of many dead camel which have miscarry amongst the rock it be also a very thievish way full of wild arab yet by the providence of God we come safe that day to Conetra where we lodge in a good cane distant from sassa eight and twenty mile in a Bazar like unto a cloister adjoin to the cane we take pleasure to walk up and walk wonder at down some few turn which the turk behold wonder at we for it be not their custom in those hot country to walk up and down as we do in cold country but to sit still on the ground like bruit beast and one of they come unto we and ask we what we mean to walk up and down in such sort and whether we be out of our way or out of our wit if your way say he lie towards the upper end of the cloister why come you downward and if at the neither end why go you back again it seem no less strange unto they to see a christian with a cut doublet and they call he fool and ask he what cut doublet he mean to make hole in his coat for they neither cut nor pink any of their garment but wear they all plain spare for no cost to guard they with lace of silver and gold if they be able and such as wear long hair on their head the turk call Slovens and account long hair they savage beast for they themselves wear no hair on their head at all but shave they every week once and keep they warm with a turban of white Shash make of cotton wool which they never uncover in their salutation to any man but bow their head with their hand on their breast but if a man have a fair long beard they reverence he and long beard say he be a wise man and a honourable personage but if they have no beard at all they call they if they be young bardasses that be sodomitical boy but if they be man grow and have no beard they call they fool and man of no credit and some of they refuse to buy or sell with such and say they have no wit and that they will not believe they etc. the three and twenty of march we have a more pleasant way for the first ten mile we ride through the field and a very pleasant park but when we come out of this park or Forrest pleasant park we be somewhat trouble partly by reason of the bad way and partly by bad people in the way the people do more trouble we then the way for there sit amongst the rock leave the mountain behind they yet still they call this mount tabor in italian santo that be the holy mountain as if there be some inherent holiness in the mountain and two day after we have be there come a jesuit and two friar with a young gentleman of Paris in France who be a Protestant and some other company with they who have a desire to ascend conference betwixt a jesuite and a Protestant to the top of this holy mountain and go all together until they be weary which be at the foot of the mountain and in the heat of the day wherefore the french gentleman say he will stay for they there until they return but be himself already weary and will go no high the jesuit and Frier reprove he and call he fool and tell he he merit-monger do not know what he may merit by go to the top of that holy mountain merit say the gentleman what may I merit thou may merit say they fifty year pardon the gentleman to break a jest with they ask they whether he may merit fifty year pardon for the time past or for the time to come if say he for the time past I be not so old for he be but twenty two year of age if for the time to come he do not think he shall live so long they answer he if he do not live so long he may give the year which remain to his friend yet can they not persuade he to go up any high when we have see enough this mount return again to the castle with good stomach to our
