spanish ambassador relate the antiquity of Persepolis and some thing by he observe in persia. chap. 11 a letter from don garcia Silua FIGVEROA ambassador from PHILIP the three king of Spain to the persian write at Spahan or Hispahan 1619. to the marquis of Bedmar touch matter of persia. weary with travel both by sea and land but otherwise well I come at length from ormuz into persia. which have wander over at the king appointment I go to Hispahan where I endure a tedious irksome delay be even tire with so unpleasant a life as I here lead for whatsoever writer report of that great and ancient monarchy of the achaemenides this be my opinion that there be nothing in all this country to be find so good but that it come short of the least commodity in our Europe and beside that every thing here be so cross to our fashion that I be without all converse with man here be not so much as any book the read whereof may somewhat refresh a man mind in so great solitariness except a few pamphlet entreat of holy confession and navarr sum which the monk of saint Augustine use Hispahan be the noble city of this kingdom and though it lie but in one and thirty degree and Hispahan a half of northerly latitude yet by reason of the subtle pierce air the cold be sharp then by the climate or situation one will imagine now in all this kingdom you can scarce see any print of antiquity no antiquity all the house be build of unburned brick or earth ram up between two board too slight stuff to last many day much less many year notwithstanding there be yet remain most of those huge wild building of the castle and palace of Persepolis so much celebrate in the monument of ancient writer these frame do the arabian Persepolis and her remayne^ and Persian in their own language call Chilminara which be as much as if you shall say in spanish or Alcoranes for so they call those high narrow round steeple which the arabian have in their mesquite this rare yea and only monument of the world which far exceed all the rest of the world miracle that we have see or hear off show itself to they that come to this city from the town of Xiria and stand about a league from the river Bradamir in time past call Araxis not that that part Media from the great Armenia whereof often mention be make by Quintus Curtius Diodorus and Plutarch which author do point we out the situation of Persepolis and do almost lead we unto it by the hand the largeness fairness and long-lasting matter of those pillar appear by the twenty which be yet leave of alike fashion which with other remaynder of those stately pile do move admiration in the mind of beholder and can but with much labour and at leisure be lay open but since it be your lordship hap to live now at Venice where you may see some resemblance of the thing which I be about to write of I will brief tell you that most of the picture of man that engrave in marble do seel the front the side and stately part of this building be deck with a very comely clothing and clad in the same fashion which the venetian magnifico go in that be in gown down to the heel with wide sleeve with round flat cap their hair spread to the shoulder and notable long beard you may see in these table some man sit with great majesty in certain lofty chair such as use to be with we in the quire and chapter-house of cathedral church appoint for the seat of the chief prelate the foot be support with a little footstool neat make about a hand high and which be very worthy of wonder in so diverse dress of so many man as be engrave in these table none Portugal captain succeed in their place and in their amity and commerce with the quiteve king of those country in those country of Sofala be many first-fruit as pomegranate tree which bear all the year some green some ripe some in flower they have also figtree which yield black fig all the year most excellent orange limb vine which bear twice a year in januarie and july Ananas indian fig which yield great branch of fig as great as cucumber yellow when they be ripe and sweet of send sometime seventy fig be see on one cluster like a bunch of grape and a man can scarce lift they from the ground they have great ground of sugarcane alongst the river husband by the cafres not for sugar but to eat for they want ingenios and be a great part of their sustenance they have many and great palmtree which yield infinite and wine they have store of Guinnie wheat and rice many inhame a very great root yield broad leaf and better in taste then potato fitch and other pulse in much variety in strain out the oil and eat the rest with their wheat instead of butter innumerable hen very good and cheap hog goat cow wild beast dear and wild swine be there ten hen be sell for two teston 2s. 6d and up in the country eighteen at the price they make oil of which burn clear than that of the olive in the realty of grow little tree on the top of hill and rock which the most part of the year be dry without leaf and greenness but have this property that if one cut off a bough and put it into water in the space of ten hour a strange tree it spring and flourish with green leaf but draw it out of the water as soon as it be dry it remain again as it be before the cafres say that though this will be gather ten year yet after all that time put into water it wil^ flourish and continue green this wood be ground and give to drink in water be good to staunch flux of blood the cafres call it Murgodao another will they call which signify the dung of a man have the another name of that send so noy some that none can endure it the same be in India the tree like a thorn tree they say it have virtue against the air or blast and therefore many person wear it in string like bead tie to the arm next the skin special child along the river of Sofala in two place wild and desert grow orange and lemon which every one may gather that will wherewith they lade boat and sell they for almost nothing to the inhabitant of the fortress which fill barrel and pot with the juice and the same lemon salt and send they for India where they be much esteem and eat with Rice the bread bread of m (...) or portugal drink common palme-wine the cafres wine of their wheat or mays which they make strong and tipsy @. 2 of QVITEVE king of that country with the strange custom observe in those part in court city and country the king of these part be of curl hair a gentile which worship nothing nor have any knowledge of God yea rather he carry himself as God of his country and so be hold and reverence of his vassal he be call quiteve a title royal and no proper name which they exchange for this so soon as they become king the quiteve have more than one hundred woman all within door amongst which one or two be as his queen the rest as concubine many of they be his own aunt cousin sister and daughter which he no less use say that his son by they be true heir of the kingdom without mixture of other blood when the quitove die his queen must die with he to do he service in the other world who accord at the instant of his death take a poison which they call lucasse and die therewith the successor succeed as well to the quiteve manner of succession and coronation the woman as the state none else but the king may upon pain of death marry his sister or daughter this successor be common one of the elder son of the decess king and of his great woman or queen and if the elder be not sufficient than the next or if none of they be fit his brother of whole blood the king common while he live make the choice and train up he to affair of state to who he destiny the succession while I live there say the king have above thirty son and yet show more respect to his brother a wise man then to any of they all honour he as apparent heir the same day the king die he be carry to a hill where all the king be inter and early see after of break the bow the next morning he who the decess have name his successor go to the king house where the king woman abide in expectation and by their consent he enter the house and seat himself with the principal of they in a public hall where the king be wont to sit to hear cause in a place draw with curtain or cover with a cloth that none may see the king nor the woman with he and thence he send his officer which go through the city and proclaim festival to the new king who be now quiet possess of the king house with the woman of the king decess and that all shall go and acknowledge he for their king which be do by all the great man then in court and the noble of the city who go to the palace now solemn guard and enter into the hall by licence of the officer where the new king abide with his woman enter some and some creep on the ground till they come to the middle of the hall and thence speak to the new king give he due obeisance without see he or his woman the king make answer from within and accept their service and after that draw the curtain and show himself to they whereat all of they clap their hand and then turn behind the curtain and go forth creep on the ground as they come in and when they be go other enter and do in like sort in this ceremony the great part of the day be spend with feast music and dance through the city the next day the king send his officer through the kingdom to declare this his succession and that all shall come to the court to see he break the bow sometime there be many competitor and then he succeed who the woman admit into the king house for none may enter by law without their leave nor can be king without peaceable entrance forceable entry forfeit his women-elector right and title by bribe therefore and other way they seek to make the woman on their side near the kingdom of quiteve be another of law and custom like thereto where the reign both which be sometime but one kingdom while I be in Sofala the the like custom be incurable sick of a leprosy declare his successor and poison himself which also be the custom there if any king have any deformity in his person the name successor seek admittance of the woman but they much distaste he have secret send by night for another prince who they better like as more valiant and better-beloved who they admit and assemble themselves with he in the public hall and cause proclamation to be make to the people of his succession the other who they have reject flee for fear of his life and be mighty assemble a great power and by force enter the king house but this be strange to all who therefore forsake he and stick to he who the woman have choose whereupon the other flee and no more lift up his head before the new king begin to govern he send for all the chief in the kingdom to come to the court and see he break the king bow which be all one with take possession of the ceremony of break the bow kingdom in those court be a custom then also to kill some of those lord or great man say that they be necessary for the service of the decess king whereupon they kill those of cruel service who they stand in fear or doubt or who they hate in stead of who they make and erect new lord this custom cause such as fear themselves to flee the land. ancient the king be wont to drink poison in any grievous disaster as in a contagious disease or natural impotency lameness the loss of their foretooth or other deformity say that king ought to have no defect which if it happen it be honour for he to die and go to better himself in that better life in which he shall be whole perfect but the quiteve which reign while I be there will not follow his predecessor herein but have lose one of his foretooth send to proclaim through his whole kingdom that one of his tooth be fall out ill custom well break and that if that they may not be ignorant when they see he want it his predecessor be such fool for such cause to kill themselves he will not do so but await his natural death hold his life necessary to conserve his estate against his enemy which example he will commend to posterity if the cafar have a suit and seek to speak with the king they creep to the place where he be have prostrate themselves at the entrance and look not on he all the while they great observance the like be use in japan to lie prostrate and not look on he speak but lie on one side clap their hand all the time a rite of obsequiousness in those part and then have finish they creep out of the door as they come in for no Cafar may enter on foot to speak to the king nor eye he in speak except the familiar and particular friend of the king. the portugal enter on their foot but unshod and be near the king prostrate themselves lie on one side almost sit and without look on he speak to he at every four word clap their hand accord to the custom both cafres and portugal be entertain by he with wine of mays or their wheat call pombe which they must drink although against stomach not to contemn the king bounty whence the portugal have have some trouble and be force to stay in the town without leave to return home with great expense of time and charge every September the quiteve at the change of the moon go from Zimbaohe his city to a high hill to perform obit or exequy to his predecessor there bury with great troop exequy to the dead king both of the city and other part of the kingdom call up therefore as soon as they be ascend they eat and drink their pombe the king beginning till they be all drink continue that eat and drink eight day one of which they call Pemberar of a kind of tilt exercise then use in this feast the king and his noble clothe themselves in their best somewhat resemble that which Aeneas perform to Anchises silk and Cotten clothes which they have with many thrum like carpet fringe wrought therein hang down on the eye and face as a horse foretop they tie about the head a large ribbon and divide into two part they run one against another on foot with bow and arrow in their hand which they shoot upward that none be hurt and thus make a thousand careere and feat till they be tire and can stir and they which hold out long be account the proper valiant man and be therefore reward with the prize propound Gaspar de melo captain of Sofala in my time cause to make a large ribbon with great fringe of silk and gold and send it with other piece of price to the quiteve who most esteem that ribbon for this pember purpose after this eight day festival they spend two day or three in mourn and then the devil enter into one of the company say he be the soul of the decease king father of the devil tyranny and oracle present to who those exequy be perform and that he come to speak to his son the Cafar thus possess fall down on the ground in a ill plight and be distract the devil speak by his as some report I believe for certain that this Caphar nation be the most brutish and barbarous in the world no form of religion neither worship God nor any idol nor have image church or sacrifice or person dedicate to religion and be hard to be convert either to christian or moor they hold the immortality of the soul and have a confuse knowledge that there be a great God who they call Molungo but they pray not to he nor do commend themselves to he when they suffer any necessity or sterility they have recourse to their king strong believe that he be the king in divine reputation able to give they all thing which they desire and that he can obtain all thing of the dead his predecessor with who he seem to have conference whereupon they sue to the king for rain if they want it and for seasonable harvest time and always when they thus petition he they bring he great present which he receive and bid they return home in a good hour for he will have care of their request to satisfy the same and though they see themselves often frustrate yet continue they to spend time and cost in such petition till rain or other their suit happen think that though he grant not at first yet by their importunity as he also for gain tell they that he have do it at last they observe certain festival rest from labour except dance appoint by the king holy day strict keep they not know when or why they call such day that be soul of saint depart in who honour they keep they on one of these day a Portugal in that city Zimbaohe which be pass to where the gold mine be cause a cow to be kill at his house call Calano which be a vessel of water make bitter with certain herb which they put into it whereof they give the accuse to drink say that if he be innocent he shall drink it all off at one gulp without any stay and cast it all up again at once without any harm if guilty he shall not be able to get down one drop without gargle and choke there have be see many experiment of all these the well know in Sofala the cafres be black as pitch curl and wear their head full of horn make of the same haire-fashion in horn hair which stand up like a distaff wear slender piece of wood within their lock to uphold they without bend without they tie they with a ribbon make of the bark of a herb which while it be fresh stick like glue and dry be like a stick with this they bind their hair in bundle from the bottom to the top of each bundle make a horn hold herein great pride and gallantry strive to excel each other and mock they which want they say they be like woman for as the male wild beast have horn which the female want so do these savage beast also the quiteve have herein a fashion which none may imitate of four horn one of a span long on the mould of the head like a unicorn and three of half a span one on the neck at each ear another all upright to the top for their horn sake they have no hat nor headcovering amongst they the apparel of the king and chief man be fine cotton or silk gird to they and hang almost to the knee and another great call Machiras which the cafres weave cast over the shoulder like a cloak wherewith they go muffle let it hang on the left hand to the ground esteem great gravity and majesty in a long train the rest of the body be naked they go all barefoot and the vulgar go naked both man and woman without shame the better sort of they wear a monkey skin hang down from the girdle like a smith apron and the woman likewise but the cafres which trade with the portugal wear a cover to the knee they have no occupation but smith which make azagay occupation spade hatchet halfe-sword weaver which make Cotton clothes for Machiras the woman make they but improper their office be ordinary to dig and weed and sow man more love their lubberly ease few help their wife a spade be as usual with their woman as a rock with our spinster the man now and then hunt for wild beast other while dance and sing and therefore poor the quiteve make some royal hunt with three or four thousand man in the desert the tartar do the like and the scot also as I have hear in the further north of this island near the city encircle all the beast in that compass tiger lion ounce elephant buffal dear wild swine and the rest drive they together and then set on their dog with cry arrow and azagaye pursue and kill what they can then may they kill the lion which at other time by the quiteve prohibition be a deadly offence because he be entitle great lion. after this they eat in the same place with great jollity but the most they carry home and * * as Bacon and martinmas beet in England house of cafar household and food hang it for the king and for themselves their house be round of unhewn timber cover with straw like a thatch country house which they remove at pleasure their good be a pan in which they boy^e their wheat two spade to dig one bow and arrow a Mat whereon they lie which they make of rush and common they sleep on the ground if it be cold they make a fire in the midst of the house lie all about it like cac so beggarly and brutish be the life if that be life of the cafres their food be common maize pulse fruit sugarcane fish and all kind of beast which they kill in the desert as monkey dog cat rat snake lizard crocodile all flesh Rice they sow rather to sell the portugal then to eat prefer their maize they steep two day in water a peck or thereabouts which in that space grow forth and then the water be put out they let it dry two or three hour and be well dry wine ho^ make they stamp it till it settle into a mass which they do in a great mortar as high as a man middle call Cuni by they by the portugal Pilano after this they set a great earthen vessel on the fire half full of water whereon when it seethe they put in above half the peck of mais-meale by little and little still stir it as when man make pottage and after it seethe a little they take the vessel of the fire and put in the rest of the say mass stir they together till their pombe be make which be let stand two day and then they drink it many of they neither eat nor drink aught else but live only hereof if it stand four or five day it become vinegar and the sour the more tipsy they say that it make they strong in some place grow certain reed which every second or three year have great ear like rye of which they gather store and be good sustenance in all there grow a certain herb which they sow call Bangue the straw and leaf whereof they cut and be well dry stamp they to powder and hereof they eat a handful and then drink water and so sustain themselves many day and if they eat much it make they drunken like to wine all these cafres before they go about any business of import as journey merchandise or sow they cast lot to divine of the success a thing use likewise to inquire of thing lot and divination steal or lose and in all doubtful case and there to give credit as we do to the gospel these lot be little round stick flat and bore through the midst less than table-man call always carry about they file on a string to use upon any occasion of doubt cast they like dice so many time for want of they they divine by stroke or line which they draw on the ground some be great witch and consult with the devil so prone to it witch that they be prohibit by the king that none shall use this witchcraft without his licence in pain of death and confiscation of wife child and good half to the king and half to the informer and yet many be such secret and all will be if they can the same penalty punishments be to thief and to adulterer it be lawful for any man to slay any of these three sort take in the fact or if any listen not to kill he which by witchcraft adultery or robbery have wrong he he may sell he or do with he what he please as his own chattel and they call the condemn such a man witch thief or adulterer the loss of good to the king be common for any fault amongst they the cafres buy of the parent their wife for cow clothes or otherwise accord to marriage their ability and therefore they which have many daughter be rich if any mislike his wife he may return she to he that sell she but with loss of the price pay and the parent may sell she again to another husband the wife have no liberty to forsake her husband the ceremony of marriage be dance and feast of the neighbour every invite guest bring his present of meal Inhames fitch or other victual for that day expense he which be able may have two wife but few be able to maintain they except the great man which have many but one be principal the rest as handmaid some of they live like wild beast and when they be near time of travel they go to the wilderness or brutish travel untilled place and there go up and down receive the savour of that wild place which cause to they quick delivery they after their delivery wash themselves and their child in a lake or river and then return to their house with they in their arm without swaddle they neither have they there wherewithal to do it or such custom nor have any bed to lie on but a Mat or lock of straw when any of they die the kindred friend and neighbour assemble and bewail he all that day in which he die and the same day lay he on a Mat or seat where he die and if funeral he have any cloth or garment bury he therein otherwise naked they make a hole in the desert or wild untilled place and set by he a vessel of water and a little maize to eat and drink they say in his journey to the other life and without more ceremony cover he with earth and lay on the hole the Mat or the Chai e in which he be bring to burial where they consume without any more respect although they be new for they hold it ominous to touch that Mat or seat in which one die as bode death or some ill the kindred and friend lament he eight day from morning to noon and a hour at sun set which mourn they perform lamentation with dance and dreary song and speech all together on foot in a round circle and now and then one of the stander by enter into the middle of the circle and make a turn or two and then take his place again and after the mourn finish they all sit in a round and eat and drink for the soul of the decease who they mourn for and then return home the next kindred be at this cost these cafar be cruel and inhuman to one another if any of they be sick and have no inhumanity famine and beggary wife kindred or friend to look to he no other Cafar will give he any thing but let he starve and die forlese without take on he any compassion although he see he ready to perish with hunger of which sickness most of they die through miserable poverty and improvident and prodigality and when they do the most some friend take the forlorn man carry he to the wild uncultivate place and lay he at some bush or at the foot of a tree with a little vessel of water to drink and a little maize to eat if he can and so leave he till he die without more care of he and although some Cafar pass by and see he groan or lament yet will he give he no help and this brutishness be so natural to they that some when they feel themselves deadly sick take order to be so carry to the wilderness and lay at the foot of a bush and their dye like beast in Mocaranga some parent as black as pitch have white goldi-locked child like fleming white cafres while I be in the country the quiteve nourish one white child in the court as a strange prodigy the Manamotapa keep two other white cafres with like admiration the cafres say such be the child of the devil beget of black woman by with any disaster they leave all these hole open they be strong and able to endure labour they go naked both man and woman and when they be apparel it be with a monkey skin or of some other beast from the body mean while in torture and when they be at the point of death devilish cruelty thrust a stake through their neck other look on with undaunted countenance which be to undergo the same butchery the king of bigub and also desire baptism which both as he of Guinala be beafare Bigub have three king vassal five and three beafare king bijag the Guinalan seven although the bijagi have take six form thus be the blossom of his hope blast and he haste away to his former friend it will not be amiss to relate the funeral mourning worthy mourning and funeral amongst numerous issue by reason of their polygamy the mane Farma the king of the Logui have seventy two son and fifty daughter so that his progeny most survive be above three thousand the old grandsire be dead news be send to all the kindred in their severell habitation every village mourn and the kindred visit the corpse with present gold clothes and what they can accomplish all with lamentable lamentation part of the present be put in the grave another part go to the king of the place the three to the heir but the king themselves be bury secret by night with a few friend attend have all their life heap treasure to that funeral purpose funeral rite and be therefore bury in unknown place as in the bottom of river turn meanwhile the stream on the other side they lose much gold this way and if they die sudden no man know where they have prepare and treasure that treasure that the wife and servant be add to the exequy we need not repeat they hope to find all ready to serve they in the next life some great man have house set over their grave cover with cloth and other thing there leave to waste with time and hither the kindred make recourse to consult with the dead and acquaint they with their affair the funeral end they return with so many stalk of straw as there reruayne month to the year end against which time they provide store of rice wine hen and if the decease be rich of cow and then assemble to a funeral feast last day and night with all excess in eat drink dance and such a noise that none in the village can sleep for which cause the Jesuit which have their church in the village have their house out of they their great glory be the number of meat beyond mouth and of drunkard beyoud tale king Peter be invite to one of these riot yet riot not but by his modest example win good opinion to his religion they have sacrifice a maid and certain cow with diabolical rite to their ancestor in a wood close before he come Barerius go to Fatema the king of the boulons and be light to he by night GRAMAYE thus much have I relate of the Jesuit and dominicans late labour in Africa Gramaye Africa 10. have late publish ten book or tractate of Africa he say that there be some relic of the ancient christian after so many inundation of heresy and mahometism both in Morocco tunes and Lybia which use the mass of the mozarabe Christianity of Barbary translate into Arabic there be also Greek and abassine and of diverse nation merchant with free use of their conscience at tune and Tripoli priest in gown monk in their cowl be permit public supplication and funeral in the kingdom of Fez their liberty be great but in all the coast of Barbaria there be no security of the public exercise of christian religion nor any monastery but at Oram and in the place subject or confederate to the spaniard in the place subject to the moor and turk there be public permit not secure both exercise church and place of burial in town sometime eclipse or disturb by the morabute in time of drought at which time as it be to appease the angry deity they spoil church Christian holy overthrow tavern for none else may sell wine which after a few day be again permit the christian churchyard or rather buriall-place be a piece of ground without the town near the jewish buriall-place not enclose yea in place bearing corne. but the sandy soil scarce secure the corpse from dog prayer and other rite be use at the grave but not at Algiers without scoff and injury special from boy priest administer sacrament without special cure or certain stipend or order yea some without order baptism be often administer by the lay-people and without the ecclesiastical ceremony and whatsoever require episcopal benediction of long time have there want seldom be there sermon never catechise vesper or lauds the beast fish and fowl of the river of the portugal mandingo and fulby there live the river gamba Gambia or Gambra be in 13. degree 30. minute the inhabitant they seem to themselves to travel southeast to 8. degr. they want instrument to make the true height as far as I can learn in my travel up the same three hundred and twenty league or nine hundred and sixty mile call it by no other name but a general name in their language to all river and water it have one sole entrance which in the mouth be about four league wide and three fathom water in the channel without any bar four league inward it spread itself into so many river bay and creek that for thirty league unto tancroval it be very intricate the main channel may easy be discern except in that with a fair stream from the mouth it flow to Baraconda or some little above which be nigh two hundred league in the low season the land-floud abridge this tide raise the water thirty tide 200. leag flood 30. foot high the reins foot upright repel the sea force and cover the flat which in the low season cause impediment these rain always proceed from the southeast begin within land where we abide in the late end of May and at the river mouth in the end of june continue three month with great violence with great wind most terrible thunder and lightning in sudden gust and storm which violence be overpass the people continue their labour of tillage they begin and go out with more gentleness the extremity be from the middle of july to the middle of August in September equinoctial the sun clear and thence till may they have no rain whereby the ground be hard and uncapable of tillage in this rainy unseasonable season be they force therefore to exercise their husbandry as also to prepare their habitation secure from the overflow of the river where the bank can discipline it and hence may the unwholsomnesse be cause whatsoever venom come from tree cause of the unwholsomnesse of rain plant serpent whereof be many kind toad and scorpion contain and continue all that time of drought in the dust and on the earth and wash in the first reins yield venomous vapour to the sun strong exhale faculty which it vomit again crude and undigested in the next reins and so the former reins be worse than the late blister the naked body whereon they fall breed worm in garment therewith wet and lay by it be therefore fit to be provide of water to drink or dress meat before these season fall and to note for hea^th prevent the hurt by keep the well cover and not to water in the open river as the saint john man do in the first voyage thereby the last to the most of they our man remain there three year and return sound free the country of the imputation the river increase when no rain be see where we abide whereby the reins fall above and further passablenesse of the river appear the shall which stay we might in another season be prevent yea with fit man and instrument cut through continue so small a space promise fair beyond so far as we have occasion to look the sea-horse and store of crocodile proclaim deep water upward and if it join above to Senaga as it be usual describe it can be far above that place of Palmita leave bind up which our negro say some people have use to pass the river there abound in this river sea-horse and crocodile or alegator this they call Bumbo river horse and crocodile who length we have measure in the impression make in the sand whence we have drive he three and thirty foot so fear of the native that they dare not wash their hand wade or swim in the great river tell of many their friend by this enemy devour neither dare they pass over their cattle but when they pass over a beef a Canoe go before whereto fear of the crocodile one hold he close with a rope fasten to his horn another hold up his tail the priest or Marybuck in the midst pray over the beast and spit on he by who stand another with bow and arrow ready and thus they pass they one by one and when we be force in a shallow place to enter the water and force the boat against the current the black will not be persuade say Bumbo will have they till at last on better consideration at a three straight they bethink themselves that a white man be more conspicuous in the water and therefore adventure yet do I never find they to assault we in all this way but when many of they lay on the sand they will avoid we as snake use the noise and sight of man with we bold in deep water their musky scent make we oft to stop our nostril it make both the water and fish also in some place to taste and relish of they that we can not eat the one nor drink the other the noise of they in that place whereby they call one to another resemble the sound of a deep well may be hear a league the river-horse be in fashion of body a complete horse have round buttock short ear wag see before in santos c 12. a large description where our man may learn to take this horse elephant crocodile etc. to his mouth two tooth stand right before on his low chap great and dangerous neigh direct like a horse four leg short the foot divide some so great that I have measure a print twenty inch over he do hurt in the rice-ground but general feed on low marish ground where the sedge be green in herd by night bold in the water snort neigh and toss the water within pistol shoot very fearful of fire as may appear by a candle end we can not spare they any shot set on a piece of wood and let down the stream on they they be most dangerous when they have their young with they which sometime they leave on the shore carry in the water by the female on her back I have see the sea-horse and crocodile to swim together without disagreement there be store of mullet and other fish amongst other with a net we take one like a english torpedo Tremedor or Thinta breme but of great thickness which one of our sailor put his hand to present cry out that he have lose the use of his hand and arm another barelegged put thereto his foot lose the sense of his leg their sense be see to return the cook be call up and bid to dress it who lay both his hand thereon sink present on his hinder part make grievous moan that he feel not his hand sandy a black come with his Canoe laugh and emblem of a flatterer tell we that they much fear this fish in the water for he benumb whatsoever he touch which he use to do stroke himself on other fish and then devour they but be dead he be good meat at that place near cassan the people will come bold into the water some great Marybuck have secure they from the Bumbo by his blessing and we may see many on the other side but never any on this one little fish there be which may be call the run fish like our roach with a red tail enforce to run a great way on the top of the run fish water light touch it by his adversary which be like a trout who to avoid he have run sometime into our Canoe there be store of foul which we see sit on the bank but never in the main river swim river foul it seem for fear of the crocodile and feed on the marsh and pond goose rather big than our tame goose with a spur on each pinion large sharp and if they be not kill dead ready for offence duck mallard heron curlews stork plover and the like the people fish their lake and pond which be many broad shallow go a whole town native fish or plantation together only the man each with a kind of basket hold the open mouth downward close one by another overspread the pond clap down their basket before they and so return most of they lade to speak of the inhabitant I will begin at the mouth of the river where dwell the black call mandingo which speak the same language fearful of any ship because many have be surprise and carry away except they know they they bring to we abundance of Bonanos which in the west indies they call plantano with beef goat hen grain and some hide among these dwell or lurk rather a certain way up the river certain portugal portugal these may be of the Tangos maos before mention some of that colour other Molatos but the most black scatter two or three in a place beget child of the black woman but have neither church nor friar nor any other religious order it appear that they be fugitive or exile from Portugal or the isle of that government which employ themselves in buy commodity especial slave a few of they have use one time of the year to go up the river in a small bark as far as Setico to trade whence they have return much gold and have not attempt further which be not half the way we have go up they say that those * * Hector Nunez etc. their paucity refuse still these native bear a sullen disaffection to the Portugal notwithstanding there be another people dwell amongst the mandingo call fulby a tawny people much like to those vagrant amongst we call egyptian the woman well feature with a long black hair more loose than that of the black woman neat apparel in the habit of the native the man be not so handsome by reason they live of and with their cattle some goat but herd of beef in abundance the keep of which be their profession in some place they have settle town most wander unite themselves in kindred and drive their herd together where they find good pasture they agree with the king and build house as the season serve during the reins betake themselves to the mountain and high ground and then succeed the river even to his severe bank their toil be continual keep their cattle in the day from stray and from the crocodile haunt in the night bring they near their house and part they in several herd make fire about they and likewise in the midst about which they lie themselves ready against the roar assailant thus be the poor Fulby almost grow beastial and when we have go to they to buy a beef he have come forth from his beast with his face and hand cover with fly as thick as here they use to sit on horse in summer and the same kind of fly but those fulby seem more senseless not remove they as we be fain with a bough in conference to do and as our beast use whisk of their tail and other motion they live in great subjection to the mandingo who will share with they if they know of base state their kill of a beef and in their commodity that when they trade with we they will draw we covert to see it lest the negro participate in his return of these the country be full every where disperse and high up they be in one part principal hold domination exclude the black but for the most part in war their language be different from the black their woman will daily bring we milk curd two sort of butter one new soft and white the other hard and of a excellent colour as good as any we have here but for a little freshness bring in goard like dish neat and clean within and without therein much unlike the irish Calios how ever otherwise resemble their course of life their return be swall bead and knife of sixteen penny the dozen with other trifle but after they have once taste ramdam so they call our salt nothing else can so well please they be this never so little if we deny trade one day we shall not have their company in a week so that we be willing to please they the black not apply himself to cattle the mandingo themselves which be the natural inhabitant be perfect black live the mandingo idle life a most idle life except two month of the year in their seedtime and harvest wander up and down at other time from one to another have little knowledge to hunt fish or foul how much soever both wood and water abound in game the beast and fowl as guinnie hen and partridge resort to their very door in the heat of the day they pass the time in company chat under the shady tree have one game with some thirty stone and hole cut in a piece of wood perform by a kind of count they ordinary make their diet but one meal a day special the vulgar and young sort or rather none their hour of meal be after the day light be in and then with fire of reed without the door they sit round and fall to their viand which for the most part be Rice or some other grame boil which be bring unto they in goard by the woman hot they put in their hand roll it up in ball and cast into their mouth flesh or fish their want of skill to get have make rarity their cock and hen be plentiful but spare to barter with we for sma^l piece of iron bead and such commodity they hold it unwholesome to eat in the heat of the day the heat and moisture then exhale to the exterior part and the inward cool and more disable for note for our man diet concoction whereby we can in that heat easy drink yea and desire it that quantity of aquavitae or hot drink which here will kill we and there we dr^n^e with more temperance and satisfaction in less quantity both morning and evening and in my opinion it be fit for we to eat early and again after the heat be past in thos^ part their usual drink be water yet have both wine of tree as also their dullo of grain like their house our ale. they place their habitation round together and for the most part have a wall of reed make up together some six foot high fortify they against ravenous^ east which yet cause often alarm and mighty cry compass their town with door of the same shut in the night some of the house within be make of the same reed but the better sort of loom reddish and remain very hard likely to yield the best brick in the world the whole country but the mountain yield the same earth the ant-hil be remarkable cast up strange ant-hil in those part by Pis^ ire some of they twenty foot in height of compass to contain a dozen man with the heat of the sun bake into that hardness that we use to hide ourselves in the ragged top of they when we take up stand to shoot at deer or wild beast the form of their house be round and cover with reed tie fast to raft that they may endure the outrageous gust and reins such be their mean town and village other they ha^e of force suitable to their war fortify and entrench of which the inland have store and fortifications cassan against which the betray ship do ride be such it be the seat of the king seat on the river enclose round with hurdle like those which our shepherd use but above ten foot high fasten to strong pole which be high than the hurdle on the inside in diverse place they have building make like turret whence to shoot arrow and cast dart against the assailant on the outside be a ditch or trench of great breadth beyond which again the town be circle with post and piece of tree set close and fast into the ground some five foot high so thick that except in style and place make purpose a single man can get through and in like manner a small distance off be the like defence which they say be to keep off the force of horse their arm be a azegay or javelin with which in their hand they walk be a reed of six foot with a iron-pike artificial make and dangerous they have other to cast like their arm azegey dart with barb head about the neck a bandelier of red or yellow cloth with a sword hang of some two foot long and a open handle the better sort carry a bow in their hand and at their back a case with many hole hold some four and twenty arrow of reed as big as a swan quill two foot long head with iron poison without neck or feather the bow also make of a reed with a flat string or stick smooth and fasten of the same bow and arrow wood and to a buff jerkin or any sleight garment of defence be little offensive the danger be in the poison we have see they likewise on horseback their horse small bridle and saddle after the spanish fashion each man have a assegie and a broad buckler hang on the right side of his horse the king house be in the middle of the town enclose by itself with his wife several house about to which you can come but by a court of guard pass through a open house where stand his chair empty in which none but himself may sit by which hang his drum which every night they use to drum on hoop sing and make a wild confuse noise till day break with fire in the house and yard which noise they use in mean town also to scar away wild beast I see and do eat and drink with six of their king or which have reference to great king live further all the southside of the river as we go their king be subject to the king of Cantore of the north-side half subject to the king of the rest to the king of woolley these we see not their neck and their bow their woman the king for great state have many time two of his wife sit by he lay their hand on his naked skin above the waste stroke and gentle pull the same he have a her child nurse adultery be severe punish the man and woman be both sell which be the punishment for great offence none be put to death the portugal buy and transport they to the west indies other man Gregory they leave not till all be out @. 2 of their marybuck and religion merchandise fiddler instrument trade husbandry with a further history of the creature in those part their marybuck or bassareas be their priest or religious person separate from other marybucke or priest of a mahometan sect differ from the common in their habitation and course of life they tell of Adam Eve Noah with other thing mention in scripture like the Levitical tribe they have their town and land proper to themselves wherein dwell none of the secular but their slave who issue be their inheritance they marry also in their own tribe breed all their child to their own profession have as mhny wife and woman as the rest accord to their degree in every marybucke town they have a principal they will put their hand to work and may be hire to do service as well as other we agree with they by the moon their habit be as that of the vulgar I visit Fodee bram the principal in his sickness who sit on his Mat or bram. see sup. 925. bed support by three of his wife to each of which I give a pewter ring which he take kind and cause a dinner to be provide and send i a hide and a elephant tooth in recompense of a present which I have give he which here cost eighteen penny they worship it seem they speak some Arabic word in which also their law be write one God and call he awl acknowledge Mahomet be circumcise observe Friday sabbath but have no meskit or mahometan church or other religious place where they celebrate the same follow therein their occasion without intermission they have open round house not decent sweep in which they teach their child to write and read paper be of great esteem with they their pen be a kind of pencil their law be write in a language differ from their vulgar none of the temporal people have any use of book or letter we slovenly cleanliness think they make use of some shady tree in the field for their assembly and one day see a marybucke come with his slave to the riverside close by our wall he first with a gourd full of water wash his member without any nicety of our see he then wash the empty gourd his slave bring he other water wherewith he wash his hand and after that a three for his face after all which make a low reverence with his body and lay his hand on his breast his face direct towards the east * * to Mecca ward kneel down and in decent form seem to utter certain prayer which end he kiss the ground rise up turn his face to the west and perform like ceremony and then return to his lodging when Fodee bram be dead he be lay in a house where a grave be dig and a great pot of water set in the room and after the irish manner much cry rather than mourn be make he be lay into the ground the woman run about in a lunatic fashion with their arm spread make a terrible spectacle of sorrow the marybucke assemble themselves in a convenient place to receive the multitude near the grave where the people sit down in a ring a marybucke come forth in the midst who betwixt say and sing seem to rehearse certain verse in the praise of the decease the people interject their applause clap hand and run in to gratify their poet or prophet with a present thus one after another every marybucke have his speech but the most popular orator carry only Marybucke oration or sermon the present the principal might also take of the grave earth and water in the pot to make a relike-ball thereof some day be thus spend a great solemnity be make for the install of his son in the succession they have great book manuscript with which we have see some of they lade as the vulgar be insatiate with hot drink these be abstenious strict devote to poor pure water their book and abstinence as also their wife and child nor will endure the least infant or play boy to taste of our liquor or raisin Sugar fruit or any sweet thing nor can the great reason in their sickness persuade a taste insomuch that my marybucke almost drown once in a whirlpool after twice sink recover scarce have any sense and yet shut his mouth to our rosa-solis whereby we seek to revive he benefit no doubt by the send and be come to himself he ask whether any have enter say he have rather have die then any shall have come within he hereby they be easy discern from the vulgar and this sobriety make they useful in their service and credible in their report they dispose themselves general to travel together with their family book and Marybucks traveller boy the country be open to they renew it seem their provision when they come to some principal place of we it be most certain they will beg and a choir of paper be a great gift to a whole company which they use to write their Gregory and when we send any of cause why paper be so esteem see sup. 1466. the people any whither he will look to have a sheet or two of paper above his covenant to buy he sustenance in the way these marybucke by their travel be experience in diverse country and how ever the country agree or have war the marybucke be always a privilege person with both side yet do they use arm as well as other but rather I think for defence against mankinde-beast then beastly unkind men. two marybucke give we much intelligence of gold one of which when I come to take leave of he take my right hand betwixt he utter over the same certain unknown word and will ever and anon spare spittle upon it and the like he do over my right shoulder the inhabitant of Setico be all marybucke and have continual trade to the king of bursall and carry slave to buy salt which be there by the sea side a dirty kind like sea-coal ash trade of slave and salt. this they make little use of among themselves but carry it up far into the country their return be gold and Cola nut the gold be say to be bury with they or by themselves king or principal person be accompany with their juddy or fiddler the most common instrument be make of a great gourd and a music and musician neck thereto fasten in some sort resemble our Bandora the string mean and unfit without fret yet with pin wound and fit to some harmony with this they have a little drum their ballards see before pag. 925. and sup. c. 12. the like in Cafraria whereon with a crooked stick in the right hand and the finger on the left they play wring the mouth and gape very deform their ballards be a foot above ground hollow under with some seventeen key on the top on which the player strike sit on the ground with two stick a foot long with ball fasten on the end the sound may be hear a english mile this instrument be one of their most ingenious to every one of these key belong a small iron a foot long as big as a quill upon which hang two gourd under the hollow like bottle which cause the sound there be few of they but not a few which resort to they and spend whole night in dance each person male or female single give to the musician whereby they be esteem rich and their wife more adorn than the king with bloodstone but these if any licentious as their carriage import these man be deny burial be set dead in a tree as conceive to have most familiarity with their door devil and be account diviner their great assembly be at the circumcision which be a set time yearly the circumcision a seal of ynrighteousnesse without faith. youth which be circumcise have licence permit to filch hen and from the fulby a beef or young cattle to make merry with in the time of their soreness it be do without religious ceremony and have no name but cut of prick the party strip naked and sit on the ground and the butcher pull the skin over very far and cut it not without the marybucke policy as I find by experience thus the devil may be belie who yet be a oracle to they as appear by one of their juddy which have tell one at pompetane how many of we and at what hour we etc. you desire to have the whole proceed of our unfortunate voyage yet fortunate to we who be here to relate what the lord have do for we the which as near as God shall enable i I will make know unto you first ten league to the southward of the north cape we be chase by a turkish man of war of four and thirty piece of ordnance and be not far from the shore it please God we recover it before he can fetch we up yet he be so near to we before he leave we that he be within shoot of we and see that we be bend to run ashore rather then to come into his hand he espy ten or twelve boat under the i will of Dones fisherman where we be chase in and leave we and put out his boat full of small shot and some of they he take and some get away and some he chase ashore upon the island and there he land his man and take they all away to the number of five and fifty person and one kill so there he keep we the space of four day at length away he go and the next day we find the wind fair come out and go along the shore within musket shoot all the way betwixt that and the isle of Bayone at length we espy this sail come out of the sea and come direct in with the isle of Bayone and we be so near the shore do not great fear because we think what ever he be we shall get the shore before he at last he come something near to we we see it be no great sail not pass one hundred ton or thereabouts and that there be no hope of run away but that we must either fight it out or run ashore I call up all my company and ask they what they will do whether they will stand by i and show themselves like man and that it may never be say that we shall run away from he be not much big than we although he have as many more ordnance as we they answer all with one consent that they will live and die with i and fear to bear in with it for fear of man of war we hold in two or three league to the northward of it see a great town by the water side we be in hope the rock a point of land at the turn in from the sea towards Lisbon to get a boat aboard before night and come with it we go as near to it as we can and lay by the lee and put out a weafe and stay there three hour and no boat will come to we then night come on we get our tack aboard and steer away for the rock again and the wind be at northwest we be fearful to hale off far from the shore for fear of man of war but steer direct for the rock and go not above half a mile without it because the wind be large enough and as soon as we be shoot to the southward of the rock in a die of rain the wind come to the west south-west and we run that way in hope to carry it away the wind southward still till we have bring ourselves so near that we have no room to bear up and have no aftersayle to make our ship stay be force be but we two to put our anchor from the bow and to break open a scuttle and go down and vere to a whole cable and bring up the ship and go up and take in our sail and get another anchor from the bow and make three or four of the turk clear the cable to we this be about twelve of the clock in the night and when the day come on the weather do begin to increase much and the sea be much grow be so near the shore as we be that we be fain to cut our mast by the board and be not able to do it of ourselves be but two of we and over-watcht for want of sleep for from Thursday night till Sunday night we never take wink of sleep I go to the cabin door and have they come to help we they tell i they will come but make no great haste for they do fear that we will have kill they at last perceive that I be very angry with they as I be cut at our mainmast and my mate at the foremast one of they come up and fall down on his knee and kiss i by the foot and beg of i that I will not kill he and I tell he that I will do none of they any hurt but they shall come and help we work and he go and tell his consort what I have say so up they come all upon the deck and every one of they one after another come and kiss we by the foot as well he that lie hurt as we and then we give they the axe to cut the mast but we keep the weapon and when our mayne-mast and foremast be cut away the ship do ride pretty easy and then we go to prayer the turk sit with we and I have no more book leave but a little prayer-book in my pocket one of the turk go to his bag and fetch i own bible and bring it to i say master here be a big book for you after prayer we do eat and drink together and be as though we have be altogether consort there we rid from twelve of the clock at night till two of the clock in the afternoon the next day and all this time there come not a boat to we yet we be but three mile from cast Cales we be not half a mile from the point which if we can have weather we may have go into Lisboa without any sail but it be not God will that it shall be so Sunday be the sevenyh day after we be take we cut our cable and with our sprit-sayle and spirit sayle-topsayle we run into a flat place be no more flat place there that there be no hope of ever save our life for the rock be as steep as a house and so some by one mean and some by another we get ashore but we do not suffer one of the turk to go till we be all ashore and then we go to a little village half a mile from the place where we come ashore and there we cause all the turk to be pinyon for not a man come to the water side all this time and so two or three of the man of the village go with we to cast Cales and there the turk be put in prison and we be very well use and they that be hurt be dress and have a chirurgeon to look to we for the space of two day till we have a little refresh ourselves and then a boat provide for we and the turk to carry we to Lisboa where after examination both of we and they the governor give they free to we and tell we we do deserve a great deal more thus have I relate unto you the whole truth of our proceed and no more but what be truth not for that I desire to be appland of man but that whosoever shall hear this discourse may not think that of our own power we can do this but that it be the hand of the lord have do it and the lord grant that I and every of we may never be unmindful of that the lord have do for we amen this letter be write to master John moulton to who also he write another which I have demand his advice about that which seem to i a strange immanity that I say not inhumanity and unchristianitie alone of man as the other be the unspeakable grace and daemon bounty of God namely that the owner of the ship so take be also the master kinsman demand and by law threaten to wring from he part of the money which they make by sale of the turk at Lisbon where yet they be not in their podsession but as the king slave and the king officer for encouragement of other in like case give they that money as alm howsoever it be reckon also as their just price neither will they give they wage which yet demand this money as if their eye have be evil because god be good and gracious like jonas in his mad anger for the spare but I hope they better bethink they afterward or else I will here name they to their everlasting reproach which I now forbear as David do shimeis punishment in regard of so great and present a escape victory triumph which even then have happen and because these Algiers pirate have bring we into the thought of turkish power the rather a preface to the ensue treatise observe that last turkish business rather than Christian charity and of Turkey we have deliver already diverse thing remarkable yet have since meet with a piece of worth I think good also to communicate it unto thou it be a royal present worth the receive namely to set thou in possession and make thou master of the grand signior seraglio a sight hitherto prohibit in manner to which live in the seraglio and first of the woman and virgin their manner of life there first I say that all they which be in the seraglio both man and woman be the grand signior slave and so be all they which be subject to his empire for as one lord the rest slave he be their only sovereign so they do all of they acknowledge that whatsoever they do possess or enjoy proceed mere and simple from his goodwill and favour this seraglio may right be term the seminary or nursery of subject for in it all they have their bring up which afterward become the principal officer and subordinate ruler of the state and affair of the whole empire they which be within the three gate call the king gate be about two thousand person 2000 within the king gate man and woman whereof the woman old and young one with another what with the king concubine old woman and woman servant may be about eleven or twelve hundred now 11. or 1200. woman virgin those which be keep up for their beauty be all young virgin say law illawheh allawh muhamed resull allawh that be there be no god but God alone and Mahomet be the messenger of God and accord as they be in age and disposition be prove and examine by a old woman call Cahiyah Cadun that be as we say the mother of the maid so they Kabiyah cadun the mother of the maid be place in a room with the other of the same age spirit and inclination to dwell and live together now in the woman lodging they live just as the nun do in their great monastery for these virgin have very large room to live in and their bedchamber will hold almost a hundred of they a piece they sleep upon Sofaes which be build long wise on their manner of life chamber bed both side of the room so that there be a large space in the midst for to walk in their bed be very course and hard and by every ten virgin there lie a old woman and all the night long there be many light burn so that one may see very plain throughout the whole room which do both keep the young wench from wantonness and serve upon any occasion which may happen in the night near unto the say bedchamber they have their bagnoe bagnoe and kitchen for their use at all time with a great abundance of fountain of which they be serve with water above over the say bedchamber there be diverse room where they sit and sew and keep their chist in which they lie up their apparel they feed by whole camaradae sew to learn to speak and read the turkish tongue to sew and play on instrument and so they spend the day with their mistress which be ancient woman some hour notwithstanding be allow they for their recreation to walk in their garden and use such recreation sport as they familiar exercise themselves withal the king do not at all frequent or see these virgin unless it be at the instant when they king come to they be first give he or else in case that he desire one of they for his bedfellow or to show he some pastime with music and tumble trick and then he give notice to the aforesaid Cahiyah cadun of his purpose who immediate choose out such as she think to be the most amiable and fair and have place they in good order in a room in two rank half on the one side and half on the other she forthwith bring in the king who walk four or five turn in the midst of they and have view they well take good notice of she which he best like but say nothing only as he go out again he throw a handkerchief into that virgin hand by which she know that she be to lie with he that night and she be wondrous glad of so good a fortune to be choose out from among so many to enjoy the preparation society of a emperor have all the be that possible may be show upon she by the Cadun in attire paint and perfume she and so at night she be bring to sleep with the grand signior in the woman lodging there be diverse chamber appropriate for that business only and be in bed they have two great wax light burn by they all bedchamber rite night one at the bed foot and the other by the door and there be appoint by the Cadun diverse old Blacke-moore woman which watch by turn that night in the chamber two at a time one to sit by the say light at the bed foot and the other by the door and when they will they change and other two supply their room without make the least noise imaginable so that the king be not any wise disturb and in the morning when his highness rise for he rise first he change all his apparel from top to toe leave those which he wear to she reward that he lay withal and all the money that be in his pocket be it never so much and so depart to his own lodging from whence also he send she immediate a present of jewel vest and money of great value accord to the satisfaction and content which he receive from she that night in the same manner he be to deal with all the other which he make use of in that kind but with some he continue long and enlarge his bounty more towards some then to other accord as his humour and affection to they increase by their fulfil his lustful desire and if it so fall out that any one of they do conceive by he and bring forth his first beget child she be call by the name of sultana queen and if the child be a sultana queen son than she be confirm and establish by great feast and solemnity and have a dwell apart assign unto she of many stately room well furnish and many servant to attend upon she the king likewise allow she a very sufficient revenue that she may give her allowance away and spend at her pleasure in whatsoever she may have occasion and all they of the seraglio do acknowledge she for queen show all the respect and duty that may be both to she and she the other woman howsoever they bring forth issue be not call queen yet they be other sultanaes call sultanaes because they have have carnal commerce with the king. and she only be call queen which be the mother of the first beget son heir to the empire the which sultanaes be frequent by the king at his pleasure have also this prerogative to be immediate remove from the common sort and to live in room apart exceed well serve and attend and have no want either of money or of apparel in conformity of their degree all these sultanaes do resort together very familiar when they please but not without great dissimulation and inward malice fear lest the one shall be better belove of the king than the other howbeit in outward show they use all kind of courtesy one towards another and if it happen that the first beget son of the queen heir to the empire shall queen change die and another of the sultanaes shall have a second son then her son be to succeed the decease heir she be immediate make queen and the former shall remain a sultana only and so the title of queen run from one sultana to another by virtue of the son succession sometime the queen be wont to be wed to the king but now she pass without the kebin that be without a assignment of any jointure or celebrate the nuptial rite nuptial rite which be nothing else but in the presence of the mufti to give each of they their assent to matrimony of which the mufti make Hoget that be a authentical write or testification not only of the consent of the two party contract but also of the dowry which the king be to allow she the reason why the queen be not now nor have not be of late espouse be not to dismember the king patrimony of five hundred thousand Chicquins a year for sultan seraglio to be sell at very easy rate yet in the end the jew have but a bad market of it for be discover to be rich ill success and their wealth to be get by deceit they oftentimes lose both good and life too the pasha and Defterdar altogether aim at such as they be think by that mean to restore to the grand signior that which have be from time to time steal from he and the rather for that they themselves seldom want their share in the estate of such delinquent the woman of the seraglio be punish for their fault very severe and extreme beat by their overseer and if they prove disobedient take from they but if they shall be find culpable for witchcraft or any such heinous offence then be they tie and put into a sack and in the night cast into the sea so that by all mean it behoove they to be very obedient and contain themselves within the bound of honesty and modesty if they mean to come to death a good end now it be not lawful for any one to bring aught in unto they with which they with unchaste thought @. v. of the agiamoglan how take distribute and employ have already speak of the woman I now will say somewhat of the agiamoglan which serve in the seraglio and of their employment they be in number about agiamoglan 700. seven hundred from twelve to five and twenty or thirty year of age at the most be all of they christian renegado as all agiamoglan be which be gather every three year in Morea and in all the province of Albania the which tithe child be dispose of in this wise they be sometime more and sometime few accord to the discretion of the capichee appoint for that service but a whole harvest of they seldom or never renegado child how take exceed the sum of two thousand and be take from such family as be think to be of a more warlike disposition they may not be when they be gather of above twelve or fourteen year of age lest they shall be unfit for a new course and too well settle in Christianity and be keep fast for a while by the capichee they be then forthwith send to Constantinople to be distribute and share out as follow so soon as they be arrive at the port they be all clothe in Salonichi cloth it skill ^ow use not of what colour and yellow cap of feel on their head in the form of a sugarloaf and be bring before the chief who at that time be accompany with the other pasha apparel and officer of the seraglio he make choice of as many as he see to be well-favoured and judge to be likely to prove soldier then this choice be make the youth choose by the chief be carry by the bustangee Bashee into the king own seraglio and election of the best circumcision there distribute to such company as want their complete number then be they circumcise and make Turk and put to learn the turkish tongue and accord as their inclination be discover by their overseer so be they encourage and suffer to proceed if it be in goodness and be teach to write and read but they be in a manner all of they teach to wrestle school to leap to run to shoot in a bow and to conclude all such exercise as be beseem a soldier now part of the residue of they be distribute by the chief into all the grand signior garden and house of pleasure and into such ship as sail for the king account and which the rest how dispose go to lade wood and such like provision for the seraglio consign they to the master of the say vessel with this condition to restore they again when he shall require they and so he do with the chief arts-man of all sort of occupation to the intent the youth may learn and practise the say art in their lodging at home when they be become janissary or else if they please abroad at the war also he give likewise to all the pasha and great man of the court as many as they please to serve they deliver they by name unto they and write they down in a book that he may have they again when there shall be occasion to make they janissary now these which be give to the pasha be the scum and refusal of all the rest and be employ only in the service of stable kitchen and such base office but the other be put into diverse serraglio under the custody and discipline of certain eunuch who be appoint to be their overseer and take care that they be bring up and train in military exercise until such time as they become fit to be accept into the number of the janissary in the room of the dead or of old one which be no long fit for the war but be make otoorack and have leave to stay at home so that I may otoorack (...) say all these be in a manner keep in a seminary to serve at all hand the king queen and chief that the Oda Bashees and bulook bashee may be know from the common sort of Agiamoglans they wear great broad silken girdle of diverse governor colour about their middle and be allow a large stipend undergo slavery whatsoever be do unto they they have their term and prerogative amongst themselves succeed or precede one another accord to the length of time which they have spend in the seraglio so that they lie near the seaside by the wall of the seraglio they take good store of fish part of which they sell and rescue the rest to themselves they sleep always in their clothes take only off their uppermost coat and their shoe accord to the ordinary custom of the poor sort of turk between a couple of rug in sleep the winter and thin blanket in summer they never see king unless it be when he not go in again until the king be depart for there must none come near the woman but himself and his black eunuch nay if any other shall but attempt by some trick in convey himself into some private corner to see the woman and shall be discover he shall immediate be put to death every one therefore so soon as they have notice of the king come into the garden with his woman run out of sight as far as they can to be free from all fear and suspicion now of this rank of Agiamoglans which be in the king seraglio they do not make janissary as they do of those which be put into the other serraglio
