I be desirous to see how they gather the cinnamon or take it from the tree that it grow on and so much the rather because the time that I be there be the season which they gather it in which be in the month of April at which time the portugal be in arm and in the field with the king of the country yet I to satisfy my desire although in great danger take a guide with i and go into a wood three mile from the city in which wood be great store of cinnamon tree grow together among other wild tree and this cinnamon tree be a small tree and not very high and have leaf like to our bay-tree in the month of march or April when the sap go up the cut and gather of cinnamon to the top of the tree than they take the cinnamon from that tree in this wise they cut the bark off the tree round about in length from knot to knot or from joint to joint above ^nd below and then easy with their hand they take it away lay it in in the sun to dry and in this wise it be gather and yet for all this the tree die not but against the next year it a rare thing will have a new bark and that which be gather every year be the best cinnamon for that which grow two or three year be great and not so good as the other be and in these wood grow much pepper from the island of Zeilan man use to go with small ship to Negapatan within the firm Negapatan land and seventy two mile off be a very great city and very populous of portugal and christian of the country and part gentile it be a country of small trade from Negapatan follow my voyage towards the east a hundred and fifty mile I find saint Thomas or San Tom s. Thomas his sepulchre the house of bless saint Thomas which be a church of great devotion and great regard of the gentile for the great miracle they have hear to have be do by that bless apostle near unto this church the portugal have build they a city in the country subject to the king of bezeneger which city although it be not very great yet in my judgement it be the fair in all that part of the Indies it be a marvelous thing to they which have not see the lade and unlade of man and merchandise in saint Tom as they do it be a place so dangerous that a man can be serve with small bark neither can they do their business with the boat of the ship because they will be beat in a thousand piece but they make certain bark of purpose high which they call masadie they be make of little board one board be sow to another with small cord and in this order be they make and when they be thus make and the owner will embark any thing in they either man or good they lade they on land and when they be lade the barkeman thrust the boat with her lade into the stream and with great speed they make haste all that they be able to row out against the huge wave of the sea that be on that shore until that they carry they to the ship and in like manner they lade these masady at the ship with merchandise and man when they come near the shore the barkman leap out of the bark into the sea to keep the bark dangerous surge and shore right that she cast not thwart the shore and be keep right the suff of the sea set her lade dry on land without any hurt or danger and sometime there be some of they that be overthrow but there can be no great loss because they lade but a little at a time all the merchandise they lade outward they emball it well with ox hide so that if it take wet it can have no great harm in my voyage return in the year of our lord 1566. one another and so eat one another and if by evil chance any ship be lose on those land as many have be there be not one man of those ship lose there that escape uneaten or unslain these people have not any acquaintance with any other people neither have they trade with any but live only of such fruit as those land yield and if any ship come near unto that place or coast as they pass that way as in my voyage it happen as I come from malacca through the channel of Sombrero there come two of their bark near unto our ship lade with fruit as with marce which we call Adam apple with fresh nut and with a fruit call which fruit be like to our turnip but be very sweet and good to eat they will not come into the ship for my thing that we can do neither will they take any money for their fruit but they will truck for old shirt or piece of old linen breech these rag they let down with a jope into their bark unto they and look what they think those thing to be worth so much fruit they will make they that be sick in four day die and I for the space of a year after have my throat so sore and hoarse that I can never satisfy my thirst in drink of water I judge the reason of my hoarseness to be a man hot wine dear water neither be they able to drink they when we begin to want water I see certain moor that be officer in the ship that sell a small dish full for (@) ducat after this I see one where the merchant gather themselves together with their trade be a hundred mile which they row in eighteen hour with the increase of the water in which river it flow and eb as it do in the Thames and when the ebb water be come they be not able to row against it by reason of the swiftness of the water yet their bark be light and arm with oar like to foist yet the can prevail against strong tide that stream but for refuge must make they fast to the bank of the river until the next flow water and they call these bark Bazaras and Patuas they row as well as a Galliot or as well as ever I have see any a good tide row before you come to Satagan you shall have a place which be call buttor and from thence upward the sip do not go because that upward the river be very shallow and little water every year at buttor they make and unmake a village with house and shop make of straw and with all thing necessary to their use and this village stand as long as the ship ride there and till they from Martavan I depart to go to the chief city in the kingdom of Pegu which be also call after the name of the kingdom which voyage be make by sea in three or four day they may go also by land but it be better for he that have merchandise to go by sea and lesser charge and in this voyage you shall have a Macareo which be one of the most marvelous admirable tide thing in the world that nature have wrought and I never see any thing so hard to be believe as this to wit the great increase and diminish of the water there at one push or instant and the horrible earthquake and great noise that the Macareo make where it come we depart from Martavan in bark which be like to our pilot-boat with the increase of the water and they go as swift as a arrow out of a bow so long as the tide run with they and when the water be at the high than they draw themselves out of the channel towards some bank and there they come to anchor and when the water be diminish than they rest on dry land and when the bark rest dry they be as high from the bottom of the channel as as any house top be high from the ground they let their bark he so high for this respect that if this tide be like to the tide in our river of se. (...) ne but it seem great there shall any ship rest or ride in the channel with such force come in the water that it will overthrow ship or bark yet for all this that the bark be so far out of the channel and though the water have lose her great strength and fury before it come so high yet they make fast their prow to the stream and oftentimes it make they very fearful and if the anchor do not hold her prow up by strength she will be over throw and lose with man and good when the water begin to increase it make such a noise and so great that you will think it a earthquake and present at the first it make three wave so that the first wash over the bark from stem to stern the second be not so furious as the first and the these tide make their just course as we do three raise the anchor and then for the space of six hour while the water increase they row with such swiftness that you will think they do fly in these tide there must be lose no ^ot of time for if you arrive not at the stagion before the tide be spend you must turn back from whence you come for there be no stay at any place but at these stagion and there be more danger at one of these place then at another as they be high and low one than another when as you return from pegu to Martavan they go but half the tide at a time because they will lay their bark up aloft on the bank for the reason aforesaid I can never gather any reason of the noise that this water make in the increase of the tide and in diminish of the water there be another Macareo in Cambaya but that be nothing in this Macareo be a tide or a current house make of cane and cover with leaf of tree godon be a place or house for merchant to lay their good (@) the form of the build of the new city of Pegu. comparison of this by the help of God we come safe to Pegu which be two city the old and the new in the old city be the merchant stranger and merchant of the country for there be the great do and the great trade this city be not very great but it have very great suburb their house be make with cane and cover with leaf or with straw but the merchant have all one house or Magason which house they call godon which be make of brick and there they put all their good of any value to save they from the often mischance that there happen to house make of such stuff in the new city be the palace of the king and his abide place with all his baron and noble and other gentleman and in the time that I be there they finish the build of the new city it be a great city very plain and flat and four square wall round about and with ditch that compass the wall about with water in which ditch be many crocodile it have no draw-bridge yet it have twenty gate five for every square on the wall there be many place make for sentinel to watch make of wood and cover or gild with gold the street thereof be the fair that I have see they be as straight as a line from one gate to another and stand at the one gate you may discover to the other and they be as broad as ten or twelve man may ride abreast in they and those street that be thwart be fair and large these street both on the one side and the other be plant at the door of the house with nut tree of India which make a very commodious shadow the house be make of wood and cover with a kind of tile in form of cup very necessary for their use the king palace be in the middle of the city make in form of a wall castle with ditch full of water round about it the lodging within be make of wood all over gild with fine pinnacle and very costly work cover with plate of gold true it may be a king house within the gate there be a fair large court from the one side a rich and stately palace to the other wherein there be make place for the strong and stout elephant he have four that be white a thing so rare that a man shall hardly find another king that have any such as if this king know any other that have white elephant he send for they as for a four white elephant gift the time that I be there there be two bring out of a far country and that cost i something the sight of they for that they command the merchant to go to see they and then they must give somewhat to the man that bring they the broker of the merchant give for every man half a ducat which they call a Tansa which amount to a great sum for this money call Tansa be half a ducat which may be three shilling and four penny the number of merchant that be in that city and when they have pay the aforesaid Tansa they may choose whether they will see they at that time or no because that when they be in the king stall every man may see they that will but at that time they must go and see they for it be the king pleasure it shall be so this king amongst all other his title be call the king of the white elephant and it be report that if this king know any other king that have any of these white elephant and will not send they unto he that he will hazard his whole kingdom to conquer they he esteem these white elephant very dear and they be have in great regard and keep with very meet service every one of they be in a house all gild over and they have their meat give they in vessel of silver and gold there be one black elephant the great that have be see and he be keep accord to his bigness he be nine cubit high which be a marvelous thing it be report that this king have four thousand elephant of war and a warlike policy all have their tooth and they use to put on their two uppermost tooth sharp pike of iron and make they fast with ring because these beast fight and make battle with their tooth he have also very many young elephant that have not their tooth sprout forth also this king have a brave devise in hunt to take these elephant when he will two mile from the city he have build a fair palace all gild and within it a fair court and within it and round a excellent devise to hunt and take wild elephant about there be make a infinite number of place for man to stand to see this hunt near unto this palace be a mighty great wood through the which the huntsman of the king ride continual on the back of the female elephant teach they in this business every hunter carry out with he five or six of these female and they say that they anoint the secret place with a certain composition that they have that when the wild elephant do smell hereunto they follow the female and can leave they when the huntsman have make provision and the elephant be so entangle they guide the female towards the palace which be call Tambell and this palace have a door which do open and shut with engine before which door there be a long straight way with tree on both the side which cover the way in such wise as it be like darkness in a corner the wild elephant when he come to this way think that he be in the wood at the end of this dark way there be a great field when the hunter have get this prey when they first come to this field they send present to give knowledge thereof to the city and with all speed there go out fifty or sixty man on horseback and do beset the field round about in the great field then the female which be teach in this business go direct to the mouth of the dark way and when as the wild elephant be enter in there the hunter shout and make a great noise as much as be possible to make the wild elephant enter in at the gate of that palace which be then open and as soon as he be in the gate be shut without any noise and so the hunter with the female elephant and the wild one be all in the court together and then within a small time the female withdraw themselves away one by one out of the court leave the wild elephant alone a excellent pastime of the elephant and when he perceive that he be leave alone he be so mad that for two or three hour to see he it be the great pleasure in the world he weep he flinge he run he iustle he thrust under the place where the people stand to see he think to kill some of they but the post and timber be so strong and great that he can hurt any body yet he oftentimes break his tooth in the grate at length when he be weary and have labour his body that he be all wet with sweat than he pluck in his trunk into his mouth and then he throw out so much water out of his belly that he sprinkle it over the head of the looker on to the uttermost of they although it be very high and then when they see he very weary there go certain officer into the court with long sharp cane in their hand and prick he that these cane be like to they in Spain which they call they make he to go into one of the house that be make alongst the court for the same purpose as there be many which be make long and narrow that when the elephant be in he can turn himself to go back again and it be requisite that these man shall be very wary and swift for although their cane belong yet the elephant will kill they if they be not swift to save themselves at length when they have get he into one of those house they stand over he in a loft and get rope under his belly and about his neck and about his leg and bind he fast and so let he stand four or five day and give he neither meat nor drink at a strange thing that a beast so wild shall in so short time be make tame the great strength that the king of Pegu have the end of these four or five day they unloose he and put one of the female unto he and give they meat and drink and in eight day he be become tame in my judgement there be not a beast so intellective as be these elephant nor of more understanding in all the world for he will do all thing that his keeper say so that he lack nothing but human speech it be report that the great strength that the king of Pegu have be in these elephant for when they go to battle they set on their back a castle of wood bind thereto with band under their belly and in every castle four man very commodious set to fight with harquebuse with bow and arrow with dart and pike and other lance weapon and they say that the skin of this elephant be so hard that a harquebusse will not pierce it unless it be in the eye temple or some other tender place of his body and beside this they a goodly order in a barbarous people be of great strength and have a very excellent order in their battle as I have see at their feast which they make in the year in which feast the king make triumph which be a rare thing and worthy memory that in so barbarous a people there shall be such goodly order as they have in their army which be distinct in square of elephant of horseman of harquebusser and pikeman that true the number of they be infinite but their armour and the order of their weapon and number of his man weapon be very naught but weak as well the one as the other they have very bad pike their sword be worse make like long knife without point his harquebuse be most excellent and always in his war he have eighty thousand harquebuse and the number of they increase daily because the king will have they shoot every day at the plank and so by continual exercise they become most excellent shot also he have great ordnance make of very good metal to conclude there be not a king on the earth that have more power or strength then this king of Pegu because he have twenty and six crown king at his command he can make in his camp a million and a half of man of war in the field against 26. crown king at h(...) command 1500000. man in one camp (@) (@) of sir ^^nts his enemy the state of his kingdom and maintenance of his army be a thing incredible to consider and the victual that shall maintain such a number of people in the war but he that know the nature and quality of that people will easy believe it I have see with my eye that those people and soldier have eat of all sort of wild beast that be on the earth whether it be very filthy or otherwise all serve for their mouth yea I have see they eat scorpion and serpent also they seed of all kind of herb and grass so that if such a great army want not water and salt they will maintain themselves a long time in a bush with root flower and leaf of tree they carry rice with they for their voyage and that serve they in stead of comfit it be so dainty unto they this king of Pegu have not any army or power by sea but in the land for people dominion (...) gold and silver he far exceed the power of the great Turk in treasure and strength this king have diverse magason full of treasure as gold and silver and every day he increase it more and more and it be never diminish also he be lord of the mine of ruby saphire the riches of the king of Pegu. and spinel near unto his royal palace there be a inestimable treasure whereof he make no account for that it stand in such a place that every one may see it and the place where this treasure be be a great court wall round about with wall of stone with two gate which stand open every day and within this place or court be four gild house cover with lead and in every one make their money of and this metal be make of copper and lead mingle together this statue also have a crown on his head like the first this treasure be of such a value as it be stand in a open place this cart be very high with a goodly canopy over it behind the cart go twenty of his lord and noble with every one a rope in his hand make fast to the cart for to hold it upright that it fall not the this king of Pegu have one principal wife which be keep in a Seralio he have three hundred concubine of who it be report that he have ninety child this king sit every day in person to hear the suit of his subject but he nor they never the order of justice. speak one to another but by supplication make in this order the king sit up aloft in a great hall on a tribunal seat and low under he sit all his baron round about than those that demand audience enter into a great court before the king and there set they down on the ground forty pace distant from the king person and amongst those people there be no difference in matter of audience before the king but all alike and there they sit with their supplication no difference of person before the king in controversy or in justice in their hand which be make of long leaf of a tree these leaf be three quarter of a yard long and two finger broad which be write with a sharp iron make for the purpose and in those leaf be their supplication write and with their supplication they have in their hand a present or gift accord to the weightiness of their matter then come the secretary down to read these supplication take they and read they before the king and if the king think it good to do to they that favour or justice that they demand than he command to take the present out of their hand but if he think their demand be not just or accord to right he command they away without take of their gift or present in the Indies there be not any merchandise that be good to bring to pegu unless it be at some time by chance to bring opium of Cambaia and if he bring money he shall lose by it now the commodity that come from saint Tom be the only merchandise for that place which be the great quantity of cloth make there which they use in Pegu which cloth be make of bombast the commodity that be venture in Pegu. weave and paint so that the more that kind of cloth be wash the more lively they show their colour which be a rare thing and there be make such account of this kind of cloth which be of so great importance that a small bale of it will cost a thousand or two thousand ducat also from saint Tom they lade great store of red yarn of bombast die with a root which they call Saia as aforesaid which colour will never out with which merchandise every year there go a great ship from s. Tom to Pegu of great importance and they usual depart from saint Tom to Pegu the eleven or twelve of September and if she stay until the twelve it be note the departure of the ship from saint Tom to Pegu. a great hap if she return not without make of her voyage their use be to depart the 6 of September and then they make sure voyage and now because there be a great labour about that kind of cloth to bring it to perfection and that it be well dry as also the greediness of the captain that will make a extraordinary gain of his freight think to have the wind always to serve their turn they stay so long that at sometime the wind turn for in those part the wind hlowe firm for certain time with the which they go to pegu with the wind in poop and if they arrive not there before the wind change and get ground to anchor perforce they must return back again for that the gale of the wind blow there for three or four month together in one place with great force but if they get the coast and anchor there then with great labour they may save their voyage also there go another great ship from Bengala every year lade with fine cloth of bombast of all sort which arrive in the harbour of Pegu grow in that country all merchant that mean to go through the Indies must carry all manner of householdstuff merchant must carry their provision for there be no inn with they which be necessary for a house because that there be not any lodging nor inn nor host nor chamber room in that country but the first thing a man do when he come to any city be to hire a house either by the year or by the month or as he mean to stay in those part in Pegu their order be to hire their house for six month now from cosmin to the city of Pegu they go in six hour with the flood and if it be ebb water than they make fast their boat to the river side and there tarry until the water flow again it be a very commodious description of the fruitfulness of that soil and pleasant voyage have on both side of the river many great village which they call city in the which hen pigeon egg milk Rice and other thing be very good cheap it be all plain and a goodly country and in eight day you may make your voyage up to Macceo distant from pegu twelve mile and there they discharge their good and lade they in cart or wane draw with ox and the merchant be carry in a closet which they call deling in the which a man shall be very well accommodate with cushion under his del be a small litter carry with man as be aforesaid head and cover for the defence of the sun and rain and there he may sleep if he have will have more or less steal from he that day they custom the good it be requisite that a man have his eye watchful and to be careful and to have many friend for when they custom in the great hall of the king there come many gentleman accompany with a number of their slave and these gentleman have no shame that their slave rob stranger whether it be cloth in show of it or any other thing they laugh at it and although the merchant help one another to keep watch and look to their good they can look thereto so narrow but one or other will rob something either more or less accord as their merchandise be more or less and yet on this day there be a worse thing than this although you have set so many eye to look there for your benefit that you escape unrob of the slave a man can choose but that he must be rob of the officer of the custom house for pay the custom with the same good oftentimes they take the best that you have and not by rate of every sort as they ought to do by which mean a man pay more than his duty at length when the good be dispatch out of the custom-house in this order the merchant cause they to be carry to his house and may do with they at his pleasure there be in pegu eight broker of the king which be call tareghe who be bind to sell all the merchandise which come to Peru at the common or the current price then if the broker merchant will sell their good at that price they sell they away and the broker have two in the hundred of every sort of merchandise and they be bind to make good the debt of those good because they be sell by their hand or mean and on their word and oftentimes the merchant know not to who he give his good yet he can lose any thing thereby for that the broker be bind in any wise to pay he and if the merchant sell his good without the consent of the broker yet nevertheless he must pay he two and be in danger of his money but this be very seldom see because the wise child and slave of the debtor be bind to the creditor and when his time be expire and payment not make the creditor may take the debtor and carry he home to his house and shut he up in a magasin whereby present he have his money and not be able to pay the creditor he may take the wife child a law for bankrupt and slave of the debtor and sell they for so be the law of that kingdom the currant money that be in this city and throughout all this kingdom be call Gansa or Ganza which be make of copper and lead it be not the money of the king but every man may stamp it that will because it have his just partition or value but they make many of they false by put overmuch lead into they and those will not pass neither will any take they with this every man may stamp what money he will money Ganza you may buy gold or silver ruby and musk and other thing for there be no other money currant amongst they and gold silver and other merchandise be at one time dear than another as all other thing be this Ganza go by weight of byze and this name of Byza go for the account of the weight and common a Byza of a Ganza be worth after our account half a ducat little more or less and albeit that gold and silver be more or less in price yet the Byza never change every Byza make a hundred Ganza of weight and so the number of the money be Byza he that go to pegu to buy jewel if he will do well it behoove he to be a whole year there to do his business for if so be that he will return with the ship he come in he can how a man may dispose himself for the trade in Pegu. do any thing so convenient for the brevity of the time because that when they custom their good in pegu that come from saint Tom in their ship it be as it be about Christmas and when they have custom their good then must they sell they for their credit sake for a month or two and then at the begin of march the ship depart the merchant that come from saint Tom take for the payment of their good gold and silver which be never want good instruction there and eight or ten day before their departure they be all satisfy also they may have ruby in payment but they make no account of they and they that will winter there for another year it be needful that they be advertise that in the sale of their good they specify in their bargain the term of two or three month payment and that their payment shall be in so many and neither gold nor silver because that with the Ganza they may buy and sell every thing with great advantage and how needful be it to be advertise when they will recover their payment in what order they shall receive their Ganza because he that be not experience may do himself great wrong in the weight of the Ganza as also in the falseness of they in the weight he may be great deceive because that from place to place it do rise and fall great and therefore when any will receive money or make payment he must take a public weigh of money a day or two before he go about his business and give he in payment for his labour two byzaes a month and for this he be bind to make good all your money and to maintain it for good for that he receive it and seal the bag with his seal and when he have receive any store than he cause it to be bring into the Magason of the merchant that be the owner of it that money be very weighty for forty Byza be a strong porter burden and also where the merchant have any payment to be make for those good which he buy the common weigh of money that receive his money must make the payment thereof so that by this mean the merchant with the charge of two byze a month receive and pay out his money without loss or trouble thing as these follow in that kingdom they spend many of these sugarcane in make of house and tent which they call vare for their idol which they call pagode whereof there be great abundance great and or idol-house great store of leafe-gold for that they overly all the top of the house with gold and some of they be cover with gold from the top to the foot in cover whereof there be great store of gold spend for that every ten year they new overly they with gold from the top to the foot so that with this vanity they spend great abundance of gold. for every ten year the rain do consume the gold from these house and by this mean they make gold dear in Pegu then it will be if they consume not so much in this vanity also it be a thing to be note in the buy of jewel in Pegu that he that have no knowledge shall have as good jewel and as good cheap as he that have be practise there a long time which be a good order and it be in this wise there be in pegu four man of good reputation which be call tareghe or broker of jewel these four man have all the jewel or rubic in their hand and the merchant that will buy come to one of these tareghe and tell he that he have so much money to employ in ruby for through the hand of these four man pass all the ruby for they have such quantity that they know not ruby exceed cheap in Pegu. what to do with they but sell they at most vile and base price when the merchant have break his mind to one of these broker or tareghe they carry he home to one of their shop although he have no knowledge in jewel and when the jeweller perceive that he will employ a good round sum they will make a bargain and if not they let he alone the use general of this city be this that when any merchant have buy any great quantity of ruby and have agree for they he carry they home to his house let they be of what value they will he shall have space to look on they and peruse they two or three day and if he have no knowledge in they he shall always have many merchant in that city that have very good knowledge in jewel with who he may always confer and take counsel and may show they unto who he will and if he find that he have not employ his money well he may return his jewel back to they who he have they of without any loss at all which thing be such a shame to the tareghe to have his jewel return that he have rather bear a blow on the face than that it shall be think that he sell they so dear to have they return for these man have always great care that they afford good pennyworth especial to those that have no knowledge this they do because they will not lose their credit and when those merchant that have knowledge in jewel buy any if they buy they dear it be their own fault and not the broker yet it be good to have knowledge in jewel by reason that it may some what ease the price there be also a very good order which they have in buy of a honest care of heathen people jewel which be this there be many merchant that stand by at the make of the bargain and because they shall not understand how the jewel be sell the broker and the merchant have their hand under a cloth and by touch of finger and nip the joint they know what bargain make with the nip of finger under a cloth be do what be bid and what be ask so that the stander by know not what be demand for they although it be for a thousand or ten thousand ducat for every joint and every finger have his signification for if the merchant that stand by shall understand the bargain it will breed great controversy amongst they and at my be in pegu in the month of August in 1569. have get well by my endeavour I be desirous to see my own country and I think it good to go by the way of saint Tom but then I shall ^arie until march. in which journey I be counsel yea and full resolve to go by the way of Bengala with a ship there ready to depart for that voyage and then we depart from Pegu to Chatigan a great harbour or port from whence there go small ship to cochin before the fleet depart for Portugal in which ship I be full determine to go to Lisbon and so to Venice when I this touffon or Tuffon be a extraordinary storm at sea. have thus resolve myself I go a board of the ship of Bengala at which time it be the year of touffon concern which touffon you be to understand that in the east indies oftentimes there be not storm as in other country but every ten or twelve year there be such tempest and storm that it be a thing incredible but to those that have see it neither do they know certain what year they will come unfortunate be they that be at sea in that year and time of the touffon because few there the touffon come but every 10. or 12 year be that escape that danger in this year it be our chance to be at sea with the like storm but it happen well unto we for that our ship be new over planck and have not any thing in she save victual and balast silver and gold which from Pegu they carry to Bengala and no other kind of merchandise this touffon or cruel storm endure three day and three night in which time it carry away our sail yard and rudder and because the ship labour in the sea we cut our mast overboard which when we have do she labour a great deal more than before in such wise that she be almost full with water that come over the high part of she and so go down and for the space of three day and three night sixty man do nothing but hale water out of she in this wise twenty man in one place and twenty man in another place and twenty in a three place and for all this storm the ship be so good that she take not one jot of water below through her side but all run down through the hatch so that those sixty man do nothing but cast the sea into the sea. and thus drive too and fro as the wind and sea will we be in a dark sea which drive we beyond the shall and when we feel the ship afloat we rise up as man revive because a manifest token of the ebb and flow in those country the sea be calm and smooth water and then sound we find twelve fathom water and within a while after we have but six fathom and then present we come to anchor with a small anchor that be leave we at the stern for all our other be lose in the storm and by and by the ship strike a ground and then we do prop she that she shall not overthrow when it be day the ship be all dry and we find she a good mile from the sea on dry land this touffon be end we discover a island not far from we and we go from the ship on the sand to see what island it be and we find it a place inhabit and to my judgement the fertile island in all the world the which be divide into two part by a channel this island be call Sondi^a which pass between it and with great trouble we bring our ship into the same channel which part the island at flow water and there we determine to stay forty day to refresh we and when the people of the island see the ship and that we be come a land present they make a place of Bazar or market with shop right over against the ship with all manner of provision of victual to ea^e which they bring down in great abundance and sell it so good cheap that we be amaze at the cheapness thereof I buy many salt cow there for the provision of the ship for half a larine a piece which Larine may be twelve smilling six penny be very good and fat and four wild hog ready dress for a larine great fat hen for a bizze a piece which be at the most a penny and the people tell we that we be deceive the half of our money because we buy thing so dear also a sack of fine rice for a thing of nothing and consequent all other thing for human sustenance be there in such abundance that it be a thing incredible but to they that have see it this island be call belong to the kingdom of Bengala distant one hundred and be the fruitfull country in all the world twenty mile from Chatigan to which place we be bind the people be moor and the king a very good man of a Moor king for if he have be a tyrant as other be he may have rob we of all because the Portugal captain of Chatigan be in arm against the retor of that place and every day there be some slay at which news we rest there with no small fear keep good watch and ward aboard every night as the use be but the governor of the town do comfort we and bid we that we shall fear nothing but that we shall repose ourselves secure without any danger although the portugal of Chatigan have slay the governor of that city and say that we be not culpable in that fact and moreover he do we every day what pleasure he can which be a thing contrary to our expectation consider that they and the people of Chatigan be both subject to one king. we depart from and come to Chatigan the great port of Bengala at the same time when the portugal have make peace and take a truce with the governor of the town Chatigan be a port in Bengala whither the portugal go with their ship with this condition that the chief captain of the portugal with his ship shall depart without any lade for there be then at that time eighteen ship of Portugal great and small this captain be a gentleman and of good courage be notwithstanding content to depart to his great hindrance rather than he will seek to hinder so many of his friend as be there as also because the time of the year be spend to go to the Indies the night before he depart every ship that have any lade therein put it aboard of the captain to help to ease his charge and to recompense his courtesy in this time there come a messenger from the king of Rachim to this Portugal captain who say in the behalf of his king that he have hear of the king of Rachim or Aracam neighbour to Bengala the courage and valour of he desire he gentle that he will vouchsafe to come with the ship into his port and come thither he shall be very well entreat this Portugal go thither and be very well satisfy of this king. this king of Rachim have his sea^e in the middle coast between Bengala and Pegu and the great enemy he have be the king of Pegu which king of Pegu devise night and day how to make this king of Rachim his subject but by no mean he be able to do it because the king of Pegu have no power or army by sea. and this king of * * or ara^am Rachim may arm two hundred galley or fust by sea and by land he have certain sluice with the which when the king of Pegu pretend any harm towards he he may at his pleasure drown a great part of the he make another voyage to Pegu here omit country so that by this mean he cut off the way whereby the king of Pegu shall come with his power to hurt he now to return to my voyage when I come to Ormus I find there master Francis Berettin of Venice and we freight a bark together to go for Basora for seventy ducat and with we there go other merchant which do ease our freight and very commodious we come to Basora and there we stay forty day for provide a Carovan of bark to go to Babylon because they use not to go two or three bark at once but five and twenty or thirty because in the night they can go but must make they fast to the bank of the river and then we must make a very good and strong guard and be well provide of armour for respect and safeguard of our good because the number of thief be great that come to spoil and rob the merchant and when we depart for Babylon we go a little with our sail and the voyage be eight and thirty or forty day long but we be fifty day on it when we come to Babylon we stay a order how to provide to go over the desert from Babylon to Aleppo there four month until the Carovan be ready to go over the wilderness or desert for Aleppo in this city we be six merchant that accompany together five venetian and a Portugal who name be as follow messer Florinasa with one of his kinsman messer Andrea de polo the Portugal and master Francis Berettin and I and so we furnish ourselves with victual and bean for our horse for forty day and we buy horse and mule for that they be very good cheap there I myself buy a horse there for eleven aken and sell he after in Aleppo for thirty ducat also we buy a tent which do we very great pleasure we have also amongst we two and thirty camel lade with merchandise for the which we pay two ducat for every camel lade and for every ten camel they make eleven for so be their use and custom we take also with we three man to serve we in the voyage which be use to go in those voyage for five ducat a man and be bind to serve we to Aleppo so that we pass very well without any trouble when the camel cry out to rest our pavilion be the first that be erect the Carovan make but small journey about twenty mile a day and they set forward every morning before day two hour and about two in the afternoon they sit down we have great good hap in our voyage for that it rain for which cause we never want water but every day find good water so that we can not take any hurt for want of water yet we carry a camel lade always with water for every good respect that may chance in the desert so that we have no want neither of one thing nor other that be to be have in the country for we come very well furnish of every thing and every day we eat fresh mutton because there come many shepherd with we with their flock who keep those sheep that we buy in Babylon and every merchant mark his sheep with his own mark and we give the shepherd a Medin which be two penny of our money for the keep and feed our sheep on the way and for kill of they and beside the Medin they have the head the skin and the entrails of every sheep they kill we fix buy twenty sheep and when we come to Aleppo we have seven alive of they and in the Carovan they use this order that the merchant do lend flesh one to another because they will not carry raw flesh with they but pleasure one another by lend one one day and another another day from Babylon to Aleppo be forty day journey of the which they make six and thirty day 36. day journey over the wilderness over the wilderness in which six and thirty day they neither see house tree nor people that inhabit it but only a plain and no sign of any way in the world the pilot go before and the Carovan follow after and when they sit down all the Carovan unlade and sit down for they know the station where the well be I say in six and thirty day we pass over the wilderness for when we depart from Babylon two day we pass by village inhabit until we have pass the river Euphrates and then within two day of Aleppo we have village inhabit in this Carovan there go always a captain that do justice unto a order how to provide for the go to jerusalem all man and every night they keep watch about the Carovan and come to Aleppo we go to Tripoli whereas master Florin and master Andrea polo and I with a friar go and hire a bark to go with we to jerusalem depart from Tripoli we arrive at jaffa from which place in a day and a half we go to jerusalem and we give order to our bark to tarry for we until our return we stay in jerusalem fourteen day to visit those holy place from whence we return to jaffa and from jaffa to Tripoli and there we ship ourselves in a ship the author return to Venice 1581. of Venice call the bagazzana and by the help of the divine power we arrive safe in Venice the five of November 1581. I will not be unmindful to put they in remembrance that have a desire to go into those part how they shall keep their good and give they to their heir at the time of their death and how this may be do very secure in all the city that a very good order that they have in those country for the recover of the good of the dead the portugal have in the Indies there be a house call the school of the governor whereof if you give they for their pain will take a copy of your will and testament which you must always carry about you and chief when you go into the Indies in the country of the moor and gentile in those voyage always there go a captain to administer justice to all christian of the portugal also this captain have authority to recover the good of those merchant that by chance die in those voyage and they that have not make their will and register they in the aforesaid school the captain will consume their good in such wise that little or nothing will be leave for their heir and friend also there go in these same voyage some merchant that be commissary of the school of that if any merchant die and have his will make and have give order that the school of shall have his good and sell they than they send the money by exchange to the school of in Lisbon with that copy of his testament then from Lisbon they give intelligence thereof into what part of Christendom soever it be and the heir of such a one come thither with testimonial that they be heir they shall receive there the value of his good in such wise that they shall not lose any thing but they that die in the kingdom of Pegu lose the three part of their good by ancient custom of the country that if any christian die in the kingdom of Pegu the king and his officer rest heir of a three of his good and there have never be any deceit or fraud use in this matter I have know many rich man that have dwell in Pegu and in their age they have desire to go into their own country to die there and have depart with all their good and substance without let or trouble in Pegu the fashion of their apparel be all one as well the nobleman as the simple the only order of apparel in Pegu. difference be in the fineness of the cloth which be cloth of bombast one fine than another and they wear their apparel in this wise first a white bombast cloth which serve for a shirt than they gird another paint bombast cloth of fourteen brace which they bind up betwixt their leg and on their head they wear a small tocke of three brace make in guise of a mitre and some go without tocke and carry as it be a hive on the head which do not pass the low part of his ear when it be lift up they go all barefooted but the nobleman never go on foot but be carry by man in a seat with great reputation with a hat make of the leaf of a tree to keep he from the rain and sun or otherwise they ride on horseback with their foot bare in the stirrup all sort of woman whatsoever they be wear a smock down the order of the woman apparel in Pegu. to the girdle and from the girdle downward to the foot they wear a cloth of three brace open before so straight that they can go but they must show their secret as it be aloft and in their go they feign to hide it with their hand but they can by reason of the straightness of their cloth they say that this use be invent by a queen to be a occasion that the sight thereof may remove from man the vice against nature which they be great give unto which sight shall cause they to regard woman the more also the woman go barefooted their arm lade with hoop of gold and jewel and their finger full of precious ring with their hair roll up about their head many of they wear a cloth about their shoulder in stead of a cloak chap. v. in 13. degree and a three part the front be towards the west very strong by reason of the blockehouse which be upon the port along towards the sea this port be so low that elephant can enter in at it for the horse enter with not a little trouble there be three church one very fair of saint Thomas which be well serve with priest the chief of they be a vicar for so they call he who be send thither seaside and I go also to see what be the matter and see this piece of timber cast upon the shore then the church of saint John Baptist be finish but because they want transome to make the roof they the mount and another of the cross here be also the church of mercy out of the town there be one of saint Lazarus and many other well serve saint Thomas be as fair a city as I see any in that country and the house join one to the other so to be able to succour one another without the city of saint Thomas be another city environ with wall make of earth and inhabit with gentile soldier who chiefraine be call Adicario who burn the dead have power to execute justice they observe the custom to burn their dead in this city as at Negapaton but near to this be a city call Casta goldsmith row they have a custom when the husband be dead to make a pit in the earth and there to place the dead corpse crosslegged and on the other side set his live wife in the same manner and their kindred wife bury alive cast earth upon she press she down that she may die also and when they wive they marry with their compere as a carpenter take the daughter of a carpenter and so of other the foresay inhabitant worship sometime the figure of a kow and otherwhiles of a serpent call brutish deity Bittia Cappella who bite be deadly and it have one part of the flesh from the middle invert towards the head the brahmin be wont to burn cow excrement and with the ash for devotion meet devotion stink with the gentile to daub their forehead and nose who so paint wash not that day for devotion of the kow the man which be devote to the pagoda or statue after they have live a whole year after their will in carnal pleasure be wont to take a bow and a arrow and shoot their own flesh aloft in the air which they slash off in morsel and when they can continue no long in this manner they cut their own throat thus sacrifice their body to the pagoda there be some also which be call Amocchi who be a kind of people call and be not of those gentile of saint Thomas but of the coast of Chiava who be weary of live set desperate themselves in the way with a weapon in their hand which they call a Crise and kill as many as they meet with till some body kill they and this they do for the least anger they conceive as desperate man these gentile be very different in their adoration for some worship the image diversify of a man some of a kow other of serpent other the sun or the moon some a tree or the water and other thing they be accustom to celebrate many feast but in the month of septemb I see one the people plant a tree in the ground like the mast of a ship with the main-yard across upon which main-yard be two hook fasten and there be many which desire all devilish to free themselves from some trouble or misery who make a vow to the pagoda to hook or ganch themselves and for this there be some depute that stand there who see any that will ganch themselves for devotion they first make a offering and then they loosen a cord and let down the hook and with they they fasten the shoulder of he that will hook himself and then they hoist he up aloft make he turn his face to the pagoda and salute it three time with his hand in suppliant wise before his breast and make he play with a weapon which he carry in his hand while he be in draw up and after a while they let he down and colour the tree with his blood say they do it in reverence to the pagoda and then they let he down and put a rope through the hole which the hook make and fasten that cord to the pagoda they draw he by little and little to the statue by that cord then the woman of the pagoda conduct he to the statue to reverence it and after this they take care to heal he if they can and this they do by a vow or promise to the pagoda to obtain any thing or in sickness to recover health they have another feast by night which dure eight night in a long street of the city full of light on both side and three or four person take one another by the hand who have on their arm certain basket full of viand make of Rice and milk and then they run and cast that meat behind they which they say the devil eat who run behind they and while they be in this motion they never look behind they for they say if they do they shall sudden die and this be sufficient for the mad custom of this country on the thirteen of September 1583. in the name of jesus Christ after we have lade our merchandise and pay our custom we go a shipboard and have sail until the three and twenty of this month we find ourselves near to Maccareo it be very strange which Macareo be a strong race of a tide in those part see fred. huge tide be report of the ebb and flow of the water and certain he which have not see they will scarce believe they certain pilot go from Martovan as swift as a arrow in the increase of the water as long as the flood last and the tide be at the height they turn out of the channel and there ride when the water be fall on dry land and the bore or tide come as some great tree and in such a time they oppose the prow against it and so expect the fury of the water which resemble the noise of a great earthquake so that maugre their strength and skill the bark be wash from head to stern and with that violence be carry swift into the channel after that the wind blow from the south-west and we sail to the northwest till the morning when we find ourselves at Bara right over Negrais they call so in their language the haven which go into pegu where we discover on the left side of the river a pagoda or Varella all gild over which be see afar off by the vessel that come from the main and especial when the sun shine which make it glister round about as far as it be see and because the rain wash it often and consume the gold the man of that place often regild it that the ship by the splendour thereof may have this benefit to know the haven and they do it for devotion and reverence to the place we then all rejoice at that time and make merry because we consider that if we have arrive there four or five day late we can not have enter the haven by reason of the continual wind which blow there Goa be the most principal city which the portugal have in India wherein the viceroy remain Goa with his court. it stand in a island which may be five and twenty or thirty mile about it be a fine city and for a indian town very fair the island be very fair full of orchard and garden and many palmer tree and have some village here be many merchant of all nation and the fleet which come every year from Portugal which be four five or six great ship come first hither and they come for the most part in September and remain there forty or fifty day and then get to cochin where they lade their pepper for Portugal oftentimes they lade one in Goa the rest go to cochin which be from Goa a hundred I this be the twenty of November league southward Goa stand in the country of Hidalcan who lie in the country six or seven day journey his chief city be call bisapor at our come we be cast into prison and examine before the justice and demand for letter and be charge to be spy but they can prove nothing by we we continue in prison until the two and twenty of December and then we be set at liberty put in surety for two thousand ducat not to depart the town which surety father Stephens a english jesuite which we find there and another religious man a friend of his procure for we our surety name be Andre^s taborer to who we pay two thousand one hundred and fifty ducat and still he demand more whereupon we make suit to the viceroy and justice to have our money again consider that they have have it in their hand near five month and can prove nothing against we the viceroy make we a very sharp answer and say we shall be better sift before it be long and that they have further matter against we whereupon we present determine rather to seek our liberty then to be in danger for ever to be slave in the country for it be tell we we shall have the strapade the five they flee from Goa see hereof Linschoten in fine lib. 1. Bellergan a town day of April 1585. in the morning we run from thence and be set over the river we go two day on foot not without fear not know the way nor have any guide for we dare trust none one of the first town which we come unto be call Bellergan where there be a great market keep of diamond ruby saphire and many other soft stone from Bellergan we go to bisapor which be a very great town where the king do keep his court. he have many gentile in his court and they be great idolater and they have their idol stand in the wood which they call Pagodes some be like a cow some like a monkey some like buffle some like peacock and some like the devil here be very many elephant which they go to war withal here they have good store of gold and silver their house be of stone very fair and high from hence we go for Gulconda the king whereof be call cu^up de lashach here and in the kingdom of Hidalcan and in the country of the king of Gulconda Dec^^ be the diamond find of the old water it be a very fair town pleasant with fair house of brick and timber it abound with great store of fruit and fresh water here the man and the woman do go with a cloth bind about their middle without any more apparel we find it here very hot apparel the winter begin here about the last of may. in these part be a port or haven call Masulipatan which stand eight day journey from hence towards the gulf of Bengula whether Masulipatan see sup. lib. 3. c. vlt. of english trade there Seruidore come many ship out of India Pegu and sumatra very rich lade with pepper spice and other commodity the country be very good and fruitful from thence I go to Seruidore which be a fine country and the king be call the king of bread. the house here be all thatch and make of lome here be many moor and gentile but there be small religion among they from thence I go to Bellapore and so to barrampore which be in the country of Zelabdim echebar in this place their money be make of a kind of silver round and bellaport thick to the value of twenty penny which be very good silver it be marvelous great and a populous country in their winter which be in june july and August there be no pass in the street but with horse the water be so high the house be make of some and thatch here be great store of cotton-cloth make and paint clothes of cotton-wool here grow great store of corn and Rice we find marriage great store both in town and village in many place where we pass of boy of eight or ten year and girl of five or six year strange marriage old they both do ride upon one horse very trim deck and be carry through the town with great pipe and play and so return home and eat of a banquet make of Rice and fruit and there they dance the most part of the night and so make a end of the marriage they lie not together until they be ten year old they say they marry their child so young because it be a order that when the man die the woman must be burn with he so that if the father die yet they may have a father in law to help to bring up the child which be marry and also that they will not leave their son without wife nor their daughter without husband from thence we go to Mandoway which be a very strong town it be besiege twelve Mandoa or Mandoway a very strong town year by Zelabdim echebar before he can win it it stand upon a very great high rock as the most part of their castle do and be of a very great circuit from hence we go to ugin and Serringe where we overtake the ambassador of Zelabdim echebar with a marvelous great company of man elephant and camel here be great trade of Cotton and cloth make of Cotton and great store of drug from thence we go to agra pass many river which by reason of the rain be so swell that we wade and swim oftentimes for our life agra be a very great city and populous build with stone have fair and large agra a great city street with a fair river run by it which fall into the gulf of Bengala it have a fair castle and a strong with a very fair ditch here be many moor and gentile the king be call Zelabdim echebar the people for the most part call he the great Mogor from thence Zeb. echebar the great Mogor father to Selim which now reign of who see sup. l. 3 and 4. in Hawkins Fincb and sir tho-roe etc. we go for fatepore which be the place where the king keep his court. the town be great than agra but the house and street be not so fair here dwell many people both moor and gentile the king have in agra and as they do credible report one thousand elephant thirty thousand horse one thousand and four hundred tame deer eight hundred concubine such store of ounce tiger buffle cock and hawk that be very strange to see he keep a great court which they call Dericcan agra and fatepore be two very great city either of they much great than London and very populous between agra and fatepore be twelve mile and all the way be a market of victual and other thing as full as though a man be still in a town and so many people as if a man be in a market they bull draw coach or cart have many fine cart and many of they carve and gild with gold with two wheel which be draw with two little bull about the bigness of our great dog in England and they will run with any horse and carry two or three man in one of these cart they be cover with silk or very fine cloth and be use here as our coach be in England hither be great resort of merchant from Persia and out of India and very much merchandise of silk and cloth and of precious stone both ruby diamond and pearl the king be apparel in a white cabie make like a shirt tie with string on the one side and a little cloth on his head colour oftentimes with red or yellow none come into his house but his eunuch which keep his woman here in fatepore we stay all three until the eight and twenty of September 1585. and newbery neigh in which it seem he die unknown how or where then master John Newberie take his journey towards the city of lahor determine from thence to go for Persia and then for Aleppo or Constantinople whether he can get soon passage unto and direct i to go to for Bengala and for Pegu and do promise i if it please God to meet i in Bengala within two year with a ship out of England I leave William Will lead serve the king of Cambaia lead the jeweller in service with the king Zelabdim echebar in fatepore who do entertain he very well and give he a house and five slave a horse and every day six s. s. in money I go from agra to Satagam in Bengala in the company of one hundred and fourscore boat lade with salt opium hinge lead carpet and diverse other commodity down the river jemena the chief merchant be moor and gentile in these country they have many strange ceremony the Bramenes which be their priest come to the water and have the superstitious ceremony of the Bramenes like those of the ancient gymnosopgist in Strabo etc. a string about their neck make with great ceremony and lade up water with both their hand and turn the string first with both their hand within and then one arm after the other out though it be never so cold they will wash themselves in cold water or in warm these gentile will eat no flesh nor kill any thing they live with Rice butter milk and fruit they pray in the water naked and dress their meat and eat it naked and for their penance they lie flat upon the earth and rise up and turn themselves about thirty or forty time and use to heave up their hand to the sun and to kiss the earth with their arm and leg stretch along out and their right leg always before the left every time they lie down they make a devotion as on bead more by tale then by weight score on the ground with their finger to know when their stint be finish the Bramenes mark themselves in the forehead ear and throat with a kind of yellow gear which they grind and every morning they do it and they have some old man which go in the street with a box of yellow powder and mark man on their head and neck as they meet they and their wife do come by ten twenty and thirty together to the water side sing and there do wash themselves and then use their ceremony and mark themselves in their forehead polygamy and face and carry some with they and so depart sing their daughter be marry at or before the age of ten year the man may have seven wife they be a kind of crafty people worse than the jew when they salute one another they heave up their hand to their head and say rame rame from agra I come to Prague where the river jemena enter into the mighty river Ganges and jemena jose his name Ganges come out of the northwest and run east into the prague Ganges gulf of Bengala in those part there be many tiger and many partridge and turtle-dove and much other fowl here be many beggar in these country which go naked and Tigris holy holy beggar the people make great account of they they call they Schesche here I see one which be a monster among the rest he will have nothing upon he his beard be very long and with the hair of his head he cover his privity the nail of some of his finger be two inch long for he will cut nothing from he neither will he speak he be accompany with eight or ten and they speak for he when any man speak to he he will lay his hand upon his breast and bow himself but will not speak he will not speak to the king. we go from Prague down Ganges the which be here very broad here be great store of fish of sundry sort and of wild fowl as of swan goose crane and many other thing the country be very fruitful and populous the man for the most part have their face shave and their head very long except some which be all shave save the crown and some of they be as though a man shall set a dish on their head and shave they round all but the crown in this river of Ganges be many land his water be very sweet and pleasant and the country Ganges water adjoin very fruitful from thence we go to Bannaras which be a great town and great store of cloth be make Bannaras there of Cotton and sash for the moor in this place they be all gentile and be the great idolater that ever I see to this town come the gentile on pilgrimage out of far a pilgrimage of the gentile to the river Ganges image country here alongst the water side be very many fair house and in all of they or for the most part they have their image stand which be evil favour make of stone and wood some like lion leopard and monkey some like man and woman and peacock and some like the devil with four arm and four hand they sit cross legged some with one thing in their hand and some another and by break of day and before there be man and woman which come out of the town and wash themselves in Ganges and there be diverse old man which upon place of earth make for the purpose sit pray and they give the people three or four straw which they take and hold they between their finger when they wash themselves and some sit to mark they in the forehead and they have in a cloth a little rice barley or money which when they have wash themselves they give to the old man which sit there pray afterward they go to diverse of their image and give they of their sacrifice and when they give the old man say certain prayer and then be all holy and in diverse place there stand a kind of image which in their language they call ada. and they have diverse great stone carve whereon they pour water and throw thereupon some rice wheat Ada a idol it may seem of Adam who some have dream to have both sex with four hand etc. after divide into male and female barley and some other thing this ada have four hand with claw moreover they have a great place make of stone like to a well with step to go down wherein the water stand very foul and stink for the great quantity of flower which continual they throw into it do make it stink there be always many people in it for they say when they wash themselves in it that their sin be forgive they because God as they say do wash himself in that place they gather up the sand in the bottom of it and say it be holy they never pray but in the water and they wash themselves over head and lade up water with both their hand and turn themselves about and then they drink a little of the water three time and so go to their god which stand in those house some of they will wash a place which be their length and then will pray upon the earth with their arm and leg at length out and will rise up and lie down and kiss the ground twenty or thirty time but they will not stir their right foot and some of they will make their ceremony with fifteen or idolatrous rite sixteen pot little and great and ring a little bell when they make their mixture ten or twelve time and they make a circle of water round about their pot and pray and diverse sit by they and one that reach they their pot and they say diverse thing over their pot many time and when they have do they go to their god and strew their sacrifice which they think be very holy and mark many of they which sit by in the forehead which they take as a great gift there come fifty and sometime a hundred together to wash they in this well and to offer to these idol they have in some of these house their idol stand and one sit by they in warm weather with a fan to blow wind upon they and when they see any company come they ring a little bell which hang by they and many give their alm but especial those which come out of the country many of they be black and have claw of brass with long nail and some ride upon peacock and other fowl which be evil favour with long hawk bill and some like one thing and some another but none with a good face among the rest there be one which they make great account of for they say he give they all thing both food and apparel and one sit always by he with a fan to make wind towards he here some be burn to ash some scorch in the fire and throw into the water and funeral by burn dog and fox do present eat they the wife here do burn with their husband when they die if they will not their head be shave and never account be make of they afterward the people go all naked save a little cloth bind about their middle their woman have their apparel neck arm and ear deck with ring of silver copper tin and with round hoop make of ivory adorn with amber stone and with many agat and they be mark with a great spot of red in their forehead and a stroke of red up to the crown and so it run three manner of way in the winter which be our may the man wear qailt gown of cotton like to our mattrace and quilt cap like to our great grocer mortar with a slit to look out at and so tie down beneath their ear if a man or a woman be sick and like foolish physic to die they will lay he before their idol all night and that shall help he or make a end of he and if he do not mend that night his friend will come and sit with he a little and cry and afterward will carry he to the water side and set he upon a little raft make of reed and so let he go down the river when they be marry the man and the woman come marriage rite to the water side and there be a old man which they call a bramane that be a priest a kow and a calf and a kow with calf then the man and the woman the kow and calf and the old man go into the water together and they give the old man a white cloth of four yard long and a basket crosse-bound with diverse thing in it the cloth he lay upon the back of the kow and then he take the kow by the end of the tail and say certain word and she have a copper or a brass pot full of water and the man do hold his hand by the old man hand and the wife hand by her husband and all have the kow by the tail this tie of new marry folk together by the clothes be use by the mexicans in old time and they pour water out of the pot upon the cow tail and it run through all their hand and they lade up water with their hand and then the old man do tie he and she together by their clothes which do they go round about the kow and calf and then they give somewhat to the poor which be always there and to the bramane or priest they give one kow and calf and afterward go to diverse of their idol and offer money and laidowne flat upon the ground and kiss it diverse time and then go their way their chief idol be black ugly idol and evill-favored their mouth monstrous their ear gild and full of jewel their tooth and eye of gold silver and glass some have one thing in their hand and some another you may not come into the house where they stand with your shoe on they have continual lamp burn before they from Bannaras I go to Patenaw down the river Ganges where in day Pegu be a city very great strong and very fair with wall of stone and great ditch round about it there be two town the old town and the new in the old town be all the merchant stranger and very many merchant of the country all the good be sell in the old town which be very great and have many suburb round about it and all the house be make of cane which cane-house they call Bambos and be cover with straw in your house you have a Warehouse which they call godon which be make of brick to put your good in for oftentimes they take fire and burn in a hour four or five hundred house so that if the godon be not you shall be in danger to have all burn if any wind shall rise at a trice in the new town be the king and all his nobility and gentry it be a city very great and populous and be make square and with very fair wall and a great ditch round about it full of water with many crocodile in it it have twenty gate and they be make of stone for every square crocodile gate 20. five gate there be also many turret for sentinel to watch make of wood and gild with gold very fair the street be the fair that ever I see as straight as a line from one gate to the other and so broad that ten or twelve man may ride afront through they on both palm-tre^streets side of they at every man door be set a palmer tree which be the nut-tree which make a very fair show and a very commodious shadow so that a man may walk in the shade all day the house be make of wood and cover with tile the king house be in the middle of the city and be wall and ditch round about and the building within be make all the wall be gild with gold within the first gate of the king house be a great large room on both side whereof be house make for the king elephant which be marvelous great and fair and be bring up title be call the king of the white elephant the king of the white elephant if any other king have one and will not send it he he will make war with he for it for he have rather lose a great part of his kingdom than not to conquer he they do very great service unto these white elephant every one of they stand in a house gild with gold and they do feed in vessel of silver and gilt one of they when he do go to the river to be wash as every day they do go under a canopy of cloth of gold or of silk carry over he by six or eight man and eight or ten man go before he play on drum shawm or other
